There was a clear difference in the morphology of the living cells from the high and low intertidal samples. Although we found Microcoleus sp. in both the low and high intertidal zones, the low intertidal-zone samples had abundant coccoid cells, whereas the high intertidal-zone samples had abundant filamentous forms. The cyanobacterial 16s rDNA analysis confirmed the identity and presence of M. chthonoplastes. Low intertidal-zone samples also had Oscillatoria spp. Two bands were also observed that did not show high homology with other published cyanobacterial sequences. Our results provided some evidence that differing communities, or at least morphologies, of cyanobacteria are found across the intertidal zone (H6).

The cyanobacteria composition described in the present study is similar to that in the north-western Dampier Archipelago (200 km north), where Microcoleus chthonoplastes and Geitlerniema sp. (previously Phormidium sp.) were also found (Paling et al. 1989). Our study adds to this species list of cyanobacteria in these arid-zone estuaries, with the occurrence of Plectonema sp., Leptolyngbya sp. and Lyngbya aestuarii in the high intertidal-zone samples.

Nitrogen fixation
The mean N fixation was 1.7 ± 0.33 nmol N cm⁻² h⁻¹, accounting for 34% of total N incorporated by the cyanobacterial mat (N fixation plus N removal during tidal inundation). This result confirms that N fixation is an important mechanism for N incorporation by the cyanobacterial mat in this region (H3). It is probable that N fixation is performed by Oscillatoria sp., Plectonema sp., Leptolyngbya sp., Lyngbya aestuarii, Geitlerniema sp. and Microcoleus. However, Leptolyngbya can fix N only if associated with heterotrophic bacteria (Li et al. 2010).

Our results indicated that cyanobacterial mats in Exmouth Gulf are capable of fixing N during the day and at night, with higher rates during the day. Thus, our hypothesis that N-fixation rates were highest at night (H4) was rejected. Diurnal N fixation would suggest the presence of heterocystous cells because of the fact that N fixation is very sensitive to oxygen, which is produced during photosynthesis. However, the species we found in the mat are non-heterocystous forms. Nevertheless, some species of non-heterocystous cyanobacteria have alternative mechanisms that allow them to fix N during both night and day, in both anaerobic and aerobic conditions. Such mechanisms include microanaerobiosis (e.g. Plectonema; Berman-Frank et al. 2003), cellular differentiation (e.g. Trichodesmus; Berman-Frank et al. 2003) or intracellular processes still to be understood (e.g. Lyngbya; Jones 1992), such as inclusion granules (Cyanothece; Reddy et al. 1993). Some species of Plectonema that lack heterocysts have been observed to require light to fix N (Misra and Rakesh 1994). Thus, the occurrence of Plectonema and Lyngbya in the high intertidal zone suggest that these species may be responsible for diurnal N fixation.

As hypothesised (H5), the cyanobacterial mat from the low intertidal zone had higher N-fixation rates than did the cyanobacterial mat at higher intertidal elevations. These results indicated that the biogeochemical function of the cyanobacterial mat varies over the intertidal zone. The difference in N-fixation rates between the low and high intertidal zones could be related to lower salinities and more frequent tidal flushing in the low intertidal zone, which favour N fixation (Paling et al. 1989; Toledo et al. 1995; Kyaruzi et al. 2003). Differences in N fixation between cyanobacterial mats from the low and high intertidal zones might also be a consequence of different cyanobacterial community compositions along the desiccation gradient, as has been observed in a subtropical arid wetland in Baja California Sur, Mexico (Rothrock and Garcia-Pichel 2005) and is suggested in the present study. Variation in N-fixation rates over tidal elevation has also been reported for an intertidal bank in the Wadden Sea (Severin and Stal 2008).

Our results showed that N fixation is temporally and spatially variable and suggested a significant role of N fixation in this ecosystem. The N-fixation rates we measured in our study site (ranging from 1.4 to 8.2 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹, mean 4.9 ± 0.77 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹) were similar to those in cyanobacterial mats in Dampier, Western Australia (0.8–6 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Paling et al. 1989), lower than those found in intertidal mudflats in California, USA (37 nmol C₂H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Joye and Paerl 1994), within the range of those found in the intertidal zone of the lagoon of Aladabra Atoll (0.6–125 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Potts and Whitton 1977) and higher than those measured in mangrove sediments in Zanzibar (0.001 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Kyaruzi et al. 2003). Thus, N fixation at our study site could be considerable, especially because of the large areas (>100 km²) occupied by cyanobacterial mats in this region.

The results from the present study have provided insights into the role of cyanobacterial mats in nutrient exchange in coastal arid wetlands during periods of rainfall. The conditions in which we conducted our experiment were very different from conditions that occur most frequently in the region because of the increase in nutrients associated with the rain brought by Cyclone Pancho. The rain and flooding could have strongly modified the nutrient exchange of the cyanobacterial mat. For example, although the N-fixation rates measured were very similar to those measured by Paling et al. (1989), they are likely to be underestimated, as the increased N input resulting from runoff during the tropical cyclone reduces N-fixation rates (Joye and Paerl 1993). Nutrient assimilation during tidal exchange may have also been particularly high during the sampling period because an increase in nutrients enhances assimilation (Joye and Paerl 1993). Thus, the contribution of N fixation to total N incorporation under normal conditions could be higher than the one reported in the present study. Furthermore, the acetylene–ethylene method used to measure N fixation has some limitations, including (1) the relatively long time required to achieve a high, stable ethylene production, (2) the inhibition of acetylene reduction at high acetylene partial pressures and (3) incomplete saturation sites for ethylene production at low partial pressures (Patriquin and Denike 1978). The acetylene–ethylene reduction method can also overestimate N-fixation rates because it measures gross N fixation, without taking into account N loss by other processes such as denitrification (Howarth et al. 1988; Mahaffey et al. 2005). Although we maintained standard conditions between runs (6 h, 25°C), adding confidence to our relative comparisons (low v. high in the intertidal; day v. night), there is potential for error in our comparison of N fixation with N incorporation during tidal inundation. N exchange are highly likely, and further studies will be necessary to characterise the ecosystem contribution of nutrient exchange of the cyanobacterial mat in the Exmouth Gulf.

In conclusion, the results from the present study show that during periods of rainfall, the cyanobacterial mat in this subtropical and arid coastal wetland incorporates N through N fixation and through removal of dissolved nutrients from the floodwater during tidal inundation. The biogeochemical function of the cyanobacterial mat varies spatially and temporally. Spatially, the cyanobacterial mat has higher N-fixation rates in the low than in the high intertidal zone; temporally, it removes more nutrients from the floodwater and fixes more N in the day than at night. The cyanobacterial mat removes nutrients from the tidal water as soon as it is flooded, regardless of previous desiccation. The composition of the cyanobacterial mat in Giralia Bay is characterised by non-heterocystous forms within the Oscillatoriaceae, including representatives of the genera Oscillatoria and Microcoleus, whereas composition of the mat varies with elevation; more species are likely to occur in the high intertidal zone.

As predicted by McKinnon and Ayukai (1996), the vast cyanobacterial mats in Exmouth Gulf are likely to contribute to nutrient exchange, especially N fluxes, between the intertidal and subtidal ecosystems. The active nutrient exchange and high abundance of cyanobacterial mats in the region are likely to result in a significant contribution to N dynamics at an ecosystem scale, although this remains to be investigated. The exchange between cyanobacterial mats and the coastal ocean could be especially important in arid oligotrophic regions, such as the one in the present study, where cyanobacterial mats could have significant effects on coastal primary and secondary production.

Epilithic nitrogen fixation in the rocky littoral zones of Lake Malawi, Africa Abstract—Rates of epilithic N₂ fixation in the rocky littoral zones of Lake Malawi, determined by in situ incubations and the acetylene reduction method, declined with depth, were highly correlated to light intensity and heterocyst biovolume, and are among the highest observed values for freshwater or marine systems. Daytime N₂ fixation rates were similar between sites at similar depths, except at sediment and nutrient impacted sites, where rates were lower and more variable. Daytime N₂ fixation rates were measurable in all transparent chambers and were negligible in opaque chambers, which indicates that phototrophic diazotrophs (organisms capable of utilizing atmospheric nitrogen) were responsible for all daytime N₂ fixation. Nocturnal N₂ fixation was ~60% of daytime fixation. A model that integrated N₂ fixation over depth and time predicted that epilithic N₂ fixation may contribute up to 35% of N inputs to the epilimnion of Lake Malawi. Lake Malawi is a large (28,000 km²), deep (>700 m) oligotrophic African rift valley lake located between latitudes 9°5'S and 14°5'S. Although only 30% of the shoreline is composed of rocky substrata, approximately one half of Lake Malawi’s 500–1,000+ species of fish reside in the rocky littoral areas (Reinthal 1990; Ribbink et al. 1983), making it a critical habitat for fish biodiversity. The vast majority of these fish are herbivorous, and both ecological studies (Reinthal 1990) and stable isotope studies (Bootsma et al. 1996) indicate that epilithic periphyton is the most important component of their diets. Photosynthetic rates by the epilithic periphyton of Lake Malawi reach maximum values near 1g C m⁻² d⁻¹, which are similar to those that occur on coral reefs (Bootsma 1993). However, rates of nutrient uptake for these algal communities are unknown. The dominance of heterocystous cyanoprokaryotes within the epilithic periphyton community, and recent evidence that ambient total nitrogen concentrations are among the lowest for freshwater or marine systems (~7 μM; Guildford & Hecky 2000), suggest that the process of nitrogen fixation could play an important role in supplying “new” nitrogen to the epilithic periphyton community and epilimnion of Lake Malawi. The purpose of this study was, first, to determine the spatial dynamics of epilithic N₂ fixation in the rocky littoral zones of Lake Malawi and to estimate its contribution to the N requirements of the epilithic periphyton community. Such information is necessary for a more complete understanding of the factors that control periphyton productivity, which in turn maintains the dense and diverse littoral fish community of Lake Malawi. Second, this study examines the relationships between epilithic N₂ fixation, heterocyst biovolume, light intensity, and chlorophyll concentration, in an attempt to identify the controlling factors and variability in epilithic N₂ fixation rates. Third, this study gives preliminary estimates for the importance of epilithic N₂ fixation in the whole lake nitrogen budget of Lake Malawi and compares rates in Lake Malawi with freshwater and marine habitats over a wide range of latitudes. Sites—To accomplish the study objectives, five rocky littoral zone sites were selected in the central and southern portions of Lake Malawi. All experiments were conducted during the dry windy seasons (May–October) of 1997 and 1998. During 1997, two sites were used for study (Maleri South and Maleri North). Because of the presence of crocodiles at these sites during 1998, these sites were abandoned, and experiments were conducted at three new sites (Likoma Island [LI]-Makalawe, LI-Membe, and Thumbi West) during 1998. A more detailed description of the physical habitat at these sites was presented in Higgins (1999) and Ribbink et al. (1983). On average, each site/depth was sampled 2–3 times monthly, with the exception of LI-Makalawe and LI-Membe, which were opportunistically sampled over a 2-d period during May 1998. Acetylene reduction assays—Epilithic nitrogen fixation was estimated by modification of the acetylene reduction technique (Stewart et al. 1967) to allow for sampling epilithic periphyton communities, in situ, over a depth gradient (2–16 m) by use of SCUBA diving. The modifications are described in detail in Higgins (1999) and include the use of 800-ml, opaque, and ultraviolet-transparent plexiglass chambers fitted with a neoprene seal and skirt and weighted with a lead sock to isolate chamber water from surrounding ambient water. Chambers were placed on rocky surfaces, injected with 100 ml (at surface temperature and pressure) of welder’s-grade acetylene, stirred vigorously by use of a built-in stirring device, and incubated for 0.5–2.5 h. After the incubation time, the chamber was stirred vigorously, and a 40-ml aqueous sample was taken by use of a glass 50-ml syringe fitted with a three-way valve. After 10 ml of surface air was drawn in, the syringe was shaken vigorously for 2 min and placed in a water bath (at lake temperature) for ~1 min before the headspace was drawn into a 7-ml vacutainer, which was later analyzed on a Shimadzu GC-8A chromatograph fitted with a 3.05 m × 6.35 mm × 5.34 mm Altech porasil C/phenyl isocyanate mesh 80/100 column. Calibration with ethylene standards was conducted both prior to and after sample analysis each day, and an interlab calibration with known ethylene concentrations and 25 random samples (Freshwater Institute, Winnipeg, Canada). A time-series experiment was conducted, and rates of ethylene production were found to be linear between 0.5 and 2.5 h. Rates of N₂ fixation were calculated by use of a theoretical 4 : 1 (C₂H₂ : N₂) conversion ratio, which is of similar magnitude to experimentally determined conversion ratios for epilithic algal communities (Reuter et al. 1986; Larkum et al. 1988). In several acetylene reduction assays, screens of different mesh sizes were placed over the chambers, to reduce the amount of solar radiation received by the periphyton com- Table 1. The amount of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) received by the algal communities within each chamber was calculated from in situ light readings, combined with the percentage of transmission through each screen, calculated by use of a LICOR LI-1800 Spectroradiometer within a tub of lake water under low wave conditions. The in situ light readings were taken concurrent to, and directly beside, the acetylene reduction assays by use of a LICOR LI-1000 Data Logger and Quantum Sensor with a flat plate collector. Algal collection, heterocyst enumeration, and chlorophyll—After most experiments, duplicate or triplicate algal samples were taken from the rock surface within each chamber by use of a periphyton-scraping device, as described by Loeb (1981). The periphyton samples were stored in the dark and returned to the laboratory, where subsamples were taken for chlorophyll a analysis and heterocyst enumeration. Chl a was extracted from filtered subsamples at −5°C for ~14 h by use of an alkaline acetone solution, according to the methods of Stainton et al. (1977), and analyzed fluorometrically. For each site and depth combination, five algal samples were randomly chosen for heterocyst enumeration. A 2-ml subsample was placed in a Utermöhl chamber, and at least 50 fields (or 100 heterocysts) were counted by use of a Zeiss Axioinvert 35 inverted phase microscope with 400× magnification. Each sample to be counted was selected randomly, such that the person counting did not know the site or depth from which it originated. Daytime N₂ fixation—During daylight hours, rates of nitrogen fixation were easily detectable in all transparent chambers (Table 1), whereas rates in opaque chambers were typically 4%–7% of rates in transparent chambers, which indicates that photosynthetic cyanoprokaryotes were responsible for the majority N₂ fixation rates noted. The dominance of heterocystous forms of Calothrix at virtually all sites and depths studied (Higgins 1999) make it highly probable that they were responsible for the majority of daytime N₂ fixation by the periphyton community. Cyanoprokaryotic endosymbionts capable of N₂ fixation were found in several species of the diatom Rhopalodia; however, their total biovolume was generally an order of magnitude less than Calothrix heterocyst biovolume (Higgins 1999); therefore, they likely do not contribute largely to the overall fixation rates noted. The range of daytime N₂ fixation rates was 1–2,920 \( \mu \)g N m⁻² h⁻¹, with variability generally <30% of the mean value for each site/depth (Table 1). The Maleri Island sites, which are known to be impacted annually by a plume of sediment- and nutrient-rich water extending from the nearby Linthipe River (Bootsma and Hecky 1999), are an exception and have much higher variability, especially at 10 m depth. At the Maleri South site, a 1–2 cm layer of silt covering rocky surfaces was noted below 7 m depth, and rocky surfaces had a relatively low total standing crop of periphyton and biovolume of heterocysts (Higgins 1999). Nitrogen fixation, Chl a, and heterocyst biovolume—Of the parameters known to influence N₂ fixation, the strongest correlation was found with heterocyst biovolume (\( R = 0.71, P < 0.005 \); Fig. 1) and solar insolation (discussed below). Both N₂ fixation rates and heterocyst biovolume showed generally decreasing values with increasing depth at all sites sampled (Fig. 2a–e, Table 1). In contrast to studies on the epilithic periphyton of five northern temperate lakes by Loeb and Reuter (1981), chlorophyll and N₂ fixation were not highly correlated in the epilithic periphyton of Lake Malawi (\( R = 0.04, P = 0.70 \)). Studies on coral reefs have shown an inverse relationship between N₂ fixation and chlorophyll, which was attributed to the grazing activity of fish keeping the periphyton community in an early succesional stage, decreasing chlorophyll concentrations while increasing rates of primary production and nitrogen fixation (Wilkinson and Sammarco 1983; Larkum 1988). This may also be the case in Lake Malawi, where densities of grazing fish can exceed 10 individuals m⁻² area (Ribbink et al. 1983). Nitrogen fixation versus light model—The results of the screen experiments indicated that rates of nitrogen fixation per heterocyst were strongly dependent on the amount of PAR reaching the periphyton community (\( R^2 = 0.75, P < 0.001 \); Fig. 3). Nonlinear regression was used to fit these data to the relationship modified from Platt et al. (1980) by Lewis and Levine (1984), \[ N = N_s (1 - e^{-(\alpha I / N_s)}) e^{-(\beta I / N_s)} + D, \] where \( N \) is the amount of nitrogen fixed per heterocyst biovolume per unit time, \( N_s \) is the parameter representing maximum nitrogen fixation per heterocyst biovolume in the absence of light inhibition, \( I \) is the light intensity (PAR), \( \alpha \) is the slope of the light-limited and linear part of the N-fixation versus PAR curve, \( \beta \) is the parameter for light inhibition, and \( D \) is the fixation rate for heterocysts in the dark (Levine and Lewis 1987). Because light inhibition of nitrogen fixation under high light intensities was not evident during any of the experiments and fixation rates in the dark (during daylight hours) were negligible, the parameters \( \beta \) and \( D \) were set to zero. The N_2 fixation model, which integrates the relationships between N_2 fixation per heterocyst versus light, solar irradiance, light extinction, and heterocyst biovolume can be used in simulations to calculate N_2 fixation over a wide variety of spatial and temporal ranges. (1980). solar insolation), and 1 January 1997 (rainy season, highest solar insolation), were calculated by use of a mean light extinction coefficient of 0.2 (\( n = 18 \), range 0.16–0.25), cloudless solar data generated by Fee’s (1990) model (14°S latitude), and the relationship between heterocyst biovolume and depth (Higgins 1999). This simulation predicts that the maximum difference in nitrogen fixation rates due to seasonal differences in solar radiation is ~15% of the annual mean value. The 1 June 1997 simulation was also used to compare model estimates with in situ estimates of hourly N_2 fixation at midday for 2, 5, and 10 m depths (Table 1, Fig. 2f). The 1 June 1997 simulation for 2 m depth predicted a N_2 fixation rate of 1,490 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, which fell within the range of N_2 fixation rates for each site, with the exception of LI-Makalawe and Thumbi West (Table 1, Fig. 2f) and agreed with the site-averaged in situ N_2 fixation rate of 1,500 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}. The model predicted values of 910 and 370 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1} for 5 and 10 m depths, which agreed closely with the site-averaged in situ estimates of 950 and 410 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}. Patch-specific and nocturnal rates of nitrogen fixation— Above 1 m depth at all sites, and from 0–5 m depth at Maleri South, visually distinct patches of epilithic periphyton dominated by Calothrix or Cladophora were observed throughout the sampling season (May–October). At other sites and depths, the epilithic periphyton community was more homogenous and was dominated by heterocystous Calothrix spp (Higgins 1999; Higgins unpubl. data). The biomass of Calothrix patches were dominated by heterocystous Calothrix species, whereas the biomass of Cladophora patches were codominated by Cladophora, Calothrix, and a variety of epiphytic diatoms (Higgins 1999). Calothrix patches at 2 m depth had significantly higher rates of nitrogen fixation (1,450 ± 540 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}; \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) than Cladophora patches (720 ± 90 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) during daylight hours (\( t \)-test, \( P = 0.03 \)). The relative patchiness in the epilithic periphyton community structure at shallow depths of the Maleri Island sites is likely responsible for the higher variability in N_2 fixation rates noted (Table 1), whereas the impacts of sediment accumulation account for the high variability at deeper depths. The mean rate of nocturnal nitrogen fixation in Calothrix patches, from 1–2 m depth, was double that for Cladophora patches, was ~60% of the daytime averages for nitrogen fixation (Tables 1, 2), and was an order of magnitude larger than rates measured in opaque chambers during the day. Although the difference in N_2 fixation rates between daytime dark box and nocturnal dark box experiments was unexpected, there are a number of plausible explanations. First, nocturnal N_2 fixation by nonheterocystous diazotrophs might occur primarily at night, when O_2 inhibition is reduced (i.e., the temporal separation of N_2 fixation and O_2 evolution processes). Second, the length of incubation during daytime dark box experiments may have been insufficient to allow a shift in adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and reductant pathways, which differ between day and night within heterocystous diazotrophs (Stewart 1973). The agreement between model estimates and in situ estimates for N₂ fixation allowed us to estimate daytime N₂ fixation throughout the littoral zone. From a maximal carbon fixation rate of 1 g m⁻² d⁻¹ (Bootsma 1993) and a “Redfield” C : N ratio of 5.68 (molar), the calculated 24-h N demand of periphyton would be 170 mg N m⁻² d⁻¹. From model estimates of daily N₂ fixation at shallow depths (1–2 m), N₂ fixation would contribute between 8% and 12% of the total 24-hr N demand of epilithic periphyton and between 13% and 18% if nocturnal N₂ fixation were included. To estimate the importance of epilithic N₂ fixation to the N budget of Lake Malawi, we employed our model to spatially and temporally integrate N₂ fixation rates over a depth gradient (under the assumption of a 45° slope) for a single year. Within the model, we multiplied area estimates over a range of factors (2–5.7), to adjust for roughness of the substrata (Higgins 1999), then extrapolated the results over the entire rocky littoral zone area in Lake Malawi, as determined from literature sources (Ribbink et al. 1983) and aerial surveys (Cooley unpubl. data). Although our model uses estimated daily PAR under 100% cloudless conditions from Fee’s (1990) model, we calculated depth-integrated rates under 70% cloudless conditions and found only a 10% difference in model output (due to light saturation at shallow depths). On the basis of these assumptions, the N₂ fixation model estimates that 4–20 × 10⁴ kg N lake⁻¹ yr⁻¹, or 40–120 mmol N m⁻² yr⁻¹, is biologically fixed by epilithic diazotrophs. This estimate for epilithic N₂ fixation is similar in magnitude to those for precipitation and riverine inputs to Lake Malawi and suggests that epilithic N₂ fixation may be a significant source of N to the epilimnion (Table 3). Furthermore, because epilithic N₂ fixation rates do not vary substantially between seasons, the relative importance of epilithic N₂ fixation increases during the dry-windy season, when riverine and atmospheric inputs of N and pelagic N₂ fixation are much reduced. Interlake comparisons—Because this study represents the first epilithic N₂ fixation estimates from a tropical lake, epilithic N₂ fixation rates from Lake Malawi are presented along with benthic N₂ fixation rates from both marine and freshwater ecosystems that encompass a wide latitudinal range (Table 4). Summertime hourly N₂ fixation rates do not appear to follow a strong latitudinal gradient for freshwater systems. During the summer insolation period, somewhat lower hour- ly rates in temperate regions are made up for by longer day lengths. As a result, daily rates in arctic regions (during summer months) may be similar to those in more temperate or tropical regions. Because of seasonal differences in solar irradiance patterns and water temperature, however, annual N\(_2\) fixation rates in tropical regions are often an order of magnitude higher than those in temperate regions. Nonetheless, the importance of benthic N\(_2\) fixation to the nitrogen budget in these systems is related to seasonal trends in primary production and N demand and therefore does not necessarily vary over latitudes. For example, Bergmann and Welch (1990) estimated that N\(_2\) fixation accounted for up to 28% of the N budget in some arctic lakes, similar to our estimates for the epilithon of Lake Malawi (Table 3). Epilithic N\(_2\) fixation rates do not show any strong differences between freshwater and marine habitats. Hourly, daily, and annual N\(_2\) fixation rates in the rocky littoral areas of Lake Malawi are similar to those in coral reef habitats. This similarity in N\(_2\) fixation can be at least partially attributed to similarities in primary productivity (Bootsma 1993), grazing rates (Wilkinson and Sammarco 1983; Larkum et al. 1988; Andre 1999), and nutrient availability (Howarth et al. 1988; Bootsma and Hecky 1999). We conclude that benthic nitrogen fixation is a quantitatively significant contribution to the nitrogen requirement of the epilithic periphyton and to dependant herbivores, as well as to the whole-lake nitrogen budget. The predictive model of N\(_2\) fixation should be tested through further studies on Lake Malawi and other tropical lakes. Scott N. Higgins,1 Robert E. Hecky, and William D. Received: 1 March 2000 Accepted: 5 March 2001 Amended: 12 March 2001 High-resolution metal gradients measured by in situ DGT/DET deployment in Black Sea sediments using an autonomous benthic lander Abstract—DET (Diffusive equilibration in thin films) and DGT (diffusive gradients in thin films) have been deployed in situ using an autonomous benthic lander to measure concentrations and induced fluxes of Fe and Mn (DET/DGT) and trace metals (DGT) in pore waters at millimeter spatial resolutions. The newly developed deployment system is described, and based on these first results, its strengths and weaknesses are discussed. Deployments were made in the Western Black Sea in shelf sediments overlain by well-oxygenated water at a water depth of 77 m. Maxima of the redox-sensitive metals at 4 and 8 cm deep within the sediment indicated that two zones of reduction dominated the geochemistry. Sharp, but systematic, features were superimposed on this general picture and were well replicated in the profiles of Mn, Co, and Cd, but the sharp features in the Fe profile were offset from those of the others elements by several millimeters. Detection of this functional discrimination between Fe and Mn as regulators of trace metals would not have been possible using more conventional sampling procedures. The sediment–water interface is chemically and microbiologically the most active site in natural waters, with steep gradients in physical, chemical, and biological properties (Santschi et al. 1990). Over the last 20 yr, the spatial resolution of measurements of solute concentrations in pore waters has been improved to a submillimeter scale for a limited range of determinands (e.g. O_2, NO_3^−, pH, pCO_2) through the development of microelectrodes and optrodes (Larsen et al. 1997; Glud et al. 1999). These techniques have demonstrated the existence of concentration gradients across the sediment–water interface over millimeter and submillimeter depth scales (Cai and Reimers 1993). Although the resolution of conventional (Carrignan et al. 1985) slicing/squeezing and dialysis procedures has been improved (Shaw et al. 1990; Aller et al. 1998) and voltametric electrodes have been used for Mn and Fe and other solutes (e.g., I^− and S(−II)) (Bren- del and Luther 1995; Luther et al. 1998), only the emerging techniques of DET (diffusive equilibration in thin films) and DGT (diffusive gradients in thin films) have provided high-resolution data for a wide range of components that include trace metals other than Fe and Mn (Davison et al. 2000). DET is directly comparable to more traditional “peeper” systems, except that diffusive equilibrium is attained between solutes in the pore waters and in a thin film of gel. The thinness (<1 mm) of the film results in much faster diffusive equilibration than with traditional peepers. DET has been used to measure Ca^{2+}, Mg^{2+}, Na^{+}, K^{+}, Fe^{2/3+}, Mn^{2+}, Cl^−, SO_4^{2−}, NO_3^−, alkalinity, and ΣCO_2 in pore waters at a resolution of 1–2 mm (Davison et al. 1994; Brunnegard 1997; Mortimer et al. 1998; Zhang et al. 1999) and Fe at a resolution of 400 μm (Fones et al. 1998) and in two dimensions (Shuttleworth et al. 1999). DGT (Davison et al. 2000) uses an extra backing layer of gel impregnated with chelating resin. Metal continuously diffuses across the outer layer of gel (95% water) and accumulates on the chelating resin. After deployment, the resin gel layer is sliced and eluted with acid, and metals are determined by atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Deployment for a given time at a known temperature allows calculation of the mean flux to the resin gel during deployment. If pore waters are effectively buffered by rapid resupply from a local source, such as a desorbing solid phase, the measured flux can be quantitatively interpreted as a concentration (Zhang et al. 1995; Harper et al. 1998). DET/DGT assemblies were initially deployed in situ in shallow waters by SCUBA divers (Davison et al. 1994; Zhang et al. 1995; Brunnegard 1997) or placed by hand (Davison et al. 1997). Epilithic nitrogen fixation in the rocky littoral zones of Lake Malawi, Africa Abstract—Rates of epilithic N₂ fixation in the rocky littoral zones of Lake Malawi, determined by in situ incubations and the acetylene reduction method, declined with depth, were highly correlated to light intensity and heterocyst biovolume, and are among the highest observed values for freshwater or marine systems. Daytime N₂ fixation rates were similar between sites at similar depths, except at sediment and nutrient impacted sites, where rates were lower and more variable. Daytime N₂ fixation rates were measurable in all transparent chambers and were negligible in opaque chambers, which indicates that phototrophic diazotrophs (organisms capable of utilizing atmospheric nitrogen) were responsible for all daytime N₂ fixation. Nocturnal N₂ fixation was ~60% of daytime fixation. A model that integrated N₂ fixation over depth and time predicted that epilithic N₂ fixation may contribute up to 35% of N inputs to the epilimnion of Lake Malawi. Lake Malawi is a large (28,000 km²), deep (>700 m) oligotrophic African rift valley lake located between latitudes 9°5'S and 14°5'S. Although only 30% of the shoreline is composed of rocky substrata, approximately one half of Lake Malawi’s 500–1,000+ species of fish reside in the rocky littoral areas (Reinthal 1990; Ribbink et al. 1983), making it a critical habitat for fish biodiversity. The vast majority of these fish are herbivorous, and both ecological studies (Reinthal 1990) and stable isotope studies (Bootsma et al. 1996) indicate that epilithic periphyton is the most important component of their diets. Photosynthetic rates by the epilithic periphyton of Lake Malawi reach maximum values near 1g C m⁻² d⁻¹, which are similar to those that occur on coral reefs (Bootsma 1993). However, rates of nutrient uptake for these algal communities are unknown. The dominance of heterocystous cyanoprokaryotes within the epilithic periphyton community, and recent evidence that ambient total nitrogen concentrations are among the lowest for freshwater or marine systems (~7 μM; Guildford & Hecky 2000), suggest that the process of nitrogen fixation could play an important role in supplying “new” nitrogen to the epilithic periphyton community and epilimnion of Lake Malawi. The purpose of this study was, first, to determine the spatial dynamics of epilithic N₂ fixation in the rocky littoral zones of Lake Malawi and to estimate its contribution to the N requirements of the epilithic periphyton community. Such information is necessary for a more complete understanding of the factors that control periphyton productivity, which in turn maintains the dense and diverse littoral fish community of Lake Malawi. Second, this study examines the relationships between epilithic N₂ fixation, heterocyst biovolume, light intensity, and chlorophyll concentration, in an attempt to identify the controlling factors and variability in epilithic N₂ fixation rates. Third, this study gives preliminary estimates for the importance of epilithic N₂ fixation in the whole lake nitrogen budget of Lake Malawi and compares rates in Lake Malawi with freshwater and marine habitats over a wide range of latitudes. Sites—To accomplish the study objectives, five rocky littoral zone sites were selected in the central and southern portions of Lake Malawi. All experiments were conducted during the dry windy seasons (May–October) of 1997 and 1998. During 1997, two sites were used for study (Maleri South and Maleri North). Because of the presence of crocodiles at these sites during 1998, these sites were abandoned, and experiments were conducted at three new sites (Likoma Island [LI]-Makalawe, LI-Membe, and Thumbi West) during 1998. A more detailed description of the physical habitat at these sites was presented in Higgins (1999) and Ribbink et al. (1983). On average, each site/depth was sampled 2–3 times monthly, with the exception of LI-Makalawe and LI-Membe, which were opportunistically sampled over a 2-d period during May 1998. Acetylene reduction assays—Epilithic nitrogen fixation was estimated by modification of the acetylene reduction technique (Stewart et al. 1967) to allow for sampling epilithic periphyton communities, in situ, over a depth gradient (2–16 m) by use of SCUBA diving. The modifications are described in detail in Higgins (1999) and include the use of 800-ml, opaque, and ultraviolet-transparent plexiglass chambers fitted with a neoprene seal and skirt and weighted with a lead sock to isolate chamber water from surrounding ambient water. Chambers were placed on rocky surfaces, injected with 100 ml (at surface temperature and pressure) of welder’s-grade acetylene, stirred vigorously by use of a built-in stirring device, and incubated for 0.5–2.5 h. After the incubation time, the chamber was stirred vigorously, and a 40-ml aqueous sample was taken by use of a glass 50-ml syringe fitted with a three-way valve. After 10 ml of surface air was drawn in, the syringe was shaken vigorously for 2 min and placed in a water bath (at lake temperature) for ~1 min before the headspace was drawn into a 7-ml vacutainer, which was later analyzed on a Shimadzu GC-8A chromatograph fitted with a 3.05 m × 6.35 mm × 5.34 mm Altech porasil C/phenyl isocyanate mesh 80/100 column. Calibration with ethylene standards was conducted both prior to and after sample analysis each day, and an interlab calibration with known ethylene concentrations and 25 random samples (Freshwater Institute, Winnipeg, Canada). A time-series experiment was conducted, and rates of ethylene production were found to be linear between 0.5 and 2.5 h. Rates of N₂ fixation were calculated by use of a theoretical 4 : 1 (C₂H₂ : N₂) conversion ratio, which is of similar magnitude to experimentally determined conversion ratios for epilithic algal communities (Reuter et al. 1986; Larkum et al. 1988). The amount of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) received by the algal communities within each chamber was calculated from in situ light readings, combined with the percentage of transmission through each screen, calculated by use of a LICOR LI-1800 Spectroradiometer within a tub of lake water under low wave conditions. The in situ light readings were taken concurrent to, and directly beside, the acetylene reduction assays by use of a LICOR LI-1000 Data Logger and Quantum Sensor with a flat plate collector. Algal collection, heterocyst enumeration, and chlorophyll—After most experiments, duplicate or triplicate algal samples were taken from the rock surface within each chamber by use of a periphyton-scraping device, as described by Loeb (1981). The periphyton samples were stored in the dark and returned to the laboratory, where subsamples were taken for chlorophyll a analysis and heterocyst enumeration. Chl a was extracted from filtered subsamples at −5°C for ~14 h by use of an alkaline acetone solution, according to the methods of Stainton et al. (1977), and analyzed fluorometrically. For each site and depth combination, five algal samples were randomly chosen for heterocyst enumeration. A 2-ml subsample was placed in a Utermöhl chamber, and at least 50 fields (or 100 heterocysts) were counted by use of a Zeiss Axioinvert 35 inverted phase microscope with 400× magnification. Each sample to be counted was selected randomly, such that the person counting did not know the site or depth from which it originated. Daytime N₂ fixation—During daylight hours, rates of nitrogen fixation were easily detectable in all transparent chambers (Table 1), whereas rates in opaque chambers were typically 4%–7% of rates in transparent chambers, which indicates that photosynthetic cyanoprokaryotes were responsible for the majority N₂ fixation rates noted. The dominance of heterocystous forms of Calothrix at virtually all sites and depths studied (Higgins 1999) make it highly probable that they were responsible for the majority of daytime N₂ fixation by the periphyton community. Cyanoprokaryotic endosymbionts capable of N₂ fixation were found in several species of the diatom Rhopalodia; however, their total biovolume was generally an order of magnitude less than Calothrix heterocyst biovolume (Higgins 1999); therefore, they likely do not contribute largely to the overall fixation rates noted. The range of daytime N₂ fixation rates was 1–2,920 \( \mu \)g N m⁻² h⁻¹, with variability generally <30% of the mean value for each site/depth (Table 1). The Maleri Island sites, which are known to be impacted annually by a plume of sediment- and nutrient-rich water extending from the nearby Linthipe River (Bootsma and Hecky 1999), are an exception and have much higher variability, especially at 10 m depth. At the Maleri South site, a 1–2 cm layer of silt covering rocky surfaces was noted below 7 m depth, and rocky surfaces had a relatively low total standing crop of periphyton and biovolume of heterocysts (Higgins 1999). Nitrogen fixation, Chl a, and heterocyst biovolume—Of the parameters known to influence N₂ fixation, the strongest correlation was found with heterocyst biovolume (\( R = 0.71, P < 0.005 \); Fig. 1) and solar insolation (discussed below). Both N₂ fixation rates and heterocyst biovolume showed generally decreasing values with increasing depth at all sites sampled (Fig. 2a–e, Table 1). In contrast to studies on the epilithic periphyton of five northern temperate lakes by Loeb and Reuter (1981), chlorophyll and N₂ fixation were not highly correlated in the epilithic periphyton of Lake Malawi (\( R = 0.04, P = 0.70 \)). Studies on coral reefs have shown an inverse relationship between N₂ fixation and chlorophyll, which was attributed to the grazing activity of fish keeping the periphyton community in an early succesional stage, decreasing chlorophyll concentrations while increasing rates of primary production and nitrogen fixation (Wilkinson and Sammarco 1983; Larkum 1988). This may also be the case in Lake Malawi, where densities of grazing fish can exceed 10 individuals m⁻² area (Ribbink et al. 1983). Nitrogen fixation versus light model—The results of the screen experiments indicated that rates of nitrogen fixation per heterocyst were strongly dependent on the amount of PAR reaching the periphyton community (\( R^2 = 0.75, P < 0.001 \); Fig. 3). Nonlinear regression was used to fit these data to the relationship modified from Platt et al. (1980) by Lewis and Levine (1984), \[ N = N_s (1 - e^{-(\alpha I / N_s)}) e^{-(\beta I / N_s)} + D, \] where \( N \) is the amount of nitrogen fixed per heterocyst biovolume per unit time, \( N_s \) is the parameter representing maximum nitrogen fixation per heterocyst biovolume in the absence of light inhibition, \( I \) is the light intensity (PAR), \( \alpha \) is the slope of the light-limited and linear part of the N-fixation versus PAR curve, \( \beta \) is the parameter for light inhibition, and \( D \) is the fixation rate for heterocysts in the dark (Levine and Lewis 1987). Because light inhibition of nitrogen fixation under high light intensities was not evident during any of the experiments and fixation rates in the dark (during daylight hours) were negligible, the parameters \( \beta \) and \( D \) were set to zero. The N_2 fixation model, which integrates the relationships between N_2 fixation per heterocyst versus light, solar irradiance, light extinction, and heterocyst biovolume can be used in simulations to calculate N_2 fixation over a wide variety of spatial and temporal ranges. This simulation predicts that the maximum difference in nitrogen fixation rates due to seasonal differences in solar radiation is ~15% of the annual mean value. The 1 June 1997 simulation was also used to compare model estimates with in situ estimates of hourly N_2 fixation at midday for 2, 5, and 10 m depths (Table 1, Fig. 2f). The 1 June 1997 simulation for 2 m depth predicted a N_2 fixation rate of 1,490 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, which fell within the range of N_2 fixation rates for each site, with the exception of LI-Makalawe and Thumbi West (Table 1, Fig. 2f) and agreed with the site-averaged in situ N_2 fixation rate of 1,500 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}. The model predicted values of 910 and 370 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1} for 5 and 10 m depths, which agreed closely with the site-averaged in situ estimates of 950 and 410 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}. Patch-specific and nocturnal rates of nitrogen fixation— Above 1 m depth at all sites, and from 0–5 m depth at Maleri South, visually distinct patches of epilithic periphyton dominated by Calothrix or Cladophora were observed throughout the sampling season (May–October). At other sites and depths, the epilithic periphyton community was more homogenous and was dominated by heterocystous Calothrix spp (Higgins 1999; Higgins unpubl. data). The biomass of Calothrix patches were dominated by heterocystous Calothrix species, whereas the biomass of Cladophora patches were codominated by Cladophora, Calothrix, and a variety of epiphytic diatoms (Higgins 1999). Calothrix patches at 2 m depth had significantly higher rates of nitrogen fixation (1,450 ± 540 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}; \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) than Cladophora patches (720 ± 90 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) during daylight hours (\( t \)-test, \( P = 0.03 \)). The relative patchiness in the epilithic periphyton community structure at shallow depths of the Maleri Island sites is likely responsible for the higher variability in N_2 fixation rates noted (Table 1), whereas the impacts of sediment accumulation account for the high variability at deeper depths. The mean rate of nocturnal nitrogen fixation in Calothrix patches, from 1–2 m depth, was double that for Cladophora patches, was ~60% of the daytime averages for nitrogen fixation (Tables 1, 2), and was an order of magnitude larger than rates measured in opaque chambers during the day. Although the difference in N_2 fixation rates between daytime dark box and nocturnal dark box experiments was unexpected, there are a number of plausible explanations. First, nocturnal N_2 fixation by nonheterocystous diazotrophs might occur primarily at night, when O_2 inhibition is reduced (i.e., the temporal separation of N_2 fixation and O_2 evolution processes). Second, the length of incubation during daytime dark box experiments may have been insufficient to allow a shift in adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and reductant pathways, which differ between day and night within heterocystous diazotrophs (Stewart 1973). The agreement between model estimates and in situ estimates for N₂ fixation allowed us to estimate daytime N₂ fixation throughout the littoral zone. From a maximal carbon fixation rate of 1 g m⁻² d⁻¹ (Bootsma 1993) and a “Redfield” C : N ratio of 5.68 (molar), the calculated 24-h N demand of periphyton would be 170 mg N m⁻² d⁻¹. From model estimates of daily N₂ fixation at shallow depths (1–2 m), N₂ fixation would contribute between 8% and 12% of the total 24-hr N demand of epilithic periphyton and between 13% and 18% if nocturnal N₂ fixation were included. To estimate the importance of epilithic N₂ fixation to the N budget of Lake Malawi, we employed our model to spatially and temporally integrate N₂ fixation rates over a depth gradient (under the assumption of a 45° slope) for a single year. Within the model, we multiplied area estimates over a range of factors (2–5.7), to adjust for roughness of the substrata (Higgins 1999), then extrapolated the results over the entire rocky littoral zone area in Lake Malawi, as determined from literature sources (Ribbink et al. 1983) and aerial surveys (Cooley unpubl. data). Although our model uses estimated daily PAR under 100% cloudless conditions from Fee’s (1990) model, we calculated depth-integrated rates under 70% cloudless conditions and found only a 10% difference in model output (due to light saturation at shallow depths). On the basis of these assumptions, the N₂ fixation model estimates that 4–20 × 10⁴ kg N lake⁻¹ yr⁻¹, or 40–120 mmol N m⁻² yr⁻¹, is biologically fixed by epilithic diazotrophs. This estimate for epilithic N₂ fixation is similar in magnitude to those for precipitation and riverine inputs to Lake Malawi and suggests that epilithic N₂ fixation may be a significant source of N to the epilimnion (Table 3). Furthermore, because epilithic N₂ fixation rates do not vary substantially between seasons, the relative importance of epilithic N₂ fixation increases during the dry-windy season, when riverine and atmospheric inputs of N and pelagic N₂ fixation are much reduced. Interlake comparisons—Because this study represents the first epilithic N₂ fixation estimates from a tropical lake, epilithic N₂ fixation rates from Lake Malawi are presented along with benthic N₂ fixation rates from both marine and freshwater ecosystems that encompass a wide latitudinal range (Table 4). Summertime hourly N₂ fixation rates do not appear to follow a strong latitudinal gradient for freshwater systems. During the summer insolation period, somewhat lower hour- ly rates in temperate regions are made up for by longer day lengths. As a result, daily rates in arctic regions (during summer months) may be similar to those in more temperate or tropical regions. Because of seasonal differences in solar irradiance patterns and water temperature, however, annual N\(_2\) fixation rates in tropical regions are often an order of magnitude higher than those in temperate regions. Nonetheless, the importance of benthic N\(_2\) fixation to the nitrogen budget in these systems is related to seasonal trends in primary production and N demand and therefore does not necessarily vary over latitudes. For example, Bergmann and Welch (1990) estimated that N\(_2\) fixation accounted for up to 28% of the N budget in some arctic lakes, similar to our estimates for the epilithon of Lake Malawi (Table 3). Epilithic N\(_2\) fixation rates do not show any strong differences between freshwater and marine habitats. Hourly, daily, and annual N\(_2\) fixation rates in the rocky littoral areas of Lake Malawi are similar to those in coral reef habitats. This similarity in N\(_2\) fixation can be at least partially attributed to similarities in primary productivity (Bootsma 1993), grazing rates (Wilkinson and Sammarco 1983; Larkum et al. 1988; Andre 1999), and nutrient availability (Howarth et al. 1988; Bootsma and Hecky 1999). We conclude that benthic nitrogen fixation is a quantitatively significant contribution to the nitrogen requirement of the epilithic periphyton and to dependant herbivores, as well as to the whole-lake nitrogen budget. The predictive model of N\(_2\) fixation should be tested through further studies on Lake Malawi and other tropical lakes. Scott N. Higgins,1 Robert E. Hecky, and William D. Received: 1 March 2000 Accepted: 5 March 2001 Amended: 12 March 2001 High-resolution metal gradients measured by in situ DGT/DET deployment in Black Sea sediments using an autonomous benthic lander Abstract—DET (Diffusive equilibration in thin films) and DGT (diffusive gradients in thin films) have been deployed in situ using an autonomous benthic lander to measure concentrations and induced fluxes of Fe and Mn (DET/DGT) and trace metals (DGT) in pore waters at millimeter spatial resolutions. The newly developed deployment system is described, and based on these first results, its strengths and weaknesses are discussed. Deployments were made in the Western Black Sea in shelf sediments overlain by well-oxygenated water at a water depth of 77 m. Maxima of the redox-sensitive metals at 4 and 8 cm deep within the sediment indicated that two zones of reduction dominated the geochemistry. Sharp, but systematic, features were superimposed on this general picture and were well replicated in the profiles of Mn, Co, and Cd, but the sharp features in the Fe profile were offset from those of the others elements by several millimeters. Detection of this functional discrimination between Fe and Mn as regulators of trace metals would not have been possible using more conventional sampling procedures. The sediment–water interface is chemically and microbiologically the most active site in natural waters, with steep gradients in physical, chemical, and biological properties (Santschi et al. 1990). Over the last 20 yr, the spatial resolution of measurements of solute concentrations in pore waters has been improved to a submillimeter scale for a limited range of determinands (e.g. O_2, NO_3^−, pH, pCO_2) through the development of microelectrodes and optrodes (Larsen et al. 1997; Glud et al. 1999). These techniques have demonstrated the existence of concentration gradients across the sediment–water interface over millimeter and submillimeter depth scales (Cai and Reimers 1993). Although the resolution of conventional (Carrignan et al. 1985) slicing/squeezing and dialysis procedures has been improved (Shaw et al. 1990; Aller et al. 1998) and voltametric electrodes have been used for Mn and Fe and other solutes (e.g., I^− and S(−II)) (Bren- del and Luther 1995; Luther et al. 1998), only the emerging techniques of DET (diffusive equilibration in thin films) and DGT (diffusive gradients in thin films) have provided high-resolution data for a wide range of components that include trace metals other than Fe and Mn (Davison et al. 2000). DET is directly comparable to more traditional “peeper” systems, except that diffusive equilibrium is attained between solutes in the pore waters and in a thin film of gel. The thinness (<1 mm) of the film results in much faster diffusive equilibration than with traditional peepers. DET has been used to measure Ca^{2+}, Mg^{2+}, Na^{+}, K^{+}, Fe^{2/3+}, Mn^{2+}, Cl^−, SO_4^{2−}, NO_3^−, alkalinity, and ΣCO_2 in pore waters at a resolution of 1–2 mm (Davison et al. 1994; Brunnegard 1997; Mortimer et al. 1998; Zhang et al. 1999) and Fe at a resolution of 400 μm (Fones et al. 1998) and in two dimensions (Shuttleworth et al. 1999). DGT (Davison et al. 2000) uses an extra backing layer of gel impregnated with chelating resin. Metal continuously diffuses across the outer layer of gel (95% water) and accumulates on the chelating resin. After deployment, the resin gel layer is sliced and eluted with acid, and metals are determined by atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Deployment for a given time at a known temperature allows calculation of the mean flux to the resin gel during deployment. If pore waters are effectively buffered by rapid resupply from a local source, such as a desorbing solid phase, the measured flux can be quantitatively interpreted as a concentration (Zhang et al. 1995; Harper et al. 1998). DET/DGT assemblies were initially deployed in situ in shallow waters by SCUBA divers (Davison et al. 1994; Zhang et al. 1995; Brunnegard 1997) or placed by hand (Davison et al. 1997). CLEAN Soil Air Water Renewables Sustainability Environmental Monitoring Research Article Influence of Crude Oil on Denitrification in Subtidal Sediments in the Northern Gulf of Mexico In this study the impact of hydrocarbons on nitrogen cycling in intertidal sediments from a barrier island in the north central Gulf of Mexico was investigated. Initial total petroleum hydrocarbon (TPH) concentrations of the sediments averaged \(49 \pm 27\ \mathrm{mg\ kg}^{-1}\) in June and \(75 \pm 48\ \mathrm{mg\ kg}^{-1}\) in November. Following the addition of crude oil, TPH concentrations increased to \(340 \pm 73\) and \(296 \pm 50\ \mathrm{mg\ kg}^{-1}\) in June and November, respectively. Sediment oxygen demand (SOD), inorganic nitrogen and phosphorus fluxes, and denitrification capacity, measured with the isotope pairing technique (IPT) within a week of oiling, were consistently higher in June compared to rates in November when temperatures were \(10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) lower. Despite significantly higher TPH concentrations in the oiled treatments, SOD, nutrient fluxes, nitrogen fixation, denitrification, and anammox, did not differ between the treatments. Potential denitrification rates, measured in the presence of excess nitrate (100 \(\mu\)M), were similar between the control and oil treatments, but significantly higher than rates measured with the IPT. The elevated rates of potential denitrification suggest the presence of an active extant microbial community capable of significant attenuation of porewater nitrate concentrations. The insignificant changes in nitrogen cycling in response to petroleum hydrocarbon additions at a site with hydrocarbons present, albeit at low concentrations, suggests resiliency in nitrogen cycling in response to additional hydrocarbon inputs in ranges investigated in this study. Keywords: Denitrification; Isotope pairing technique; Marine sediments; Nitrogen fixation; Total petroleum hydrocarbons Received: August 10, 2016; revised: December 12, 2016; accepted: June 7, 2017 DOI: 10.1002/clen.201600546 1 Introduction In the aftermath of an oil spill, the abundance of the microbial communities capable of metabolizing petroleum hydrocarbons as a carbon source increases [1]. But because of the overabundance of carbon relative to nitrogen or phosphorus in hydrocarbons, there is an increase in demand for inorganic nutrients, especially nitrogen, by microorganisms capable of degrading hydrocarbons [2]. Changes in three microbially driven processes following oil spills, namely nitrogen fixation, denitrification, and anammox, can affect the availability of nitrogen in sediments. As opposed to nitrogen fixation, which supplies bioavailable nitrogen to the sediments, denitrification and anammox transform bioavailable nitrogen to dinitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}_2\)) gas that is then lost to the atmosphere. While denitrification and anammox both result in the production of dinitrogen gas, denitrification is the dissimilatory process by which nitrate or nitrite is used as electron acceptors [3], whereas anammox is the anaerobic oxidation of ammonium with nitrite serving as the terminal electron acceptor [4]. Understanding changes in these processes following an oil spill is of particular interest because of their impact on nitrogen availability and how they can affect hydrocarbon degradation. Previous investigations have shown that changes in rates of nitrogen fixation [5] or denitrification [6–10] depend on the quantity and quality of the oil and habitat type where an oil spill occurs. Potential denitrification rates in marsh and coastal sediments exposed to crude oil, for example, were lower, and the decline in rates were much more pronounced the longer the sediments were exposed to crude oil [6, 7], or when the sediments were exposed to fresh crude as opposed to weathered oil [7]. However, because denitrification is an anaerobic process, others have suggested that following exposure to hydrocarbons and reduced oxygen availability in the sediments, denitrification would be enhanced. For example, in contaminated sediments within the vicinity of the Deepwater Horizon (DWH) accident site, and in naturally occurring oil seeps in the Gulf of Mexico, Scott et al. [8] noted a shift in the metabolic flow of nitrogen to the denitrification pathways. Similarly, laboratory experiments have demonstrated that following oil contamination in marsh sediments mineralization and potential denitrification rates increased, and these increases were attributed to the enhanced supply of carbon from the oil [9], and a change in redox conditions that favored denitrification [8, 10]. Our goal was to determine how oiling with weathered crude oil changes nitrogen cycling, particularly denitrification, nitrogen fixation and anammox, in a coastal region. Current strategies for remediation of oiled beaches and wetlands include application of nitrogen and/or nitrogen and phosphorus [11, 12] with the ultimate goal of keeping porewater bioavailable nutrient concentrations at levels that are adequate for the microbial community capable of hydrocarbon degradation [13, 14]. A better understanding of the impact of hydrocarbons on nitrogen cycling in marine sediments can lead to better predictions of the impacts of oil spills on biogeochemical cycles and improved remediation strategies of impacted ecosystems. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study site Samples were collected in June and November 2014 from a subtidal sandy site on the east end of Dauphin Island, AL, USA (30°15′3″N, 88°4′40″W); a barrier island located in the northern Gulf of Mexico (Fig. 1). Point measurements of temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen were recorded with a YSI 556 Multiparameter Meter during each sampling event. 10 mL of site water was collected in triplicate and filtered through a GF/F (0.7 μm pore size) and frozen until analyses were performed for dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN: NO\(_2^-\), NO\(_3^-\), NO\(_4^-\)) and PO\(_4^{3-}\) with standard wet chemical techniques modified for the Skalar SAN\(^+\) Autoanalyzer. 2.2 Porewater nutrients Sediments were collected in triplicate with a 2.6 cm id corer and sectioned in 1 cm segments to a depth of 6 cm for the determination of total extractable porewater nutrients. Nutrients were extracted with 10 mL of 1 M NaCl [15] after shaking at 60 rpm on a shaker table for 4 h. Samples were then centrifuged at 4500 rpm for 10 min and the supernatant was GF/F filtered and frozen for analysis for DIN and PO\(_4^{3-}\) as described above. 2.3 Chlorophyll-\( \alpha \) (chl-\( \alpha \)) Samples for sediment chl-\( \alpha \) concentrations were collected in triplicate with a corer (1.4 cm id) to a depth of 1 cm. Sediment wet weights were recorded prior to being stored at –80°C. Sediments were freeze-dried, dry weight was recorded, and were extracted in 10 mL of 90% acetone for 24 h. Both surface water and sediment chl-\( \alpha \) concentrations were determined fluorometrically [16]. 2.4 Crude oil weathering and analysis The crude oil was weathered by placing an aliquot of Louisiana sweet crude oil in an open container on a mechanical shaker at ca. 85 rpm for five days under a fume-hood in a dark environment. Total petroleum hydrocarbons (THP) in the sediments were extracted according to the EPA SW-846-3550 and standard method SM 5520F [17] and analyzed by Fourier transform IR spectroscopy (FTIR) at Envirochem, Mobile, AL. 2.5 Application of the oil In June and November, ten cores (9.5 cm id, 24 cm height) were collected from subtidal bare sediments to a depth of ~20 cm for ![Map of the study site on Dauphin Island, AL, USA.](page_101_1342_1342_670.png) Figure 1. Map of the study site on Dauphin Island, AL, USA. determination of sediment oxygen consumption (SOD), nutrient fluxes, and denitrification rates. In addition, six cores for measuring rates of potential denitrification and nitrogen fixation were collected. All cores were brought back to the laboratory and the overlying water was gently removed. Half of the cores were oiled, while the remainder served as controls. The oil was applied by injecting 0.1 mL of the oil at a depth of 5 cm in ten evenly spaced locations across the cores. After oiling, cores were inundated for 12 h by gently adding 100 mL of unfiltered site water. Overlying water was then removed and sediments were exposed to air for 12 h. This cycle of inundation and air exposure was similar to the timing of semidiurnal tides at this location and was repeated for 3 days with the same water from each core. 2.6 Potential N₂ fixation and denitrification The top 5 cm from triplicate oiled and control cores were homogenized following the application of the oil and a 3-day inundation/exposure period and used for rate measurements. Nitrogen fixation rates were determined with the acetylene reduction technique [18]. Approximately 20 g of sediment from each core was measured into 70 mL serum vials and mixed with 40 mL GF/F filtered site water. Samples were sealed with butyl rubber stoppers, flushed with N₂ gas for 10 min and injected with 7 mL acetylene. Vials were incubated in the dark for 24 h, and then thoroughly shaken, before the headspace concentration of ethylene (C₂H₄) was determined on a Shimadzu gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector. Bunsen gas solubility coefficients for ethylene for the appropriate salinity and temperature were used to calculate the total amount of ethylene produced [19]. Production rates of ethylene were converted to N₂ fixation rates with a 3:1 ethylene to N₂ reduction ratio [18]. Rates of potential denitrification were determined with the acetylene inhibition technique [20] as previously described [21]. Briefly, 20 g of sediment from each core was measured into 70 mL serum vials and mixed with 35 mL GF/F filtered site water. Samples were amended with nitrate to a final concentration of 100 μM, sealed with butyl rubber stoppers and flushed with nitrogen gas for 10 min. 7 mL of acetylene was injected into each vial and incubated for 1 h. Vials were shaken vigorously prior to sampling the headspace. Headspace N₂O concentrations were measured on a gas chromatograph, Shimadzu 2014, equipped with an electron capture detector and used to calculate potential denitrification rates. The nitrous oxide solubility coefficients [22] were used to calculate total nitrous oxide produced (headspace and dissolved). Potential denitrification as well nitrogen fixation rates were converted from a gram basis to an areal basis. 2.7 Experimental setup for benthic flux measurements Five oiled and five control cores were placed underwater in an environmental chamber set to the average water temperature and allowed to equilibrate for 3 days with aerobic overlying water to ensure that no bubbles would be formed when the cores were capped. Incubations were carried out in the dark to prevent interference by photosynthetic algae [23] or bubble formation. Cores were capped underwater ensuring no air bubbles were formed and each core was equipped with a magnetic stir bar to mix the overlying water. GF/F filtered site water, enriched to a final concentration of 50 μM of isotopically labeled sodium nitrate (Na⁺¹⁵NO₃⁻), was then flowed through each core at a rate of ~2.5 mL min⁻¹. The positive displacement of the overlying water exited the core through an outflow tube ("outflow") and was collected in a reservoir. After 24 h of flow through, water samples were collected from the outflow and inflow from each core for determination of oxygen, nutrients and nitrogen gas isotope concentrations (described below). Following the sample collections, the cores were gently uncapped and the top 5 cm from each was sectioned and homogenized for THP analysis. 2.8 Benthic fluxes Sediment oxygen demand was determined from inflow and outflow water based on O₂ concentrations measured with a Unisense® multimeter equipped with a calibrated O₂ (Ox-500) sensor. Water samples were collected in triplicate from the inflow and outflow lines, filtered through GF/F and immediately frozen until analysis for inorganic nutrient concentrations as previously described. Inflow and outflow samples from each core were collected in triplicate in 12 mL Exetainers® by overflowing the vial's volume twice for the analysis of isotopes of nitrogen gas with membrane inlet MS (MIMS), equipped with an in-line quartz column packed with copper turnings and heated to 600°C [24], to remove oxygen upstream of the mass spectrometer. Samples were then preserved with 250 μL of 50% w/v ZnCl₂, capped and stored underwater until analysis within 48 h. Denitrification was determined according to the isotope pairing technique (IPT) as described in [25]. In this approach, denitrification is explicitly calculated from the \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2\) fluxes calculated from dissolved \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2/^{28}\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2/^{28}\mathrm{N}_2\) measured with the MIMS. Denitrification of \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) (\(D_{15}\)) was calculated directly: \[ D_{15} = F^{29} + 2F^{30} \] where \(F^{29}\) and \(F^{30}\) represent the steady state \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2\) fluxes. Denitrification of \(^{14}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) (\(D_{14}\)) was calculated using the expression of Nielsen [25]: \[ D_{14} = \frac{F^{29}}{2F^{30}} D_{15} \] Total denitrification was then calculated as the sum of \(D_{14}\) and \(D_{15}\), and hereafter referred to as "denitrification capacity." Benthic fluxes were calculated according to: \[ F = (C_e - .C_i)V/A \] where \(C_e\) is the outflow concentration, \(C_i\) is the inflow concentration, V is the flow rate, and A is the surface area of the sediment. 2.9 Anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) Anammox slurries were created in duplicate 1 L bottles of artificial seawater at the same salinity as the site water and autoclaved for 1 h. Once cooled, homogenized surface sediments from 0 to 5 cm depth were added for the control and the oil treatment cores, and the slurry was continuously stirred for 1 h while being purged with N₂ gas. Slurries were then amended with Na¹⁵NO₃ to a final concentration of 50 μM. The contents of the slurry were then dispensed into 12 mL Exetainers® and incubated at in situ temperature. Triplicate samples for each treatment were preserved with 250 μL of 50% w/v ZnCl₂ over six time points over a 48-h period, analyzed on the MIMS, with anammox rates calculated from the equations of Thamdrup and Dalsgaard [26]. 2.10 Statistical analysis Two-way ANOVA was used to test the seasonal and treatment effects across the study sites for denitrification and nutrient fluxes, chlorophyll content, extractable nutrients, and potential denitrification and nitrogen fixation rates. ANOVA was run with R-software routine. When necessary, data were log10 transformed to meet the homoscedasticity assumption. 3 Results 3.1 Nitrogen fixation, potential denitrification, and anammox Despite higher TPH concentrations in the oil treatment (Fig. 2) as well as differing salinity, temperatures, sediment chl-α concentrations, water column and pore water nutrient concentrations (Table 1, Fig. 3), nitrogen fixation and potential denitrification did not differ between the treatments (Table 2). The contribution of anammox to N₂ production was <4% during the sampling date in both treatments (Table 2). Nitrogen fixation averaged 1.79 ± 0.44 and 3.03 ± 0.80 μmol N m⁻² h⁻¹ in June and November, respectively, and was lower than potential denitrification by orders of magnitude (average 959 ± 49 and 782 ± 45 μmol N m⁻² h⁻¹ in June and November, respectively) (Table 2). The range of variability in the water column nutrients was overshadowed by those in the sediments where sediment ammonium concentrations, for example, varied by as much as 200 nmol g⁻¹ dry sediment. 3.2 Benthic fluxes SOD and inorganic nutrient fluxes did not differ between the oil and control treatments (Table 2). However, consistent with warmer temperatures in June, SOD was 48% higher compared to rates measured in November (Table 2). Inorganic nutrient fluxes were also temporally variable, with more than two times higher sediment nitrate uptake and more than three times higher ammonium efflux in June than in November (Table 2). Sediments were a phosphorus source to the water column in June, but this pattern was reversed in November. Similar to SOD and inorganic nitrogen fluxes, denitrification in June exceeded rates in November (Table 2). Denitrification capacity increased with increasing SOD with a greater slope in June (0.085, \( r^2 = 0.43, \ p = 0.037 \)) than in November (0.016, \( r^2 = 0.44, \ p = 0.034 \)) (Fig. 4a). Denitrification capacity also increased with greater sediment nitrate uptake but with a more constrained range of variability in November compared to June (Fig. 4b) and rates did not differ between the treatments (Table 2).

For examples, chl-a inventories, which are an indicator of the abundance of microphytobenthos and are often used as a proxy for labile organic matter in the sediments, were similar to prior measurements in this region, which generally range from 20 to 150 mg m⁻² [21, 27, 28]. Sediment oxygen consumption and nutrient fluxes were within the range of fluxes measured in other temperate and tropical estuaries [27–29] in both oiled and control sediments. Sediment TPH concentrations measured in coastal Alabama in the aftermath of the Deepwater Horizon spill reached concentrations of 200 mg kg⁻¹. The oil additions to the study cores increased TPH concentrations to levels much greater than those measured in Alabama marshes affected by the DWH spill [30, 31]. Despite this increase, nitrogen fixation and denitrification were unaffected. The rates of denitrification capacity measured with the IPT were on the lower range of values measured with the same technique [32, 33] and significantly exceeded anammox. The minor contribution of anammox to N₂ production is consistent with other studies, suggesting that anammox does not appear to be a significant pathway for nitrogen loss in estuarine environments [21, 34, 35] that could be affected by oil contamination. Rates of potential denitrification, when nitrate concentrations were elevated compared to in situ pore water concentrations, increased substantially compared to rates measured with IPT. This higher rate of denitrification when nitrate is abundant, suggests the presence of an extant microbial community capable of responding to increased nitrate availability. Interestingly, the presence of oil did not affect the magnitude of the increase in denitrification in response to higher nitrate availability. This extant microbial community carrying out denitrification can greatly contribute to nitrogen removal in the sediments and potentially limit the Figure 3. Concentrations of total extractable pore water ammonium, nitrate + nitrite, and phosphate in the surficial sediments (\( n = 3 \) for each depth, average \( \pm \) standard error). availability of nitrogen to hydrocarbon degrading microorganisms, which are often nitrogen limited [36]. Gilbert et al. [37] were able to experimentally link oxygen availability and potential denitrification in coastal sediments after exposure to hydrocarbons. The authors initially measured a reduction (83%) of potential denitrification in contaminated sediments, with a gradual increase over time. The sharp decline was attributed to lower oxygen availability and the increase in denitrification with time was attributed to the bioturbating fauna that (i) increased the oxygen supply, which could enhance coupled nitrification–denitrification within the sediments at the oxic anoxic microzones; and (ii) the supply of nitrate from the water column to deeper regions within the sediments where denitrification could occur. This observation of a higher slope for denitrification capacity versus SOD in the summer compared to the fall is also indicative of a tighter coupling of nitrification-denitrification in June than in November, and furthermore suggests that oil spills at concentrations that negatively impact the nitrifiers [38] or sediment oxygen availability, which is required for nitrification, will have a larger effect in the summer than in the winter months on denitrification. In a previous investigation with sediments from a nearby marsh exposed to high hydrocarbon loads (4000 mg kg\(^{-1}\)), nitrogen fixation was enhanced [31], but interestingly, at oil additions of 500 mg kg\(^{-1}\) nitrogen fixation rates were unaffected. In mesocosm experiments, Horel et al. [31] also reported that potential denitrification rates in marsh sediments exposed to hydrocarbons were higher than controls with sediments incubated at 10 and 30°C, with the highest potential denitrification measured in sediments contaminated with highly weathered crude oil at 4000 mg kg\(^{-1}\). However, similar to results for nitrogen fixation, rates of denitrification in sediments contaminated at lower levels (500 mg kg\(^{-1}\)) and at concentrations similar to the current study were not affected. Others have also noted a threshold of contamination affecting nitrogen cycling. Schafer et al. [39] exposed sediments from the sub-Antarctic region to a range of oil concentrations (0–50–000 mg kg\(^{-1}\)), and found that while denitrification potentials were unaffected, nitrification was inhibited at hydrocarbon concentrations exceeding 190 mg kg\(^{-1}\). The impacts of oil on nitrogen cycling in marine sediments have been variable with several studies reporting declines in denitrification [7, 8], while other have shown increased denitrification [9, 10], or still no changes in rates of denitrification in oiled sediments [6]. Several of the studies that show minor effects of crude oil contamination on processes in the nitrogen cycle are from regions that have been previously exposed to crude oil. For example, Bonin et al. [7] showed that changes in potential denitrification at six sites on the Mediterranean coast following exposure to oil at a concentration of 10 g kg\(^{-1}\) of sediment varied depending on the sites. While rates of denitrification declined at five of the sites, rates remained high and invariant at the site located near a refinery that had been a chronic source of hydrocarbon contamination. Deni and Penninckx [40] also reported that nitrification was not affected by additional oil inputs in sediments collected from areas previously exposed to hydrocarbon and attributed this finding to a higher affinity for ammonium by microbes at the contaminated sites. In our study region, Horel et al. [41] measured moderately high background hydrocarbon degrader microorganisms, as well as a large temporal variability in abundances of hydroclastic microorganisms in the sediments. Horel et al. [41] suggested that these findings were consistent with prior exposure to hydrocarbons caused by accidental marine fuel from the naval traffic at this location, as well as an active microbial community that is predisposed to oil contamination. The resiliency in nitrogen cycling to further contamination at our site is, therefore, consistent with prior results that show minor changes in rates Table 2. Current remediation strategies of oiled ecosystems include application of nitrogen, or nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers to oiled sediments [12, 13]. Increasing the supply of inorganic nutrients to sediments lowers the nutrient limitation of the hydrocarbonoclastic microbial community and leads to enhanced rates of hydrocarbon degradation. Optimizing the concentrations of pore water inorganic nutrients by application of fertilizers that result in the greatest hydrocarbon degradation, however, remains challenging [14, 42]. This data suggests that while additional input of oil at a site with a prior history of contamination does not lead to increased denitrification; however, denitrification increases substantially in response to higher nitrate availability. Therefore, if the remediation of a chronically oiled site relies on the application of fertilizers, monitoring pore water nitrate availability will be necessary to ensure that concentrations are maintained at levels that are adequate for optimal hydrocarbon degradation.
