Epiphytic Nitrogen Fixation Associated With Standing Dead Shoots of Smooth Cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora CAROLYN A. CURRIN1 National Marine Fisheries Service National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Beaufort Laboratory 101 Pivers Island Road Beaufort, North Carolina 28516 HANS W. PAERL University of North Carolina Institute of Marine Sciences Morehead City, North Carolina 28516 ABSTRACT: N_2 fixation associated with the epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora shoots was examined in both a natural and transplanted salt marsh in North Carolina. Acetylene reduction (AR) assays were conducted over a 24-mo period to estimate N_2 fixation rates on standing dead stems and leaves. In the natural salt marsh, mean AR rates ranged from 0.5 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 14 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, while in the transplanted marsh mean AR rates ranged from 1 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 33 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}. Diel AR activity of epiphytic communities in both marshes varied seasonally. Midday incubations yielded higher AR rates than nighttime incubations in the spring, while midday incubations in late summer and fall generally yielded AR rates equal to or lower than nighttime incubations. Desiccation during low tides occasionally repressed AR activity, although AR rates quickly rebounded with wetting. AR activity was localized in the epiphytic community, rather than in the underlying Spartina stem material. Based on the measured AR rates and the density of standing dead stems, the annual input of new N to the natural salt marsh via epiphytic N_2 fixation is estimated to be 2.6 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. The estimate of annual input of new N to the transplanted marsh is 3.8 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. These estimates should be added to previous estimates of N_2 fixation in marsh sediments to estimate the total contribution of new nitrogen to salt marsh nitrogen budgets. Introduction Salt marsh primary production is often limited by the availability of fixed nitrogen (Valiela 1983). Accordingly, there have been numerous efforts to quantify the amount of new N added to salt marsh ecosystems via N_2 fixation (Valiela 1983; Capone 1985; Howarth et al. 1988). The majority of previous studies have focused on sedimentary N_2 fixation, including surface and subsurface sediments, and rhizospheric N_2 fixation associated with live Spartina alterniflora. Epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina stems and leaves has also been recorded (Green and Edmisten 1974; Hanson 1977; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Talbot et al. 1988; Newell et al. 1992). Of these studies, three provide estimates of the annual N input from epiphytic N_2 fixation, which vary by over two orders of magnitude. Two lower estimates are from Georgia and Louisiana salt marshes, where epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina leaves and stems was estimated to yield 0.47 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} and 0.66 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}, respectively (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981). In a Florida salt marsh, epiphytic N_2 fixation was estimated to yield 287 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} (Green and Edmisten 1974, but see Newell et al. 1992). The Louisiana and Georgia epiphytic communities were dominated by diatoms and eukaryotic, filamentous and coccoid algae. Cyanobacteria represented an average of 4% of the total epiphytic biovolume in Georgia (Fallon et al. 1985), and were absent from the Louisiana epiphytic community (Day et al. 1973). Two genera of N_2-fixing bacteria (Rhodospirillum and Rhodopseudomonas) were cultured from the epiphytic community examined in Florida, while cyanobacteria were only isolated from sediment samples (Green and Edmisten 1974). The epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora in North Carolina salt marshes includes cyanobacteria (Calothrix spp. and Lyngbya spp. were dominant), diatoms, green algae, and heterotrophic and photosynthetic bacteria (Currin and Paerl 1997). Results from diel experiments suggest that N_2 fixation in this community is light-dependent, and that cyanobacteria are the microorganisms primarily responsible for the observed N_2-fixing activity. On an areal basis, estimated daily N_2 fixation rates (acetylene reduction assays) on standing dead Spartina stems were as high as 50 mg N m^{-2} d^{-1} (Currin and Paerl 1997), comparable to the highest rates recorded from other salt marsh environments (Capone 1983, 1985). Environmental factors controlling epiphytic N_2 fixation have been examined utilizing standing dead leaves and stems collected from Sapelo Island, Georgia (Newell et al. 1992). In that study, N_2 fixation rates as estimated by acetylene reduction (AR) assays were lowest during the winter on leaves with low ash content (<15%), while leaves collected May–August contained a higher ash content (>40%) and exhibited AR rates that were 10 times higher than the winter AR rates. Standing dead stems and leaves demonstrated similar AR rates on an ash-free dry weight (AFDW) basis. Newly senescent leaves had very low AR rates until 4 wk after tagging, and AR rates continued to rise throughout the 12-wk period after tagging. Other investigators have also documented higher rates of AR on dead stems than on live stems (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The objectives of this research were to determine seasonal patterns in AR rates associated with standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems collected from both a mature, natural salt marsh and a transplanted salt marsh. Although results from diel experiments strongly implicated epiphytic cyanobacteria as the primary N_2-fixing microorganisms on standing dead Spartina stems (Currin and Paerl 1997), separate incubations of the epiphytic film and underlying stem were made to determine the physical location of the N_2-fixing activity. In addition, the effects of desiccation, ash content, and shoot part (stem versus leaf) on AR rates were examined. An estimate of the annual N input by the epiphytic community is made for both a mature, natural marsh and a young (<3 yr old), transplanted marsh. Materials and Methods Standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems were collected from adjacent natural and transplanted marshes in the Newport River Estuary, North Carolina. The created marsh was planted with Spartina alterniflora in June 1990 (Currin et al. 1996). Collections from the natural marsh were made from five sites in a transect extending from a short Spartina zone (one site), through tall Spartina (two sites), and ending in another short Spartina zone (two sites) in the upper intertidal. Spartina stems were also collected from five sites established in the transplanted marsh, which included tall-form and short-form Spartina zones. A survey of the marshes demonstrated that there is <0.3 m difference in tidal elevation among all of the collection sites (C. Currin unpublished data). Standing dead stems were defined as the stem portion of Spartina shoots that is yellow-brown to brown in color, may include old sheaths but not blades, and remains upright on the marsh surface. Stems were chosen either randomly, using quadrants and random numbers, or arbitrarily with no selection criteria other than that described above. On several occasions, newly senescent stems (yellow-brown color, leaves intact, height >40 cm) were distinguished from old dead stems (brown color, leaves absent, height <25 cm). For AR assays (described below), 4-cm stem sections were removed from the zone between 5 cm and 15 cm from the base of the stem. Sample collections in the adjacent natural marsh were made in April, June, and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May, and June 1993. Samples were collected from the transplanted marsh in April and October 1991; February, August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May and June 1993. Additionally, results from submerged and aerial incubations from diel experiments run in March, July, and October 1992 and May 1993 (Currin and Paerl 1997) were included in estimates of annual N_2 fixation rates. The majority of incubations were done at midday (MD), defined as the period 1100–1500 hours. Incubations designated as evening (PM) were begun at or shortly after sunset (1730–2030 hours). Incubations designated as morning (AM) were begun near sunrise (0545–0800 hours). AR assays were used to estimate N_2 fixation rates (Hardy et al. 1968). All incubations were done in air, with the exception of submerged incubations in diel experiments (see Currin and Paerl 1997). After immersion in seawater (30–35%o) for 5 s, a 4-cm stem section was placed in a clean (HCl-soaked, distilled water rinsed) glass 38-ml serum bottle sealed with a rubber stopper. Seven ml of the headspace was withdrawn with a syringe, and replaced with 7.4 ml of CaC_2-generated acetylene. Bottles were incubated upright in a running water bath at ambient temperatures, when possible. Many of the incubations were done in the field, without access to running water, and so the bath water was changed periodically to minimize temperature changes. After a 2–3 h incubation, assays were terminated by injecting 9 ml distilled water, mixing, and withdrawing 9 ml of the headspace to an evacuated 9.6-ml serum bottle. The ethylene content of the headspace was determined by injecting 0.3-ml subsamples into a Shimadzu GC 8A gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector and a Poropak T column maintained at 80°C. N2 served as the carrier gas, and ethylene concentrations were determined by comparisons to standards prepared from pure ethylene (Matheson Gas Company). Upon termination of the AR assay, stems were removed from sample bottles and stem length and diameter recorded. Acetylene reduction rates are reported on a cm^2 basis, reflecting the stem surface area. In some instances, stem dry mass and organic matter content were obtained by drying for 48 h at 95°C, followed by ashing for 8 h at 500°C. The effect of desiccation on stem AR rates was examined on four occasions in September 1992 and once in December 1992. In the first experiment, stems from both marshes were collected during low and high tide periods of two consecutive tidal cycles, and incubated without any pretreatment (i.e., no seawater submergence). In subsequent experiments, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes ca. 60 min after slack low tide. Half of the stems from each marsh were immersed in seawater prior to AR assay (standard protocol), while the other half were placed in incubation bottles without the seawater immersion pretreatment. AR incubations were otherwise as described above. The potential locus of standing dead stem N2 fixation was determined in June 1991 and December 1992 by dissecting the epiphytic film away from the stem, and assaying both portions for AR. In June, 10 stems were collected from the natural marsh, and five stems were divided into epiphytic film and underlying stem portions. Dissection was done using a scalpel, and some fibrous Spartina material was retained in the epiphytic film. The remaining five stems were incubated intact. In December, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes and were treated as in June. Leaf blades attached to standing dead stems were assayed for AR on four occasions. The first or second leaf closest to the stem base was collected from the transplanted marsh in February, May, November, and December. Similar collections were made in the natural marsh in May and November. Leaves were immersed for 5 s in seawater prior to AR assay and treated as described above for stem incubations. The density of standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems was measured twice in the course of this study. On each occasion, 0.0625-m^2 quadrats were located randomly adjacent to the transects normally sampled for stem collections. The number of standing dead stems was measured in 10 replicate quadrats in each marsh. Statistical analysis was conducted with SAS software (SAS Institute Co., Cary North Carolina). One-way analysis of variance was used to determine significance of effects when class variables had three or more levels, and Tukey's test was used to determine the significance of differences between selected treatment means. Pairwise comparisons were done with t-tests. Data were log-transformed when necessary (fmax test), and significance was determined at p < 0.05. Results AR Rates in Natural and Transplanted Marshes There was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) between newly senescent and old standing stems in either marsh at any sampling time (t-test, p > 0.05). Therefore, data from senescent and old stems are combined in subsequent analyses. Leaves collected from standing dead stems in the natural and transplanted marshes had AR rates similar to stems, both on an areal (cm^2) and ash-free dry weight basis (p > 0.05). The only exception to this occurred in May 1993 when transplanted marsh stems had AR rates (4.26 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) which were significantly higher than AR rates on leaves (1.31 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, t-test, p < 0.01). On an ash-free dry weight basis, however, standing dead stem and leaf AR rates were not significantly different at any sampling time. The average AR activity on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems incubated at midday ranged from <1 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} in the natural marsh during November and December to 17 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} on stems collected from the transplanted marsh in July (Table 1; Fig. 1). Midday AR rates were significantly higher than morning or evening AR rates in December and May in the transplanted marsh and in March in the natural marsh. However, in the period July to October, midday AR incubations were equal to or significantly lower than morning or evening incubations (Fig. 1). On most sampling days, AR rates associated with standing dead stems from the natural marsh were equal to or lower than rates associated with stems from the transplanted marsh. The most distinct break in this pattern occurred in April 1991, when AR rates on stems from the natural marsh were significantly higher than those from the transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p < 0.05). This occurred on the first sampling date, after only one growing season, and was the only occasion when well-developed epiphytic films were not observed in the transplanted marsh. TABLE 1. Data from dates on which both natural and transplanted marshes were sampled were used to determine whether marsh type had a significant effect on AR rates (April and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; January, March, and May 1993). The mean AR rates of each marsh type on the selected dates were compared using one-way analysis of variance. This reduced the degrees of freedom but avoided invalid assumptions due to an unbalanced dataset. This conservative approach does not reject the null hypothesis (p = 0.067). As noted above, April 1991 differed from all other sampling dates in that, after only one growing season, no epiphytic films were observed on transplanted marsh stems. Excluding this point from the analysis results in a significant difference in epiphytic AR rates between the natural and transplanted marsh (p = 0.013, 25 d.f.). There also appears to be a temporal pattern in the difference in AR rates between the two marshes. Mean AR rates are most similar from December to June. Mean AR rates are most dissimilar from July to November, when standing dead stems in the transplanted marsh may exhibit AR rates 2–5 times higher than natural marsh stems. DESICCATION EFFECTS In September, exposed stems collected at an early morning low tide, and incubated aerially without prior wetting, exhibited measurable AR rates that were comparable to rates measured on submerged stems collected at the next high tide and incubated aerially (Fig. 2). However, exposed stems collected during the afternoon low tide were visibly more desiccated than the early morning exposed stems, and did not exhibit measurable AR activity. Stems collected at the next high tide had completely recovered AR activity (Fig. 2). Measurable AR activity was detected on exposed, unwetted stems collected from both marshes on four other dates (Fig. 3a,b). In the natural marsh, AR rates associated with exposed, unwetted stems were not significantly different from exposed, wetted stems on any occasion (t-test, p > 0.05). Exposed stems from the transplanted marsh which were wetted prior to incubation always had higher AR rates than unwetted stems, although the differences were significant (p < 0.05) on only two occasions (September 16 and December 9; Fig. 4b). Variability in AR rates was particularly high in these experiments, with the average coefficient of variation equal to 70%. CHARACTERISTICS OF STANDING DEAD MATERIAL The contribution of the epiphytic film to standing dead stem N2 fixation was evaluated in June and December. In June, there was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 4-cm section−1 h−1) between intact stems and epiphytic films removed from the stem (ANOVA, p > 0.05) (Fig. 4). However, stems from which the epiphytic film had been removed had significantly lower AR rates (p < 0.05). In December, similar results were obtained, although the differences were only significant for samples from the transplanted marsh (Fig. 4). Organic matter (OM) content of standing dead stems from the natural marsh averaged 66.5%, while transplanted stems averaged 70.5% OM. The OM content of leaves attached to standing dead Fig. 1. There was no difference in OM content between natural and transplanted leaves. No significant relationships were observed between ash content and standing dead stem AR rates at any sampling time in either the natural or transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p > 0.05), nor was there a significant relationship when all the data were combined. However, when all leaf data were combined, a small but statistically significant positive relationship between ash content and AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) emerged (Fig. 5, p = 0.01, r^2 = 0.2221). In October 1991, the ash content of the epiphytic film was determined separately from that of the underlying stem. The mean ash content of epiphytic films (36.6% ash) was significantly higher than that of the underlying stems (10.1% ash, t-test, p < 0.05). However, there was no significant relationship between the ash content of epiphytic film and AR rates (nmol C2H4 g AFDW^{-1} h^{-1}, ANOVA, p > 0.05). The average number of standing dead stems in the natural marsh was 264 stems m^{-2}, while in the transplanted marsh, average standing dead stem density was 135 stems m^{-2} (Table 2). Discussion Barring physical perturbation, Spartina alterniflora plants undergo a period of aerial senescence and decomposition after the growing season. In ice-free marshes, standing dead stems may persist for a year or more after senescence, while in more northern latitudes the aerial senescent-decomposition period may be shortened if ice cover pushes stems to the sediment surface. Several previous investigations have demonstrated that standing dead Spartina shoots support greater epiphytic N2 fixation than live shoots (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The only critical examination of the relationship between plant senescence and epiphytic N2 fixation was a study by Newell et al. (1992), in which epiphytic N2 fixation rates associated with leaves became detectable 2 wk after senescence, and continued to increase over a 12-wk period. In our study, newly senescent stems, which still retained their upper leaves, did not have significantly different AR rates than older standing dead stems. These observations suggest that not only does epiphytic colonization begin shortly before or just after plant senescence, but that epiphytic N2 fixation rates do not decrease as shoot decomposition progresses. Perhaps only the exterior portion of the older, thicker film supports active N₂ fixation. This is analogous to laminated microbial mats, in which microorganisms are buried by subsequent communities, reducing their activity by limiting light and organic matter supplies (Stal and Caumette 1994). On an areal basis, rates of N₂ fixation by the epiphytic microbial community on standing dead Spartina stems in this study ranged from 1 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ to 30 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ (Table 1). Utilizing a 3:1 conversion for ethylene:N₂ reduction (Currin 1994), this results in an estimated 0.4–14 mg N m⁻² h⁻¹. These estimates are comparable to published values of N₂ fixation in salt marsh surface sediments (Jones 1974; Hanson 1977; Carpenter et al. 1978; Patriquin and Denike 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Currin et al. 1996). Our finding of higher N₂ fixation rates associated with the epiphytic community in the transplanted marsh than the natural marsh is consistent with previous results demonstrating higher rates of N₂ fixation in transplanted marsh sediments than natural marsh sediments (Currin et al. 1996). The annual N input from epiphytic N₂ fixation can be estimated utilizing the monthly AR rates in Table 1 and the following assumptions: molar ratio of C₂H₄:N₂ fixed is 3:1 (Currin 1994), midday rates represent the average AR rate for the entire daylight period, and evening rates represent the average AR rate for the entire dark period. For the months in which we have no data for nighttime fixation, we assumed that from December to May nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at half the daytime rate, and that in the period July–November nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at a rate equal to the daytime rate (Fig. 1). This last assumption incorporates observations from diel experiments in which nighttime submerged AR incubations yielded lower AR rates than nighttime aerial incuba- Fig. 3. Thus, although July–November nighttime rates sometimes exceed daytime rates in aerial incubations, that difference may not exist when high tides occur at night. Given these assumptions, the estimated annual N input by the N2-fixing epiphytic community in the transplanted marsh represents 6.3 g N m−2 stem surface yr−1. In the natural marsh, the estimated annual N input is 2.5 g N m−2 stem surface yr−1. These community N2 fixation rates are comparable to annual N inputs from intertidal benthic cyanobacterial mats (Capone 1983). The areal extent of the epiphytic film on standing dead stems varies considerably from stem to stem, but usually occurs on most of the lower 20 cm of the stem and on any leaves attached to that part of the stem. Assuming 20 cm of stem with 0.5 cm diameter, plus an additional 5 cm length of leaf, the average epiphyte coverage per standing dead stem is 39 cm2. Further, assuming standing dead stem densities of 150 stems m−2 in the transplanted marsh and 265 stems m−2 in the adjacent natural marsh, estimated N2 fixation by the epiphytic film on stems would be 3.8 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the transplanted marsh and 2.6 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the natural marsh. These annual estimates are 5–10 times higher than estimates of annual epiphytic N2 fixation in Louisiana and Georgia salt marshes (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981) but are almost two orders of magnitude lower than estimates from a Florida salt marsh (Green and Edmisten 1974). The latter is probably an overestimate as it exceeds that reported from any other marine or agricultural ecosystem (see Newell et al. 1992). However, most rhizospheric AR assays exhibit a considerable lag time before enzyme activity is measurable (several hours to days), and the above estimates have been criticized as probably being overestimates by as much as an order of magnitude (Howarth et al. 1988). The AR assays conducted in this study to estimate N\(_2\) fixation associated with standing dead Spartina stems lasted 2–3 h and did not display a lag period; nor did those reported by Newell et al. (1992). Seasonal shifts in the N\(_2\)-fixing community, resulting in changes in diel patterns of N\(_2\) fixation, have been reported from several benthic marine habitats (Paerl et al. 1994; Pinckney et al. 1995). The seasonal patterns in day-night N\(_2\) fixation that we observed are similar to those that occur on surface sediments on North Carolina intertidal flats (Pinckney et al. 1995). On standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems, higher midday AR rates in the spring are attributed to the N\(_2\)-fixing activity of heterocystous cyanobacteria, primarily Calothrix spp. (Curran and Paerl 1997). It appears that a spring bloom of heterocystous or coccoid cyanobacteria occurs in both marshes, as epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates are similar in early spring incubations. However, during late summer and early fall, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation in the transplanted marsh is greater than in the natural marsh. One possible explanation is that light becomes limiting in the natural marsh as the Spartina canopy develops. Stem density and biomass was greater in the natural marsh than in the transplanted marsh during this study (Table 2; S. Broome unpublished data), and stem biomass is directly related to canopy light attenuation (Morris 1989). The potential inhibitory effect of desiccation on AR rates was not accounted for in the annual estimates of N\(_2\) fixation reported here. However, the data suggest that exposure, or emergence, inhibits AR rates only during extreme low tides, and that periods of emergence during low tide periods do not necessarily correspond with decreased epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates (Figs. 2 and 3). When desiccation does cause a decrease in AR activity, the activity is restored immediately after resubmergence (Fig. 2). Other studies of intertidal microalgal communities have also demonstrated that these microorganisms are resilient following desiccation. Jones (1980) examined the effect of desiccation on photosynthetic CO\(_2\) fixation by the epiphytic community on standing dead stems in a Georgia salt marsh, and determined that even severely desiccated stems recover CO\(_2\) fixation immediately after wetting. Similarly, Jones (1974) and Pulich and Rabalais (1987) found that desiccated intertidal ben- thic cyanobacteria responded almost immediately to the addition of water by resuming N\(_2\) fixation rates comparable to submerged specimens. Apart from any inhibitory effects on epiphytic growth or activity, desiccation probably plays an important role in maintaining the species composition of the epiphytic community on standing dead stems. Calothrix, the dominant cyanobacterial genus in most sampling periods (Curran and Paerl 1997), is often restricted to the upper intertidal in marine environments (Hanson 1977; Javor and Castenholz 1981; Stal et al. 1994), and was never identified in the surface sediment of the marshes we sampled (Curran et al. 1996). In a review of aquatic N\(_2\) fixation, Howarth et al. (1988) suggested that this process was unimportant to salt marsh N budgets, because the amount of N fixed in salt marsh sediments was less than 10% of the total N input. The calculated annual contribution of new N fixed by epiphytic communities on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems in this study (2–4 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)) represents an amount almost equal to the total marsh sedimentary N\(_2\) fixation calculated by Howarth et al. (1988) (2–8 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)), in effect nearly doubling the estimated amount of annual marsh N\(_2\) fixation. In contrast to N fixed in the rhizosphere, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation is probably of little direct benefit to Spartina. However, its potential importance to grazers and salt marsh nutrient cycles is not trivial. The epiphytic community provides a source of new nitrogen which may be utilized by marsh consumers, or exported from the marsh as dissolved or particulate organic N. In addition, nitrogen fixed by epiphytic microorganisms may become incorporated into standing dead Spartina tissue via fungal or bacterial activity, increasing the N content of aboveground Spartina detritus. White and Howes (1994) calculated that over half of the N in standing dead Spartina tissue is derived from external sources, and suggested that N\(_2\)-fixing microorganisms may contribute new N to detrital Spartina. Similarly, the \(^{15}\)N values of standing dead Spartina tissue collected from the North Carolina marshes examined in this study indicated that microbial N\(_2\) fixation supplied N which was incorporated into detrital Spartina tissue (Curran et al. 1995). Epiphytic microalgae and the associated microbial community may be an important, although often overlooked, food resource for marsh consumers. Multiple stable isotope analysis demonstrated the role of N\(_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria in the food webs of several marsh consumers (Littorina, Uca, Fundulus spp.) in North Carolina marshes (Curran et al. 1995). Other studies have described a diverse meiofaunal community associated with algal epiphytes on Spartina stems, and the utilization of stem-dwelling meiofauna by shrimp and fish (Rutledge and Fleeger 1993; Walters et al. 1996; Gregg and Fleeger in review). Results from this study and from Newell et al. (1992) demonstrate that active N_2-fixing communities develop on standing dead Spartina stems and leaves, and that these communities can differ markedly in species composition. Further research is necessary to determine how widespread these epiphytic communities are in North American Spartina marshes, and to delineate environmental controls on their development, community composition, and N_2-fixing potential. Epiphytic Nitrogen Fixation Associated With Standing Dead Shoots of Smooth Cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora CAROLYN A. CURRIN1 National Marine Fisheries Service National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Beaufort Laboratory 101 Pivers Island Road Beaufort, North Carolina 28516 HANS W. PAERL University of North Carolina Institute of Marine Sciences Morehead City, North Carolina 28516 ABSTRACT: N_2 fixation associated with the epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora shoots was examined in both a natural and transplanted salt marsh in North Carolina. Acetylene reduction (AR) assays were conducted over a 24-mo period to estimate N_2 fixation rates on standing dead stems and leaves. In the natural salt marsh, mean AR rates ranged from 0.5 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 14 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, while in the transplanted marsh mean AR rates ranged from 1 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 33 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}. Diel AR activity of epiphytic communities in both marshes varied seasonally. Midday incubations yielded higher AR rates than nighttime incubations in the spring, while midday incubations in late summer and fall generally yielded AR rates equal to or lower than nighttime incubations. Desiccation during low tides occasionally repressed AR activity, although AR rates quickly rebounded with wetting. AR activity was localized in the epiphytic community, rather than in the underlying Spartina stem material. Based on the measured AR rates and the density of standing dead stems, the annual input of new N to the natural salt marsh via epiphytic N_2 fixation is estimated to be 2.6 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. The estimate of annual input of new N to the transplanted marsh is 3.8 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. These estimates should be added to previous estimates of N_2 fixation in marsh sediments to estimate the total contribution of new nitrogen to salt marsh nitrogen budgets. Introduction Salt marsh primary production is often limited by the availability of fixed nitrogen (Valiela 1983). Accordingly, there have been numerous efforts to quantify the amount of new N added to salt marsh ecosystems via N_2 fixation (Valiela 1983; Capone 1985; Howarth et al. 1988). The majority of previous studies have focused on sedimentary N_2 fixation, including surface and subsurface sediments, and rhizospheric N_2 fixation associated with live Spartina alterniflora. Epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina stems and leaves has also been recorded (Green and Edmisten 1974; Hanson 1977; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Talbot et al. 1988; Newell et al. 1992). Of these studies, three provide estimates of the annual N input from epiphytic N_2 fixation, which vary by over two orders of magnitude. Two lower estimates are from Georgia and Louisiana salt marshes, where epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina leaves and stems was estimated to yield 0.47 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} and 0.66 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}, respectively (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981). In a Florida salt marsh, epiphytic N_2 fixation was estimated to yield 287 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} (Green and Edmisten 1974, but see Newell et al. 1992). The Louisiana and Georgia epiphytic communities were dominated by diatoms and eukaryotic, filamentous and coccoid algae. Cyanobacteria represented an average of 4% of the total epiphytic biovolume in Georgia (Fallon et al. 1985), and were absent from the Louisiana epiphytic community (Day et al. 1973). Two genera of N_2-fixing bacteria (Rhodospirillum and Rhodopseudomonas) were cultured from the epiphytic community examined in Florida, while cyanobacteria were only isolated from sediment samples (Green and Edmisten 1974). The epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora in North Carolina salt marshes includes cyanobacteria (Calothrix spp. and Lyngbya spp. were dominant), diatoms, green algae, and heterotrophic and photosynthetic bacteria (Currin and Paerl 1997). Results from diel experiments suggest that N_2 fixation in this community is light-dependent, and that cyanobacteria are the microorganisms primarily responsible for the observed N_2-fixing activity. On an areal basis, estimated daily N_2 fixation rates (acetylene reduction assays) on standing dead Spartina stems were as high as 50 mg N m^{-2} d^{-1} (Currin and Paerl 1997), comparable to the highest rates recorded from other salt marsh environments (Capone 1983, 1985). Environmental factors controlling epiphytic N_2 fixation have been examined utilizing standing dead leaves and stems collected from Sapelo Island, Georgia (Newell et al. 1992). In that study, N_2 fixation rates as estimated by acetylene reduction (AR) assays were lowest during the winter on leaves with low ash content (<15%), while leaves collected May–August contained a higher ash content (>40%) and exhibited AR rates that were 10 times higher than the winter AR rates. Standing dead stems and leaves demonstrated similar AR rates on an ash-free dry weight (AFDW) basis. Newly senescent leaves had very low AR rates until 4 wk after tagging, and AR rates continued to rise throughout the 12-wk period after tagging. Other investigators have also documented higher rates of AR on dead stems than on live stems (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The objectives of this research were to determine seasonal patterns in AR rates associated with standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems collected from both a mature, natural salt marsh and a transplanted salt marsh. Although results from diel experiments strongly implicated epiphytic cyanobacteria as the primary N_2-fixing microorganisms on standing dead Spartina stems (Currin and Paerl 1997), separate incubations of the epiphytic film and underlying stem were made to determine the physical location of the N_2-fixing activity. In addition, the effects of desiccation, ash content, and shoot part (stem versus leaf) on AR rates were examined. An estimate of the annual N input by the epiphytic community is made for both a mature, natural marsh and a young (<3 yr old), transplanted marsh. Materials and Methods Standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems were collected from adjacent natural and transplanted marshes in the Newport River Estuary, North Carolina. The created marsh was planted with Spartina alterniflora in June 1990 (Currin et al. 1996). Collections from the natural marsh were made from five sites in a transect extending from a short Spartina zone (one site), through tall Spartina (two sites), and ending in another short Spartina zone (two sites) in the upper intertidal. Spartina stems were also collected from five sites established in the transplanted marsh, which included tall-form and short-form Spartina zones. A survey of the marshes demonstrated that there is <0.3 m difference in tidal elevation among all of the collection sites (C. Currin unpublished data). Standing dead stems were defined as the stem portion of Spartina shoots that is yellow-brown to brown in color, may include old sheaths but not blades, and remains upright on the marsh surface. Stems were chosen either randomly, using quadrants and random numbers, or arbitrarily with no selection criteria other than that described above. On several occasions, newly senescent stems (yellow-brown color, leaves intact, height >40 cm) were distinguished from old dead stems (brown color, leaves absent, height <25 cm). For AR assays (described below), 4-cm stem sections were removed from the zone between 5 cm and 15 cm from the base of the stem. Sample collections in the adjacent natural marsh were made in April, June, and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May, and June 1993. Samples were collected from the transplanted marsh in April and October 1991; February, August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May and June 1993. Additionally, results from submerged and aerial incubations from diel experiments run in March, July, and October 1992 and May 1993 (Currin and Paerl 1997) were included in estimates of annual N_2 fixation rates. The majority of incubations were done at midday (MD), defined as the period 1100–1500 hours. Incubations designated as evening (PM) were begun at or shortly after sunset (1730–2030 hours). Incubations designated as morning (AM) were begun near sunrise (0545–0800 hours). AR assays were used to estimate N_2 fixation rates (Hardy et al. 1968). All incubations were done in air, with the exception of submerged incubations in diel experiments (see Currin and Paerl 1997). After immersion in seawater (30–35%o) for 5 s, a 4-cm stem section was placed in a clean (HCl-soaked, distilled water rinsed) glass 38-ml serum bottle sealed with a rubber stopper. Seven ml of the headspace was withdrawn with a syringe, and replaced with 7.4 ml of CaC_2-generated acetylene. Bottles were incubated upright in a running water bath at ambient temperatures, when possible. Many of the incubations were done in the field, without access to running water, and so the bath water was changed periodically to minimize temperature changes. After a 2–3 h incubation, assays were terminated by injecting 9 ml distilled water, mixing, and withdrawing 9 ml of the headspace to an evacuated 9.6-ml serum bottle. The ethylene content of the headspace was determined by injecting 0.3-ml subsamples into a Shimadzu GC 8A gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector and a Poropak T column maintained at 80°C. N2 served as the carrier gas, and ethylene concentrations were determined by comparisons to standards prepared from pure ethylene (Matheson Gas Company). Upon termination of the AR assay, stems were removed from sample bottles and stem length and diameter recorded. Acetylene reduction rates are reported on a cm^2 basis, reflecting the stem surface area. In some instances, stem dry mass and organic matter content were obtained by drying for 48 h at 95°C, followed by ashing for 8 h at 500°C. The effect of desiccation on stem AR rates was examined on four occasions in September 1992 and once in December 1992. In the first experiment, stems from both marshes were collected during low and high tide periods of two consecutive tidal cycles, and incubated without any pretreatment (i.e., no seawater submergence). In subsequent experiments, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes ca. 60 min after slack low tide. Half of the stems from each marsh were immersed in seawater prior to AR assay (standard protocol), while the other half were placed in incubation bottles without the seawater immersion pretreatment. AR incubations were otherwise as described above. The potential locus of standing dead stem N2 fixation was determined in June 1991 and December 1992 by dissecting the epiphytic film away from the stem, and assaying both portions for AR. In June, 10 stems were collected from the natural marsh, and five stems were divided into epiphytic film and underlying stem portions. Dissection was done using a scalpel, and some fibrous Spartina material was retained in the epiphytic film. The remaining five stems were incubated intact. In December, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes and were treated as in June. Leaf blades attached to standing dead stems were assayed for AR on four occasions. The first or second leaf closest to the stem base was collected from the transplanted marsh in February, May, November, and December. Similar collections were made in the natural marsh in May and November. Leaves were immersed for 5 s in seawater prior to AR assay and treated as described above for stem incubations. The density of standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems was measured twice in the course of this study. On each occasion, 0.0625-m^2 quadrats were located randomly adjacent to the transects normally sampled for stem collections. The number of standing dead stems was measured in 10 replicate quadrats in each marsh. Statistical analysis was conducted with SAS software (SAS Institute Co., Cary North Carolina). One-way analysis of variance was used to determine significance of effects when class variables had three or more levels, and Tukey's test was used to determine the significance of differences between selected treatment means. Pairwise comparisons were done with t-tests. Data were log-transformed when necessary (fmax test), and significance was determined at p < 0.05. Results AR Rates in Natural and Transplanted Marshes There was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) between newly senescent and old standing stems in either marsh at any sampling time (t-test, p > 0.05). Therefore, data from senescent and old stems are combined in subsequent analyses. Leaves collected from standing dead stems in the natural and transplanted marshes had AR rates similar to stems, both on an areal (cm^2) and ash-free dry weight basis (p > 0.05). The only exception to this occurred in May 1993 when transplanted marsh stems had AR rates (4.26 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) which were significantly higher than AR rates on leaves (1.31 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, t-test, p < 0.01). On an ash-free dry weight basis, however, standing dead stem and leaf AR rates were not significantly different at any sampling time. The average AR activity on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems incubated at midday ranged from <1 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} in the natural marsh during November and December to 17 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} on stems collected from the transplanted marsh in July (Table 1; Fig. 1). Midday AR rates were significantly higher than morning or evening AR rates in December and May in the transplanted marsh and in March in the natural marsh. However, in the period July to October, midday AR incubations were equal to or significantly lower than morning or evening incubations (Fig. 1). On most sampling days, AR rates associated with standing dead stems from the natural marsh were equal to or lower than rates associated with stems from the transplanted marsh. The most distinct break in this pattern occurred in April 1991, when AR rates on stems from the natural marsh were significantly higher than those from the transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p < 0.05). This occurred on the first sampling date, after only one growing season, and was the only occasion when well-developed epiphytic films were not observed in the transplanted marsh. TABLE 1. Data from dates on which both natural and transplanted marshes were sampled were used to determine whether marsh type had a significant effect on AR rates (April and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; January, March, and May 1993). The mean AR rates of each marsh type on the selected dates were compared using one-way analysis of variance. This reduced the degrees of freedom but avoided invalid assumptions due to an unbalanced dataset. This conservative approach does not reject the null hypothesis (p = 0.067). As noted above, April 1991 differed from all other sampling dates in that, after only one growing season, no epiphytic films were observed on transplanted marsh stems. Excluding this point from the analysis results in a significant difference in epiphytic AR rates between the natural and transplanted marsh (p = 0.013, 25 d.f.). There also appears to be a temporal pattern in the difference in AR rates between the two marshes. Mean AR rates are most similar from December to June. Mean AR rates are most dissimilar from July to November, when standing dead stems in the transplanted marsh may exhibit AR rates 2–5 times higher than natural marsh stems. DESICCATION EFFECTS In September, exposed stems collected at an early morning low tide, and incubated aerially without prior wetting, exhibited measurable AR rates that were comparable to rates measured on submerged stems collected at the next high tide and incubated aerially (Fig. 2). However, exposed stems collected during the afternoon low tide were visibly more desiccated than the early morning exposed stems, and did not exhibit measurable AR activity. Stems collected at the next high tide had completely recovered AR activity (Fig. 2). Measurable AR activity was detected on exposed, unwetted stems collected from both marshes on four other dates (Fig. 3a,b). In the natural marsh, AR rates associated with exposed, unwetted stems were not significantly different from exposed, wetted stems on any occasion (t-test, p > 0.05). Exposed stems from the transplanted marsh which were wetted prior to incubation always had higher AR rates than unwetted stems, although the differences were significant (p < 0.05) on only two occasions (September 16 and December 9; Fig. 4b). Variability in AR rates was particularly high in these experiments, with the average coefficient of variation equal to 70%. CHARACTERISTICS OF STANDING DEAD MATERIAL The contribution of the epiphytic film to standing dead stem N2 fixation was evaluated in June and December. In June, there was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 4-cm section−1 h−1) between intact stems and epiphytic films removed from the stem (ANOVA, p > 0.05) (Fig. 4). However, stems from which the epiphytic film had been removed had significantly lower AR rates (p < 0.05). In December, similar results were obtained, although the differences were only significant for samples from the transplanted marsh (Fig. 4). Organic matter (OM) content of standing dead stems from the natural marsh averaged 66.5%, while transplanted stems averaged 70.5% OM. The OM content of leaves attached to standing dead Fig. 1. Error bars represent the standard error of replicate samples. stems averaged 39.4%, which was significantly lower than stem OM content (t-test, p < 0.01). There was no difference in OM content between natural and transplanted leaves. No significant relationships were observed between ash content and standing dead stem AR rates at any sampling time in either the natural or transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p > 0.05), nor was there a significant relationship when all the data were combined. However, when all leaf data were combined, a small but statistically significant positive relationship between ash content and AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) emerged (Fig. 5, p = 0.01, r^2 = 0.2221). In October 1991, the ash content of the epiphytic film was determined separately from that of the underlying stem. The mean ash content of epiphytic films (36.6% ash) was significantly higher than that of the underlying stems (10.1% ash, t-test, p < 0.05). However, there was no significant relationship between the ash content of epiphytic film and AR rates (nmol C2H4 g AFDW^{-1} h^{-1}, ANOVA, p > 0.05). The average number of standing dead stems in the natural marsh was 264 stems m^{-2}, while in the transplanted marsh, average standing dead stem density was 135 stems m^{-2} (Table 2). Discussion Barring physical perturbation, Spartina alterniflora plants undergo a period of aerial senescence and decomposition after the growing season. In ice-free marshes, standing dead stems may persist for a year or more after senescence, while in more northern latitudes the aerial senescent-decomposition period may be shortened if ice cover pushes stems to the sediment surface. Several previous investigations have demonstrated that standing dead Spartina shoots support greater epiphytic N2 fixation than live shoots (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The only critical examination of the relationship between plant senescence and epiphytic N2 fixation was a study by Newell et al. (1992), in which epiphytic N2 fixation rates associated with leaves became detectable 2 wk after senescence, and continued to increase over a 12-wk period. In our study, newly senescent stems, which still retained their upper leaves, did not have significantly different AR rates than older standing dead stems. These observations suggest that not only does epiphytic colonization begin shortly before or just after plant senescence, but that epiphytic N2 fixation rates do not decrease as shoot decomposition progresses. Although older, more decayed stems frequently ex- Fig. 2. Effect of tidal stage on average acetylene reduction (AR) rates associated with standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems in September. Stems were collected over two tidal cycles from a) natural and b) transplanted salt marshes in North Carolina. Solid bars represent the mean AR rate of submerged stems collected at high tide. Lined bars represent the mean AR rate of exposed stems collected at low tide. Error bars represent the standard error of five replicate samples. Absence of bars indicates AR rates below detection limits. hibited a thicker epiphytic layer (3–5 mm), these stems did not have higher N₂ fixation rates on a surface area basis. Perhaps only the exterior portion of the older, thicker film supports active N₂ fixation. This is analogous to laminated microbial mats, in which microorganisms are buried by subsequent communities, reducing their activity by limiting light and organic matter supplies (Stal and Caumette 1994). On an areal basis, rates of N₂ fixation by the epiphytic microbial community on standing dead Spartina stems in this study ranged from 1 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ to 30 nmol C₂H₄ cm⁻² h⁻¹ (Table 1). Utilizing a 3:1 conversion for ethylene:N₂ reduction (Currin 1994), this results in an estimated 0.4–14 mg N m⁻² h⁻¹. These estimates are comparable to published values of N₂ fixation in salt marsh surface sediments (Jones 1974; Hanson 1977; Carpenter et al. 1978; Patriquin and Denike 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Currin et al. 1996). Our finding of higher N₂ fixation rates associated with the epiphytic community in the transplanted marsh than the natural marsh is consistent with previous results demonstrating higher rates of N₂ fixation in transplanted marsh sediments than natural marsh sediments (Currin et al. 1996). The annual N input from epiphytic N₂ fixation can be estimated utilizing the monthly AR rates in Table 1 and the following assumptions: molar ratio of C₂H₄:N₂ fixed is 3:1 (Currin 1994), midday rates represent the average AR rate for the entire daylight period, and evening rates represent the average AR rate for the entire dark period. For the months in which we have no data for nighttime fixation, we assumed that from December to May nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at half the daytime rate, and that in the period July–November nighttime N₂ fixation proceeded at a rate equal to the daytime rate (Fig. 1). This last assumption incorporates observations from diel experiments in which nighttime submerged AR incubations yielded lower AR rates than nighttime aerial incuba- Fig. 3. All collections were made during low tide periods when stems were exposed to the atmosphere. Solid bars represent the mean AR rate of exposed stems wetted with seawater prior to acetylene incubation. Lined bars represent the mean AR rate of nonwetted, exposed stems. Error bars represent the standard error of 5–10 replicate samples. Fig. 4. Hatched bars represent epiphytic film dissected from stems. Lined bars represent Spartina stems from which the epiphytic film had been removed. Solid bars represent intact standing dead stems. tions (Currin and Paerl 1997). Thus, although July–November nighttime rates sometimes exceed daytime rates in aerial incubations, that difference may not exist when high tides occur at night. Given these assumptions, the estimated annual N input by the N2-fixing epiphytic community in the transplanted marsh represents 6.3 g N m−2 stem surface yr−1. In the natural marsh, the estimated annual N input is 2.5 g N m−2 stem surface yr−1. These community N2 fixation rates are comparable to annual N inputs from intertidal benthic cyanobacterial mats (Capone 1983). The areal extent of the epiphytic film on standing dead stems varies considerably from stem to stem, but usually occurs on most of the lower 20 cm of the stem and on any leaves attached to that part of the stem. Assuming 20 cm of stem with 0.5 cm diameter, plus an additional 5 cm length of leaf, the average epiphyte coverage per standing dead stem is 39 cm2. Further, assuming standing dead stem densities of 150 stems m−2 in the transplanted marsh and 265 stems m−2 in the adjacent natural marsh, estimated N2 fixation by the epiphytic film on stems would be 3.8 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the transplanted marsh and 2.6 g N m−2 marsh surface yr−1 in the natural marsh. These annual estimates are 5–10 times higher than estimates of annual epiphytic N2 fixation in Louisiana and Georgia salt marshes (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981) but are almost two orders of magnitude lower than estimates from a Florida salt marsh (Green and Edmisten 1974). The latter is probably an overestimate as it exceeds that reported from any other marine or agricultural ecosystem (see Newell et al. 1992). However, most rhizospheric AR assays exhibit a considerable lag time before enzyme activity is measurable (several hours to days), and the above estimates have been criticized as probably being overestimates by as much as an order of magnitude (Howarth et al. 1988). The AR assays conducted in this study to estimate N\(_2\) fixation associated with standing dead Spartina stems lasted 2–3 h and did not display a lag period; nor did those reported by Newell et al. (1992). Seasonal shifts in the N\(_2\)-fixing community, resulting in changes in diel patterns of N\(_2\) fixation, have been reported from several benthic marine habitats (Paerl et al. 1994; Pinckney et al. 1995). The seasonal patterns in day-night N\(_2\) fixation that we observed are similar to those that occur on surface sediments on North Carolina intertidal flats (Pinckney et al. 1995). On standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems, higher midday AR rates in the spring are attributed to the N\(_2\)-fixing activity of heterocystous cyanobacteria, primarily Calothrix spp. (Curran and Paerl 1997). It appears that a spring bloom of heterocystous or coccoid cyanobacteria occurs in both marshes, as epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates are similar in early spring incubations. However, during late summer and early fall, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation in the transplanted marsh is greater than in the natural marsh. One possible explanation is that light becomes limiting in the natural marsh as the Spartina canopy develops. Stem density and biomass was greater in the natural marsh than in the transplanted marsh during this study (Table 2; S. Broome unpublished data), and stem biomass is directly related to canopy light attenuation (Morris 1989). The potential inhibitory effect of desiccation on AR rates was not accounted for in the annual estimates of N\(_2\) fixation reported here. However, the data suggest that exposure, or emergence, inhibits AR rates only during extreme low tides, and that periods of emergence during low tide periods do not necessarily correspond with decreased epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation rates (Figs. 2 and 3). When desiccation does cause a decrease in AR activity, the activity is restored immediately after resubmergence (Fig. 2). Other studies of intertidal microalgal communities have also demonstrated that these microorganisms are resilient following desiccation. Jones (1980) examined the effect of desiccation on photosynthetic CO\(_2\) fixation by the epiphytic community on standing dead stems in a Georgia salt marsh, and determined that even severely desiccated stems recover CO\(_2\) fixation immediately after wetting. Similarly, Jones (1974) and Pulich and Rabalais (1987) found that desiccated intertidal ben- thic cyanobacteria responded almost immediately to the addition of water by resuming N\(_2\) fixation rates comparable to submerged specimens. Apart from any inhibitory effects on epiphytic growth or activity, desiccation probably plays an important role in maintaining the species composition of the epiphytic community on standing dead stems. Calothrix, the dominant cyanobacterial genus in most sampling periods (Curran and Paerl 1997), is often restricted to the upper intertidal in marine environments (Hanson 1977; Javor and Castenholz 1981; Stal et al. 1994), and was never identified in the surface sediment of the marshes we sampled (Curran et al. 1996). In a review of aquatic N\(_2\) fixation, Howarth et al. (1988) suggested that this process was unimportant to salt marsh N budgets, because the amount of N fixed in salt marsh sediments was less than 10% of the total N input. The calculated annual contribution of new N fixed by epiphytic communities on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems in this study (2–4 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)) represents an amount almost equal to the total marsh sedimentary N\(_2\) fixation calculated by Howarth et al. (1988) (2–8 g N m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\)), in effect nearly doubling the estimated amount of annual marsh N\(_2\) fixation. In contrast to N fixed in the rhizosphere, epiphytic N\(_2\) fixation is probably of little direct benefit to Spartina. However, its potential importance to grazers and salt marsh nutrient cycles is not trivial. The epiphytic community provides a source of new nitrogen which may be utilized by marsh consumers, or exported from the marsh as dissolved or particulate organic N. In addition, nitrogen fixed by epiphytic microorganisms may become incorporated into standing dead Spartina tissue via fungal or bacterial activity, increasing the N content of aboveground Spartina detritus. White and Howes (1994) calculated that over half of the N in standing dead Spartina tissue is derived from external sources, and suggested that N\(_2\)-fixing microorganisms may contribute new N to detrital Spartina. Similarly, the \(^{15}\)N values of standing dead Spartina tissue collected from the North Carolina marshes examined in this study indicated that microbial N\(_2\) fixation supplied N which was incorporated into detrital Spartina tissue (Curran et al. 1995). Epiphytic microalgae and the associated microbial community may be an important, although often overlooked, food resource for marsh consumers. Multiple stable isotope analysis demonstrated the role of N\(_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria in the food webs of several marsh consumers (Littorina, Uca, Fundulus spp.) in North Carolina marshes (Curran et al. 1995). Other studies have described a diverse meiofaunal community associated with algal epiphytes on Spartina stems, and the utilization of stem-dwelling meiofauna by shrimp and fish (Rutledge and Fleeger 1993; Walters et al. 1996; Gregg and Fleeger in review). Results from this study and from Newell et al. (1992) demonstrate that active N_2-fixing communities develop on standing dead Spartina stems and leaves, and that these communities can differ markedly in species composition. Further research is necessary to determine how widespread these epiphytic communities are in North American Spartina marshes, and to delineate environmental controls on their development, community composition, and N_2-fixing potential. Effects of Lake Size on Nutrient Availability in the Mixed Layer during Summer Stratification E.J. Fee, R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Central and Arctic Region, Freshwater Institute, 501 University Crescent, Winnipeg, MB R3T 2N6, Canada Fee, E.J., R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson. 1994. Effects of lake size on nutrient availability in the mixed layer during summer stratification. Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 51: 2756–2768. Fluxes to the summer mixed layer of N, Si, and P were estimated in a size series of northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes. Increasing turbulence caused upward fluxes through the thermocline to increase with lake size for nutrients that increased in concentration below the thermocline (soluble reactive Si, total inorganic N, and NO_3^−; but not total N or any form of P). Precipitation and terrestrial runoff were equally important sources of N and P in all but very small lakes (<100 ha), where precipitation supplied much more than runoff. Runoff was the only important source of Si, except in very large lakes (> 100 000 ha) where mixing through the thermocline was important. N_2-fixation was unimportant except in intermediate-sized lakes (700–2000 ha). Si fluxes nearly equaled phytoplankton requirements, but N and P were below requirements, and recycling within the mixed layer must be the most important source of these nutrients. N and P deficits increased progressively with lake size, implying that the efficiency of nutrient recycling increased with lake size; mixed layers in large lakes are more turbulent and thicker than in small lakes and these processes increase the probability of nutrient regeneration within the mixed layer. Les flux de N, de Si et de P vers la couche de mélange estivale ont été estimés dans des lacs de différentes tailles du Bouclier canadien dans le nord-ouest de l’Ontario. Une turbulence accrue donne lieu à une augmentation proportionnelle à la taille des lacs des flux ascendants dans la thermocline dans le cas des éléments nutritifs dont la concentration augmente sous la thermocline (Si réactif soluble, N inorganique total, et NO_3^−); mais non le N total et aucune forme de P). Les précipitations et le ruissellement de surface étaient des sources de N et de P d’égale importance dans tous les lacs, sauf dans les très petits (<100 ha), où la contribution des précipitations étaient beaucoup plus importante à cet égard. Le ruissellement était la seule source importante de Si, sauf sans les très grands lacs (> 100 000 ha), où le mélange dans la thermocline apportait une contribution importante. La fixation du N_2 n’était pas importante sauf dans les lacs de taille intermédiaire (700–2 000 ha). Les flux de Si satisfaisaient presque les besoins du phytoplancton alors que ceux de N et de P étaient insuffisants, le recyclage dans la couche de mélange assurant probablement le principal apport de ces deux derniers éléments. Les carences en N et en P allaient en s’accroissant avec la taille des lacs, ce qui implique que la contribution du recyclage des éléments nutritifs s’accroît avec la taille des lacs; en effet, les couches de mélange des grands lacs sont plus turbulentes et plus épaisses que celles des petits lacs, ce qui accroît les possibilités de régénération des éléments nutritifs dans la couche de mélange. Received September 21, 1993 Accepted July 12, 1994 (J12098) Reçu le 21 septembre 1993 Accepté le 12 juillet 1994 When Johnson and Vallentyne (1971) introduced the Experimental Lakes Area (ELA) program in the scientific literature, they clearly recognized that extrapolation of results obtained from the observation and manipulation of very small lakes to larger, more economically important ones was a fundamental assumption of ELA’s design. They presented several examples of how a lake’s size might affect critical limnological processes and stated that these “... must be taken into account in any extrapolation.” Yet for nearly two decades, ELA results have been extrapolated to larger lakes without any explicit consideration of such effects. The Northwest Ontario Lake Size Series (NOLSS) program (Fee and Hecky 1992) was designed to remedy this deficiency; specifically, the purpose of NOLSS is to investigate physical gradients associated with lake size and to determine their biological significance. In an initial NOLSS publication, Fee et al. (1992) reported that annual rates of phytoplankton photosynthesis (PP) per unit of lake surface area (i.e., areal PP) increased progressively with lake size simply because larger lakes were ice free for longer periods and had thicker mixed layers than small lakes. In contrast, these authors showed that annual rates of PP per unit volume of the mixed layer (volumetric PP) varied with lake size in a bell-shaped pattern, i.e., rates in the smallest and largest lakes (29 ha ELA Lake 373 and 8 × 10^6 ha Lake Superior, respectively) were low and similar, whereas midsized lakes had rates nearly an order of magnitude greater. Fee et al. (1992) hypothesized that this pattern resulted from systematic changes of turbulence and water temperature with increasing lake size. According to this hypothesis, the increasing intensity of turbulence with 1This is one in a series of papers describing work of the Freshwater Institute Science Laboratory on a lake-size series in Northwest Ontario. It is also a contribution to the series honoring the 25th anniversary of the Experimental Lakes Area. lake size (Ward 1977; Quay et al. 1980) stimulates volumetric PP by increasing nutrient availability in the mixed layer, but decreasing water temperature with increasing lake size (Fee and Hecky 1992) simultaneously depresses it; the opposite effects of these two gradients on PP results in optimum conditions for PP in midsized lakes. This paper investigates one of the basic assumptions of this hypothesis: viz., that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP by making nutrients more available within the mixed layer. It is well documented that algal growth and biomass in Canadian Shield lakes is limited by nutrients; more specifically, PP is primarily phosphorus (P) limited (Schindler 1977; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1987; Hecky et al. 1993; and especially S. Guildford and L. Hendzel, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Winnipeg, MB, unpublished data for the NOLSS lakes). Theoretically, turbulence should be positively and causally related to nutrient availability in the mixed layer because: (1) more turbulent mixed layers retain particles longer, and thus recycle nutrients more effectively and (2) turbulence is the physical process responsible for the upward transport of nutrients through the summer thermocline. The second mechanism is more conditional than the first, however, because the turbulent (mixing) flux through the thermocline is not solely a function of the intensity of turbulence. That is, the flux of a substance S through a plane at depth z is \[ \text{Flux} = K_z \frac{dS}{dz} \] where \( K_z \) is the coefficient of vertical eddy diffusion (i.e., turbulence). Hence, turbulence can result in a net upward flux to the mixed layer only if the concentration of S increases with depth in the region of the thermocline. In this paper, we examine all major nutrient fluxes to the summer mixed layer in a size series of hydrologically and morphometrically similar lakes, during the period 1986-1991. Our purpose is to compare the magnitude of the only flux that depends explicitly on lake size, the turbulence-mediated upward flux through the summer thermocline, with fluxes that are independent of lake size: precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation. We then assess the ecological importance of these fluxes by comparing them with the nutrient requirements of algae residing in the mixed layer. Study Sites Table 1 summarizes morphometric features of the study lakes and defines morphometric symbols used throughout the text. All the lakes are located on the Canadian Shield in northwestern Ontario, have water renewal times >5 yr, and are deep enough to fully stratify during the summer. Except for Lakes Nipigon and Superior, whose basins are sparsely populated, there are no permanent residents in the drainage basins of the lakes. More detailed descriptions are given by Fee and Hecky (1992) and Fee et al. (1992). Methods Unless otherwise stated, field and laboratory methods follow Fee et al. (1989) and Stainton et al. (1977). Temperature-depth stratification was measured with an electronic temperature logger (R. Brancker Research Ltd., Ottawa, ON; 1 sample·s\(^{-1}\), precision of depth sensor ~0.05 m) that was lowered at a rate of ~0.5 m·s\(^{-1}\). This instrument was calibrated on several occasions with a manual resistance thermometer accurate to 0.1°C. The planar thermocline depth is defined as that depth where the rate of change of temperature with depth is greatest (normally >1°C·m\(^{-1}\)). The coefficient of eddy diffusivity, \( K_z \), was estimated using Ward's (1977) equation \[ K_z = 4.9 \times 10^{-12} \frac{g \sqrt{A_0}}{N} \] where g is the gravitational acceleration constant (9.81 m·s\(^{-2}\)), \( A_0 \) is the lake surface area, and N is the Brunt-Väisälä frequency: \[ N = \sqrt{\frac{d\rho}{dz} \cdot \frac{g}{\rho}} \] where \( \rho \) is the density of water. In oligotrophic Canadian Shield waters, \( \rho \) can be assumed to be solely a function of temperature (Quay et al. 1980) and we calculated it using Benson and Krause's (1980) equation \[ \rho = \exp(-0.589581 + 326.785/T - 45284.1/T^2) \] where T is \( ^0K \). Units throughout are metres and seconds, except for \( \rho \) which has units of grams per cubic centimetre. Results The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the hypolimnia of small lakes (top three panels in the left columns of Fig. 2 and 3); gradients were much smaller in larger lakes (right column of panels in Fig. 2 and 3). However, mixing fluxes through the thermocline depend only on concentration gradients at the depth of the thermocline (Equation (1)), and there was no obvious relationship between gradients at this depth and lake size (Table 2). Thus, lake-to-lake differences in the upward flux of individual nutrients through the thermocline depend almost entirely on \( K_z \), which was more than two orders of magnitude greater in the largest lake (Nipigon) than in the smallest (ELA Lake 373) (Table 2). Fluxes increased progressively with lake size for those nutrients that increased in concentration with depth in the region of the thermocline (NO₃⁻, TIN, and SRSi) but were nil for nutrients that had zero or negative gradients (TN, TDP, TP). Over a 21-yr period, the summer mixed layer of ELA Lake 239 received similar amounts of TN and TP from precipitation and terrestrial runoff (Fig. 4). There was always much more TIN and NO₃⁻ in precipitation than in runoff, but runoff was by far the most important source of Si. In 1990, upward mixing through the thermocline was an important source of nutrients (compared with precipitation and runoff) only in lakes >1000 ha (Table 3). The amount of N supplied by N₂-fixation was much less than that supplied by precipitation and runoff except in intermediate-sized lakes; why higher N₂-fixation rates occurred in these lakes is unclear, because other fluxes of N to them were not unusually low. Interannually, fluxes from precipitation and terrestrial runoff varied by about the same amount as did nutrient concentration gradients in the thermocline of Lake 239 (Fig. 5); the coefficients of variation of NO₃⁻ in precipitation and of concentration gradients of NO₃⁻ in the Lake 239 thermocline were both 40%. Figure 5 also shows that in 1990 (the only year for which we have the chemistry depth profile data required to estimate vertical mixing fluxes in the NOLSS lakes) vertical concentration gradients in Lake 239 were unusually low. If interannual variations of chemical concentration gradients in Lake 239 also occur in larger lakes, then mixing fluxes would be about double those given in Table 2 in an average year, and up to three times greater in high years. In 1990, fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer fell far short of phytoplankton requirements (Table 3 and left column of panels in Fig. 6), but the deficit of Si was slight. Discussion Turbulent mixing through the thermocline, the only nutrient flux to the mixed layer that is explicitly dependent on lake size, supplied less TN and TP than did those fluxes that are independent of lake size (precipitation, terrestrial runoff, N\(_2\)-fixation; Fig. 6). Mixing supplied more of some forms of N (NO\(_3^-\) and TIN) and of SRSi in larger than in smaller lakes (Table 3), but terrestrial runoff more than made up for the SRSi that turbulence failed to supply in small lakes. Thus, the only mixing fluxes of potential ecological importance are of NO\(_3^-\) and TIN. Although N plays an important role in determining phytoplankton community composition (Schindler 1977), it rarely limits algal biomass in unperturbed Canadian Shield lakes (Hecky and Kilham 1988). We, therefore, conclude that the turbulence-mediated upward flux of nutrients through the summer thermocline was an insignificant component of mixed-layer nutrient budgets in all sizes of Canadian Shield lakes in 1990. We did not measure concentrations of PO\(_4^{3-}\), the form of P most readily assimilated by phytoplankton, because standard chemical methods for measuring it always overestimate actual concentrations in Canadian Shield lakes (Stainton 1980). Moreover, when special radiochemical methods have been used to measure it, concentrations in these lakes were always minute (<0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler 1980). Nevertheless, if PO\(_4^{3-}\) did increase in concentration with depth in the thermoclines of the lakes we studied, we may have missed an important source of this critical element. We obtained an upper bound on the magnitude of this flux by assuming that concentrations increase from 0 in the mixed layer to the highest summer values ever measured in the hypolimnia of unperturbed northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes (0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler, 1980) over a distance of 1 m in all the lakes. These extremely generous assumptions yield upward (mixing) fluxes of P on the order of 0.002 \( \mu \)mol·m\(^{-2}\)·d\(^{-1} \), which amounts to only ~0.001% of the amount of P that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer require. We thus confidently conclude that the upward flux of PO\(_4^{3-}\) through the thermocline is insignificant in Canadian Shield lakes. None of the foregoing conclusions depend critically on our use of Equation (2) to estimate \( K_z \), which is a statistical fit to the results of Mortimer (1941), Jassby and Powell (1975), Hutchinson (1957), Hesslein and Quay (1973), and Ward (1977). Two of these papers (Mortimer’s and Hutchinson’s), in turn, summarize results from many other independent studies. A possible objection to these results, however, is that with one exception they are all based on measurements of the rate at which heat moved downward through the thermocline. The exception was Hesslein and Quay (1973), who found that in a very small, deep lake (ELA Lake 227; \( A_0 = 5 \) ha, \( z_m = 10 \) m) \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of a dissolved material (radon gas) was much smaller than \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of heat. This happened because turbulence was so low that transport was almost entirely the result of molecular diffusion, and heat has a higher coefficient of molecular conductivity than radon gas. Because all of our lakes are much larger than Lake 227, they have \( K_z \) values substantially greater than the molecular conductivity of heat, and this cannot be a problem here. Moreover, if \( K_z \) were smaller than the values we derived from Equation (2), vertical fluxes would be even smaller than those we calculated, which we have already concluded to be insignificant. Finally, because concentration gradients of all forms of P in the region of the thermocline were negligible, our conclusion that vertical fluxes of this critical element were nil in all lake sizes is completely independent of \( K_z \). Figure 6 shows that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer required much more P and N than all of the fluxes measured in 1990. The deficit of supply relative to demand was notably greater for P than for N, further confirming that P is the most limiting nutrient in Canadian Shield lakes (Schindler 1977, 1988; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1988; Levine and Schindler 1992; Hecky et al. 1993; S.
