Another possible problem with our approach is that we assume that Fee et al.’s (1992) \(^{14}\)C-based PP values estimate daily net C fixation into particles. We emphasize that our use of the term “net” is distinct from another common use of this term, i.e., the amount of material exported from the primary trophic level during an entire growing season (stored in sediments, flushed out of the lake, or converted into the flesh of higher trophic levels). We make no assumption about what happens to particles over periods longer than a day. Bower et al. (1987) showed that in an ELA whole-lake \(^{14}\)C experiment, Fee et al.’s (1992) PP method closely approximated net daily incorporation of C into particles; all losses of \(^{14}\)C from particles occurred at night, and these losses averaged only 8% of the daytime rate of incorporation of inorganic C into particulate matter (range 3–17%, \(n = 13\)). Essentially, we explicitly ignore this small and variable correction, and assume that the \(^{14}\)C method used by Fee et al. (1992) yields estimates of daily net particulate C fixation; Peterson (1978) reported that this is true for rapidly growing algal cultures. The final critical basic assumption for our analysis is that all major nutrient fluxes to the mixed layer were measured. One potential nutrient source that we did not measure is that from epilimnion sediments. However, studies at ELA have repeatedly demonstrated that epilimnion sediments return little or no P to the water column (\(^{32}\)P measurements: Schindler et al. 1975; Levine et al. 1986; mass balance calculations: Schindler et al. 1973, 1987; Levine and Schindler 1989; porewater gradient measurements: Schindler et al. 1977; L. Hendzel, unpublished data). Levine and Schindler (1989) did find that littoral sediments supplied N to the mixed layer, but as mentioned above, N rarely limits phytoplankton biomass in Canadian Shield lakes. Moreover, Levine and Schindler (1992) showed that the N returned to the water column from epilimnetic sediments was almost entirely derived from materials recently deposited at the sediment–water interface, rather than from deep within the sediment itself; in our view, this constitutes nutrient recycling within the mixed layer. We thus conclude that Fig. 6 can be accepted at face value, and that fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer were a small fraction of the physiological requirements of phytoplankton in 1990. Indeed, these fluxes would be capable of meeting phytoplankton needs only in small lakes and if the most generous assumptions about supply and demand are made. The major implication is that recycling within the mixed layer must be the major source of N and P for algae living there. This is scarcely a new or surprising conclusion. Harrison (1980, and see references therein) showed that external inputs of N, P, and Si to the sea could account for <1% of the amounts required by phytoplankton, and he concluded that recycling supplied the remainder. In fresh water, Levine and Schindler (1980) found that in an unfertilized, stratified ELA lake (Lake 302S; \(A_0 = 10.9\) ha, \(z_m = 10.6\) m) an average P atom recycled through epilimnetic seston 17 times prior to being lost from the mixed layer, and Levine et al. (1986, p. 376) stated that “... the predominant source of phosphate for phytoplankton in the epilimnion is not external supply, but recycling.” This result has been corroborated by so many independent studies (see Planas and Hecky 1984, and references therein) that it would have been extremely surprising if our results contradicted it. Figure 6 illustrates what may be our single most important result, viz., the fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements accounted for by all estimated fluxes to the mixed layer systematically decreases with increasing lake size. That is, nutrient recycling within the mixed layer supplies a progressively increasing fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements as lake size increases. This is logical, because both the intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the thickness of the mixed layer increase with lake size. As a consequence, mixed-layer particle residence times increase with lake size; this increases the probability that particle-bound nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than being lost to the sediments. A lower bound on the magnitude of this effect can be derived using Hesslein et al.’s (1980) value of 0.18 m·d\(^{-1}\) for the settling rate of particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 224 (\(A_0 = 25.9\) ha, \(z_m = 27\) m). Applying this figure to all lake sizes, it would take 33 d for settling to remove all particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 373 (\(z_{th} = 6\) m) compared with 72 d in Trout Lake (\(z_{th} = 13\) m). However, because large lakes have much more turbulent mixed layers than small ones, the actual difference in particle residence times in large versus small lakes is undoubtedly even greater. The percent organic C in deep-water sediments declines in a strikingly regular fashion with increasing lake size (Fig. 7). This result strongly supports our conclusion that the rate of nutrient recycling within the mixed layer increases with increasing lake size. The longer that particles are retained in the mixed layer, the more likely it is that the C they contain will be respired back to CO\(_2\) and lost to the atmosphere rather than falling through the thermocline and accumulating in deep-water sediments. We do not believe that recycling is the only process responsible for producing this pattern. Indeed, such regularity is probably the product of many processes acting in concert (e.g., longer retention in the mixed layer, increasing total depth of the water column, decreasing terrestrial influence, etc.). Nevertheless, it is fully consonant with our conclusion that large lakes recycle nutrients more efficiently than small ones. The greater efficiency of nutrient recycling in the mixed layer in large than in small lakes has important implications for Fee's (1979) theory that the rate of nutrient recycling is a function of basin morphometry. He found that in small ELA lakes, the area of epilimnion sediments (\(A_e\)) divided by the volume of the epilimnion (\(V_e\)) was strongly correlated with rates of volumetric PP. He demonstrated that, if all other factors are equal, \(A_e/V_e\) is mathematically equivalent to the probability of retention of particles in the mixed layer and thus parameterized the rate of nutrient recycling. He cautioned that this might not be true in larger lakes, where processes that are negligible in small lakes could affect nutrient recycling. Our results bear out this prediction; as lakes increase in size, the increasing intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the increasing thickness of the mixed layer both retard sedimentation losses through the thermocline, thereby increasing mixed layer particle residence time. Consequently, a large lake with a low \(A_e/V_e\) value and a small lake with a high \(A_e/V_e\) value could have the same mixed layer particle residence times and similar rates of nutrient recycling. An important corollary is that large and small lakes with similar \(A_e/V_e\) values should respond differently to the same external P loading. Productivity should be higher in the large lake because of its higher rate of nutrient recycling. These results lend strong support to Margalef's (1974) theory that physical energy levels directly control food-web structures and the biogeochemical characteristics of water bodies. The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the water column of small lakes (Fig. 2 and 3); in contrast, large lakes had relatively well-mixed hypolimnia with maximum gradients at or just below the thermocline. This difference is probably the result of several processes: (1) Internal waves, which are the primary source of hypolimnetic turbulence, are significant only in lakes with surface areas >1000 ha (Boyce 1974); thus, in small lakes, nutrients from particles remineralized near the bottom of the water column move upward very slowly compared with larger lakes. (2) Sediment focussing is very important in small lakes (Anderson et al. 1987) and causes particles that fall through the thermocline to move rapidly to great depths. (3) Because small lakes have shallow mixed layers, significant quantities of light penetrate below their thermoclines (Fee et al. 1991), permitting large algal populations to develop deep in their water columns (Fee 1976). These algal populations intercept nutrients diffusing up from below and prevent them from reaching the thermocline. Schindler and Nighswander (1970) and Bayley et al. (1992) reported that precipitation was the major source of N and P to Canadian Shield lakes. However, their conclusion was based on results obtained from the study of quite small lakes. Our results (Fig. 6) indicate that this does not apply to Canadian Shield lakes >300 ha, where fluxes of N and P from terrestrial runoff and precipitation were very similar in magnitude. Unlike N and P, there was virtually no Si in precipitation, and mixing supplied substantial quantities of this nutrient only in very large lakes (Fig. 6). However, terrestrial runoff of Si was large, particularly in small and midsized lakes, and the sum of all the fluxes that we measured apparently match phytoplankton requirements. There must, therefore, be some reason, other than a lack of supply, for why diatoms are unimportant components of the summer phytoplankton community in small, stratified Canadian Shield lakes (Kling and Holmgren 1972; Findlay and Kasian 1990). Again, the most likely explanation is based on the low mixed-layer turbulence and shallow mixed-layer depths in small lakes. Theoretically, the higher specific gravity of diatoms gives them a selective advantage over nonsinking or weakly motile competitors because by sinking they increase the rate at which they contact dissolved nutrients (by thinning the nutrient-depleted boundary layer that surrounds them: Hutchinson 1967; Margalef 1974; Titman and Kilham 1976). This strategy works well in large lakes, where high turbulence and deep mixed layers keep cells from being rapidly lost by sedimentation through the thermocline. Diatoms are also well represented in small, unstratified lakes, which lack a hypolimnion sedimentation trap altogether (Kling and Holmgren 1972). However, this strategy apparently fails in small, stratified lakes where shallow mixed layers and relatively stable water columns lead to rapid removal of sinking cells from the mixed layer. Conclusion The increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size acted in concert with positive concentration gradients of NO\(_3^-\), TDN, and SRSi in the region of the thermocline to result in more of these nutrients being transported upwards through the thermoclines in large than in small lakes (Table 2). These nutrients, however, rarely limit phytoplankton growth in Canadian Shield lakes. Because concentration gradients of P, the nutrient that does limit algal growth in Canadian Shield lakes, were nil in the region of the thermocline in all of these lakes (Fig. 2 and 3; Table 2), upward fluxes of P were essentially zero in all lake sizes. Our results support Fee et al.'s (1992) hypothesis that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP. It does this by acting in concert with the increasing depth of the mixed layer to cause particles to be retained in the mixed layer longer, thus increasing the probability that nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than lost to the sediments. Our results do not, however, rule out the possibility that the greater rates of volumetric PP in midsized lakes reported by Fee et al. (1992) are caused by lake-to-lake differences of external P loading. That is, although our results show that, all other things being equal, higher turbulence and thicker mixed layers enhance nutrient recycling and lead to higher rates of areal PP in larger lakes, the approach we have taken of using runoff and precipitation data measured in the basin of one small ELA lake to estimate P loading in all the other lakes has inherent inaccuracies (Fee and Hecky 1992). External P loading within this lake-size series could vary enough to explain the observed differences of volumetric PP. Nevertheless, Fee et al. (1992) showed that it is unlikely that areal PP, which theoretically sets potential yields of higher trophic levels, is the result of lake-to-lake differences in external P loading. Our main conclusion, that the probability of regeneration of nutrients within the mixed layer increases with lake size, has an important corollary: external nutrient loads should be converted into higher trophic levels, including especially valued organisms such as fish, more efficiently in large than in small lakes. This prediction is in harmony with Nixon's (1988) conclusion that the greatest standing crops of benthos and highest fish yields come from the most energetic marine environments. He further noted that, as we found in large lakes, sediments from these highly productive regions contained less C than did sediments from less energetic environments. His interpretation of these observations was also the same as ours, viz., that energetic mixed layers recycle nutrients more efficiently than less energetic ones. Effects of Lake Size on Nutrient Availability in the Mixed Layer during Summer Stratification E.J. Fee, R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Central and Arctic Region, Freshwater Institute, 501 University Crescent, Winnipeg, MB R3T 2N6, Canada Fee, E.J., R.E. Hecky, G.W. Regehr, L.L. Hendzel, and P. Wilkinson. 1994. Effects of lake size on nutrient availability in the mixed layer during summer stratification. Can. J. Fish. Aquat. Sci. 51: 2756–2768. Fluxes to the summer mixed layer of N, Si, and P were estimated in a size series of northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes. Increasing turbulence caused upward fluxes through the thermocline to increase with lake size for nutrients that increased in concentration below the thermocline (soluble reactive Si, total inorganic N, and NO_3^−; but not total N or any form of P). Precipitation and terrestrial runoff were equally important sources of N and P in all but very small lakes (<100 ha), where precipitation supplied much more than runoff. Runoff was the only important source of Si, except in very large lakes (> 100 000 ha) where mixing through the thermocline was important. N_2-fixation was unimportant except in intermediate-sized lakes (700–2000 ha). Si fluxes nearly equaled phytoplankton requirements, but N and P were below requirements, and recycling within the mixed layer must be the most important source of these nutrients. N and P deficits increased progressively with lake size, implying that the efficiency of nutrient recycling increased with lake size; mixed layers in large lakes are more turbulent and thicker than in small lakes and these processes increase the probability of nutrient regeneration within the mixed layer. Les flux de N, de Si et de P vers la couche de mélange estivale ont été estimés dans des lacs de différentes tailles du Bouclier canadien dans le nord-ouest de l’Ontario. Une turbulence accrue donne lieu à une augmentation proportionnelle à la taille des lacs des flux ascendants dans la thermocline dans le cas des éléments nutritifs dont la concentration augmente sous la thermocline (Si réactif soluble, N inorganique total, et NO_3^−); mais non le N total et aucune forme de P). Les précipitations et le ruissellement de surface étaient des sources de N et de P d’égale importance dans tous les lacs, sauf dans les très petits (<100 ha), où la contribution des précipitations étaient beaucoup plus importante à cet égard. Le ruissellement était la seule source importante de Si, sauf sans les très grands lacs (> 100 000 ha), où le mélange dans la thermocline apportait une contribution importante. La fixation du N_2 n’était pas importante sauf dans les lacs de taille intermédiaire (700–2 000 ha). Les flux de Si satisfaisaient presque les besoins du phytoplancton alors que ceux de N et de P étaient insuffisants, le recyclage dans la couche de mélange assurant probablement le principal apport de ces deux derniers éléments. Les carences en N et en P allaient en s’accroissant avec la taille des lacs, ce qui implique que la contribution du recyclage des éléments nutritifs s’accroît avec la taille des lacs; en effet, les couches de mélange des grands lacs sont plus turbulentes et plus épaisses que celles des petits lacs, ce qui accroît les possibilités de régénération des éléments nutritifs dans la couche de mélange. Received September 21, 1993 Accepted July 12, 1994 (J12098) Reçu le 21 septembre 1993 Accepté le 12 juillet 1994 When Johnson and Vallentyne (1971) introduced the Experimental Lakes Area (ELA) program in the scientific literature, they clearly recognized that extrapolation of results obtained from the observation and manipulation of very small lakes to larger, more economically important ones was a fundamental assumption of ELA’s design. They presented several examples of how a lake’s size might affect critical limnological processes and stated that these “... must be taken into account in any extrapolation.” Yet for nearly two decades, ELA results have been extrapolated to larger lakes without any explicit consideration of such effects. The Northwest Ontario Lake Size Series (NOLSS) program (Fee and Hecky 1992) was designed to remedy this deficiency; specifically, the purpose of NOLSS is to investigate physical gradients associated with lake size and to determine their biological significance. In an initial NOLSS publication, Fee et al. (1992) reported that annual rates of phytoplankton photosynthesis (PP) per unit of lake surface area (i.e., areal PP) increased progressively with lake size simply because larger lakes were ice free for longer periods and had thicker mixed layers than small lakes. In contrast, these authors showed that annual rates of PP per unit volume of the mixed layer (volumetric PP) varied with lake size in a bell-shaped pattern, i.e., rates in the smallest and largest lakes (29 ha ELA Lake 373 and 8 × 10^6 ha Lake Superior, respectively) were low and similar, whereas midsized lakes had rates nearly an order of magnitude greater. Fee et al. (1992) hypothesized that this pattern resulted from systematic changes of turbulence and water temperature with increasing lake size. According to this hypothesis, the increasing intensity of turbulence with 1This is one in a series of papers describing work of the Freshwater Institute Science Laboratory on a lake-size series in Northwest Ontario. It is also a contribution to the series honoring the 25th anniversary of the Experimental Lakes Area. lake size (Ward 1977; Quay et al. 1980) stimulates volumetric PP by increasing nutrient availability in the mixed layer, but decreasing water temperature with increasing lake size (Fee and Hecky 1992) simultaneously depresses it; the opposite effects of these two gradients on PP results in optimum conditions for PP in midsized lakes. This paper investigates one of the basic assumptions of this hypothesis: viz., that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP by making nutrients more available within the mixed layer. It is well documented that algal growth and biomass in Canadian Shield lakes is limited by nutrients; more specifically, PP is primarily phosphorus (P) limited (Schindler 1977; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1987; Hecky et al. 1993; and especially S. Guildford and L. Hendzel, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, Winnipeg, MB, unpublished data for the NOLSS lakes). Theoretically, turbulence should be positively and causally related to nutrient availability in the mixed layer because: (1) more turbulent mixed layers retain particles longer, and thus recycle nutrients more effectively and (2) turbulence is the physical process responsible for the upward transport of nutrients through the summer thermocline. The second mechanism is more conditional than the first, however, because the turbulent (mixing) flux through the thermocline is not solely a function of the intensity of turbulence. That is, the flux of a substance S through a plane at depth z is \[ \text{Flux} = K_z \frac{dS}{dz} \] where \( K_z \) is the coefficient of vertical eddy diffusion (i.e., turbulence). Hence, turbulence can result in a net upward flux to the mixed layer only if the concentration of S increases with depth in the region of the thermocline. In this paper, we examine all major nutrient fluxes to the summer mixed layer in a size series of hydrologically and morphometrically similar lakes, during the period 1986-1991. Our purpose is to compare the magnitude of the only flux that depends explicitly on lake size, the turbulence-mediated upward flux through the summer thermocline, with fluxes that are independent of lake size: precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation. We then assess the ecological importance of these fluxes by comparing them with the nutrient requirements of algae residing in the mixed layer. Study Sites Table 1 summarizes morphometric features of the study lakes and defines morphometric symbols used throughout the text. All the lakes are located on the Canadian Shield in northwestern Ontario, have water renewal times >5 yr, and are deep enough to fully stratify during the summer. Except for Lakes Nipigon and Superior, whose basins are sparsely populated, there are no permanent residents in the drainage basins of the lakes. More detailed descriptions are given by Fee and Hecky (1992) and Fee et al. (1992). Methods Unless otherwise stated, field and laboratory methods follow Fee et al. (1989) and Stainton et al. (1977). Temperature-depth stratification was measured with an electronic temperature logger (R. Brancker Research Ltd., Ottawa, ON; 1 sample·s\(^{-1}\), precision of depth sensor ~0.05 m) that was lowered at a rate of ~0.5 m·s\(^{-1}\). This instrument was calibrated on several occasions with a manual resistance thermometer accurate to 0.1°C. The planar thermocline depth is defined as that depth where the rate of change of temperature with depth is greatest (normally >1°C·m\(^{-1}\)). The coefficient of eddy diffusivity, \( K_z \), was estimated using Ward's (1977) equation \[ K_z = 4.9 \times 10^{-12} \frac{g \sqrt{A_0}}{N} \] where g is the gravitational acceleration constant (9.81 m·s\(^{-2}\)), \( A_0 \) is the lake surface area, and N is the Brunt-Väisälä frequency: \[ N = \sqrt{\frac{d\rho}{dz} \cdot \frac{g}{\rho}} \] where \( \rho \) is the density of water. In oligotrophic Canadian Shield waters, \( \rho \) can be assumed to be solely a function of temperature (Quay et al. 1980) and we calculated it using Benson and Krause's (1980) equation \[ \rho = \exp(-0.589581 + 326.785/T - 45284.1/T^2) \] where T is \( ^0K \). Units throughout are metres and seconds, except for \( \rho \) which has units of grams per cubic centimetre. Water chemistry depth profiles were determined twice: once at the beginning and again at the end of summer stratification (mid-June and late August, except in Trout Lake and Lake Nipigon, where corresponding temperature stratification conditions occurred in early July and mid-September); chemistry profiles were not measured on Orange Lake or Lake Superior. A PVC Van Dorn bottle was used to collect water samples, which were transported to the laboratory in polyethylene bottles precleaned with dilute HCl, followed by three rinses of distilled water, and then air-dried. Total inorganic N (TIN = \( NO_3^- + NO_2^- + NH_4^+ \)), total P (TP = TDP + SPP), and total N (TN = TDN + SPN) were obtained arithmetically. Orthophosphate (\( PO_4^{3-} \)) is undetectable in these waters (Stainton 1980). Turbulence-mediated nutrient fluxes up through the thermocline (mass\(\cdot\)m\(^{-2}\)\(\cdot\)d\(^{-1}\)) were multiplied by the ratio of the area of the lake at the depth of the thermocline (\( A_{th} \)) to the surface area of the lake (\( A_0 \)) (Table 2); this renders them directly comparable with other fluxes to the mixed layer (precipitation, terrestrial runoff, and N\(_2\)-fixation) and to the nutrient requirements of phytoplankton, which were based on the rate of phytoplankton photosynthesis per square metre of lake surface, corrected for the diminution of lake volume with depth (Fee 1980). Chemical concentrations were not measured in Orange Lake or Lake Superior; mixing fluxes thus cannot be calculated for these lakes directly. Mixing fluxes in Orange Lake were estimated by interpolating linearly (lake surface area being the independent variable) from those measured in Green and Linge Lakes. Because Lake Superior is the largest member of the size series, this method cannot be used and mixing fluxes are not available for this lake. Results The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the hypolimnia of small lakes (top three panels in the left columns of Fig. 2 and 3); gradients were much smaller in larger lakes (right column of panels in Fig. 2 and 3). However, mixing fluxes through the thermocline depend only on concentration gradients at the depth of the thermocline (Equation (1)), and there was no obvious relationship between gradients at this depth and lake size (Table 2). Thus, lake-to-lake differences in the upward flux of individual nutrients through the thermocline depend almost entirely on \( K_z \), which was more than two orders of magnitude greater in the largest lake (Nipigon) than in the smallest (ELA Lake 373) (Table 2). Fluxes increased progressively with lake size for those nutrients that increased in concentration with depth in the region of the thermocline (NO₃⁻, TIN, and SRSi) but were nil for nutrients that had zero or negative gradients (TN, TDP, TP). Over a 21-yr period, the summer mixed layer of ELA Lake 239 received similar amounts of TN and TP from precipitation and terrestrial runoff (Fig. 4). There was always much more TIN and NO₃⁻ in precipitation than in runoff, but runoff was by far the most important source of Si. In 1990, upward mixing through the thermocline was an important source of nutrients (compared with precipitation and runoff) only in lakes >1000 ha (Table 3). The amount of N supplied by N₂-fixation was much less than that supplied by precipitation and runoff except in intermediate-sized lakes; why higher N₂-fixation rates occurred in these lakes is unclear, because other fluxes of N to them were not unusually low. Interannually, fluxes from precipitation and terrestrial runoff varied by about the same amount as did nutrient concentration gradients in the thermocline of Lake 239 (Fig. 5); the coefficients of variation of NO₃⁻ in precipitation and of concentration gradients of NO₃⁻ in the Lake 239 thermocline were both 40%. Figure 5 also shows that in 1990 (the only year for which we have the chemistry depth profile data required to estimate vertical mixing fluxes in the NOLSS lakes) vertical concentration gradients in Lake 239 were unusually low. If interannual variations of chemical concentration gradients in Lake 239 also occur in larger lakes, then mixing fluxes would be about double those given in Table 2 in an average year, and up to three times greater in high years. In 1990, fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer fell far short of phytoplankton requirements (Table 3 and left column of panels in Fig. 6), but the deficit of Si was slight. Discussion Turbulent mixing through the thermocline, the only nutrient flux to the mixed layer that is explicitly dependent on lake size, supplied less TN and TP than did those fluxes that are independent of lake size (precipitation, terrestrial runoff, N\(_2\)-fixation; Fig. 6). Mixing supplied more of some forms of N (NO\(_3^-\) and TIN) and of SRSi in larger than in smaller lakes (Table 3), but terrestrial runoff more than made up for the SRSi that turbulence failed to supply in small lakes. Thus, the only mixing fluxes of potential ecological importance are of NO\(_3^-\) and TIN. Although N plays an important role in determining phytoplankton community composition (Schindler 1977), it rarely limits algal biomass in unperturbed Canadian Shield lakes (Hecky and Kilham 1988). We, therefore, conclude that the turbulence-mediated upward flux of nutrients through the summer thermocline was an insignificant component of mixed-layer nutrient budgets in all sizes of Canadian Shield lakes in 1990. We did not measure concentrations of PO\(_4^{3-}\), the form of P most readily assimilated by phytoplankton, because standard chemical methods for measuring it always overestimate actual concentrations in Canadian Shield lakes (Stainton 1980). Moreover, when special radiochemical methods have been used to measure it, concentrations in these lakes were always minute (<0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler 1980). Nevertheless, if PO\(_4^{3-}\) did increase in concentration with depth in the thermoclines of the lakes we studied, we may have missed an important source of this critical element. We obtained an upper bound on the magnitude of this flux by assuming that concentrations increase from 0 in the mixed layer to the highest summer values ever measured in the hypolimnia of unperturbed northwestern Ontario Canadian Shield lakes (0.003 \( \mu \)mol·L\(^{-1} \); Levine and Schindler, 1980) over a distance of 1 m in all the lakes. These extremely generous assumptions yield upward (mixing) fluxes of P on the order of 0.002 \( \mu \)mol·m\(^{-2}\)·d\(^{-1} \), which amounts to only ~0.001% of the amount of P that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer require. We thus confidently conclude that the upward flux of PO\(_4^{3-}\) through the thermocline is insignificant in Canadian Shield lakes. None of the foregoing conclusions depend critically on our use of Equation (2) to estimate \( K_z \), which is a statistical fit to the results of Mortimer (1941), Jassby and Powell (1975), Hutchinson (1957), Hesslein and Quay (1973), and Ward (1977). Two of these papers (Mortimer’s and Hutchinson’s), in turn, summarize results from many other independent studies. A possible objection to these results, however, is that with one exception they are all based on measurements of the rate at which heat moved downward through the thermocline. The exception was Hesslein and Quay (1973), who found that in a very small, deep lake (ELA Lake 227; \( A_0 = 5 \) ha, \( z_m = 10 \) m) \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of a dissolved material (radon gas) was much smaller than \( K_z \) as determined by measuring the transport of heat. This happened because turbulence was so low that transport was almost entirely the result of molecular diffusion, and heat has a higher coefficient of molecular conductivity than radon gas. Because all of our lakes are much larger than Lake 227, they have \( K_z \) values substantially greater than the molecular conductivity of heat, and this cannot be a problem here. Moreover, if \( K_z \) were smaller than the values we derived from Equation (2), vertical fluxes would be even smaller than those we calculated, which we have already concluded to be insignificant. Finally, because concentration gradients of all forms of P in the region of the thermocline were negligible, our conclusion that vertical fluxes of this critical element were nil in all lake sizes is completely independent of \( K_z \). Figure 6 shows that phytoplankton living in the mixed layer required much more P and N than all of the fluxes measured in 1990. The deficit of supply relative to demand was notably greater for P than for N, further confirming that P is the most limiting nutrient in Canadian Shield lakes (Schindler 1977, 1988; Fee 1979; Hecky and Kilham 1988; Levine and Schindler 1992; Hecky et al. 1993; S. Another possible problem with our approach is that we assume that Fee et al.’s (1992) \(^{14}\)C-based PP values estimate daily net C fixation into particles. We emphasize that our use of the term “net” is distinct from another common use of this term, i.e., the amount of material exported from the primary trophic level during an entire growing season (stored in sediments, flushed out of the lake, or converted into the flesh of higher trophic levels). We make no assumption about what happens to particles over periods longer than a day. Bower et al. (1987) showed that in an ELA whole-lake \(^{14}\)C experiment, Fee et al.’s (1992) PP method closely approximated net daily incorporation of C into particles; all losses of \(^{14}\)C from particles occurred at night, and these losses averaged only 8% of the daytime rate of incorporation of inorganic C into particulate matter (range 3–17%, \(n = 13\)). Essentially, we explicitly ignore this small and variable correction, and assume that the \(^{14}\)C method used by Fee et al. (1992) yields estimates of daily net particulate C fixation; Peterson (1978) reported that this is true for rapidly growing algal cultures. The final critical basic assumption for our analysis is that all major nutrient fluxes to the mixed layer were measured. One potential nutrient source that we did not measure is that from epilimnion sediments. However, studies at ELA have repeatedly demonstrated that epilimnion sediments return little or no P to the water column (\(^{32}\)P measurements: Schindler et al. 1975; Levine et al. 1986; mass balance calculations: Schindler et al. 1973, 1987; Levine and Schindler 1989; porewater gradient measurements: Schindler et al. 1977; L. Hendzel, unpublished data). Levine and Schindler (1989) did find that littoral sediments supplied N to the mixed layer, but as mentioned above, N rarely limits phytoplankton biomass in Canadian Shield lakes. Moreover, Levine and Schindler (1992) showed that the N returned to the water column from epilimnetic sediments was almost entirely derived from materials recently deposited at the sediment–water interface, rather than from deep within the sediment itself; in our view, this constitutes nutrient recycling within the mixed layer. We thus conclude that Fig. 6 can be accepted at face value, and that fluxes of N and P to the mixed layer were a small fraction of the physiological requirements of phytoplankton in 1990. Indeed, these fluxes would be capable of meeting phytoplankton needs only in small lakes and if the most generous assumptions about supply and demand are made. The major implication is that recycling within the mixed layer must be the major source of N and P for algae living there. This is scarcely a new or surprising conclusion. Harrison (1980, and see references therein) showed that external inputs of N, P, and Si to the sea could account for <1% of the amounts required by phytoplankton, and he concluded that recycling supplied the remainder. In fresh water, Levine and Schindler (1980) found that in an unfertilized, stratified ELA lake (Lake 302S; \(A_0 = 10.9\) ha, \(z_m = 10.6\) m) an average P atom recycled through epilimnetic seston 17 times prior to being lost from the mixed layer, and Levine et al. (1986, p. 376) stated that “... the predominant source of phosphate for phytoplankton in the epilimnion is not external supply, but recycling.” This result has been corroborated by so many independent studies (see Planas and Hecky 1984, and references therein) that it would have been extremely surprising if our results contradicted it. Figure 6 illustrates what may be our single most important result, viz., the fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements accounted for by all estimated fluxes to the mixed layer systematically decreases with increasing lake size. That is, nutrient recycling within the mixed layer supplies a progressively increasing fraction of phytoplankton nutrient requirements as lake size increases. This is logical, because both the intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the thickness of the mixed layer increase with lake size. As a consequence, mixed-layer particle residence times increase with lake size; this increases the probability that particle-bound nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than being lost to the sediments. A lower bound on the magnitude of this effect can be derived using Hesslein et al.’s (1980) value of 0.18 m·d\(^{-1}\) for the settling rate of particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 224 (\(A_0 = 25.9\) ha, \(z_m = 27\) m). Applying this figure to all lake sizes, it would take 33 d for settling to remove all particles from the mixed layer of ELA Lake 373 (\(z_{th} = 6\) m) compared with 72 d in Trout Lake (\(z_{th} = 13\) m). However, because large lakes have much more turbulent mixed layers than small ones, the actual difference in particle residence times in large versus small lakes is undoubtedly even greater. The percent organic C in deep-water sediments declines in a strikingly regular fashion with increasing lake size (Fig. 7). This result strongly supports our conclusion that the rate of nutrient recycling within the mixed layer increases with increasing lake size. The longer that particles are retained in the mixed layer, the more likely it is that the C they contain will be respired back to CO\(_2\) and lost to the atmosphere rather than falling through the thermocline and accumulating in deep-water sediments. We do not believe that recycling is the only process responsible for producing this pattern. Indeed, such regularity is probably the product of many processes acting in concert (e.g., longer retention in the mixed layer, increasing total depth of the water column, decreasing terrestrial influence, etc.). Nevertheless, it is fully consonant with our conclusion that large lakes recycle nutrients more efficiently than small ones. The greater efficiency of nutrient recycling in the mixed layer in large than in small lakes has important implications for Fee's (1979) theory that the rate of nutrient recycling is a function of basin morphometry. He found that in small ELA lakes, the area of epilimnion sediments (\(A_e\)) divided by the volume of the epilimnion (\(V_e\)) was strongly correlated with rates of volumetric PP. He demonstrated that, if all other factors are equal, \(A_e/V_e\) is mathematically equivalent to the probability of retention of particles in the mixed layer and thus parameterized the rate of nutrient recycling. He cautioned that this might not be true in larger lakes, where processes that are negligible in small lakes could affect nutrient recycling. Our results bear out this prediction; as lakes increase in size, the increasing intensity of turbulence within the mixed layer and the increasing thickness of the mixed layer both retard sedimentation losses through the thermocline, thereby increasing mixed layer particle residence time. Consequently, a large lake with a low \(A_e/V_e\) value and a small lake with a high \(A_e/V_e\) value could have the same mixed layer particle residence times and similar rates of nutrient recycling. An important corollary is that large and small lakes with similar \(A_e/V_e\) values should respond differently to the same external P loading. Productivity should be higher in the large lake because of its higher rate of nutrient recycling. These results lend strong support to Margalef's (1974) theory that physical energy levels directly control food-web structures and the biogeochemical characteristics of water bodies. The largest nutrient concentration gradients occurred deep in the water column of small lakes (Fig. 2 and 3); in contrast, large lakes had relatively well-mixed hypolimnia with maximum gradients at or just below the thermocline. This difference is probably the result of several processes: (1) Internal waves, which are the primary source of hypolimnetic turbulence, are significant only in lakes with surface areas >1000 ha (Boyce 1974); thus, in small lakes, nutrients from particles remineralized near the bottom of the water column move upward very slowly compared with larger lakes. (2) Sediment focussing is very important in small lakes (Anderson et al. 1987) and causes particles that fall through the thermocline to move rapidly to great depths. (3) Because small lakes have shallow mixed layers, significant quantities of light penetrate below their thermoclines (Fee et al. 1991), permitting large algal populations to develop deep in their water columns (Fee 1976). These algal populations intercept nutrients diffusing up from below and prevent them from reaching the thermocline. Schindler and Nighswander (1970) and Bayley et al. (1992) reported that precipitation was the major source of N and P to Canadian Shield lakes. However, their conclusion was based on results obtained from the study of quite small lakes. Our results (Fig. 6) indicate that this does not apply to Canadian Shield lakes >300 ha, where fluxes of N and P from terrestrial runoff and precipitation were very similar in magnitude. Unlike N and P, there was virtually no Si in precipitation, and mixing supplied substantial quantities of this nutrient only in very large lakes (Fig. 6). However, terrestrial runoff of Si was large, particularly in small and midsized lakes, and the sum of all the fluxes that we measured apparently match phytoplankton requirements. There must, therefore, be some reason, other than a lack of supply, for why diatoms are unimportant components of the summer phytoplankton community in small, stratified Canadian Shield lakes (Kling and Holmgren 1972; Findlay and Kasian 1990). Again, the most likely explanation is based on the low mixed-layer turbulence and shallow mixed-layer depths in small lakes. Theoretically, the higher specific gravity of diatoms gives them a selective advantage over nonsinking or weakly motile competitors because by sinking they increase the rate at which they contact dissolved nutrients (by thinning the nutrient-depleted boundary layer that surrounds them: Hutchinson 1967; Margalef 1974; Titman and Kilham 1976). This strategy works well in large lakes, where high turbulence and deep mixed layers keep cells from being rapidly lost by sedimentation through the thermocline. Diatoms are also well represented in small, unstratified lakes, which lack a hypolimnion sedimentation trap altogether (Kling and Holmgren 1972). However, this strategy apparently fails in small, stratified lakes where shallow mixed layers and relatively stable water columns lead to rapid removal of sinking cells from the mixed layer. Conclusion The increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size acted in concert with positive concentration gradients of NO\(_3^-\), TDN, and SRSi in the region of the thermocline to result in more of these nutrients being transported upwards through the thermoclines in large than in small lakes (Table 2). These nutrients, however, rarely limit phytoplankton growth in Canadian Shield lakes. Because concentration gradients of P, the nutrient that does limit algal growth in Canadian Shield lakes, were nil in the region of the thermocline in all of these lakes (Fig. 2 and 3; Table 2), upward fluxes of P were essentially zero in all lake sizes. Our results support Fee et al.'s (1992) hypothesis that the increasing intensity of turbulence with lake size stimulates PP. It does this by acting in concert with the increasing depth of the mixed layer to cause particles to be retained in the mixed layer longer, thus increasing the probability that nutrients will be recycled within the mixed layer rather than lost to the sediments. Our results do not, however, rule out the possibility that the greater rates of volumetric PP in midsized lakes reported by Fee et al. (1992) are caused by lake-to-lake differences of external P loading. That is, although our results show that, all other things being equal, higher turbulence and thicker mixed layers enhance nutrient recycling and lead to higher rates of areal PP in larger lakes, the approach we have taken of using runoff and precipitation data measured in the basin of one small ELA lake to estimate P loading in all the other lakes has inherent inaccuracies (Fee and Hecky 1992). External P loading within this lake-size series could vary enough to explain the observed differences of volumetric PP. Nevertheless, Fee et al. (1992) showed that it is unlikely that areal PP, which theoretically sets potential yields of higher trophic levels, is the result of lake-to-lake differences in external P loading. Our main conclusion, that the probability of regeneration of nutrients within the mixed layer increases with lake size, has an important corollary: external nutrient loads should be converted into higher trophic levels, including especially valued organisms such as fish, more efficiently in large than in small lakes. This prediction is in harmony with Nixon's (1988) conclusion that the greatest standing crops of benthos and highest fish yields come from the most energetic marine environments. He further noted that, as we found in large lakes, sediments from these highly productive regions contained less C than did sediments from less energetic environments. His interpretation of these observations was also the same as ours, viz., that energetic mixed layers recycle nutrients more efficiently than less energetic ones. Do cyanobacteria dominate in eutrophic lakes because they fix atmospheric nitrogen?

L. R. FERBER,* S. N. LEVINE,* A. LINI† AND G. P. LIVINGSTON*
*Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, U.S.A.
†Department of Geology, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, U.S.A.

SUMMARY

1. The sources of nitrogen for phytoplankton were determined for a bloom-prone lake as a means of assessing the hypothesis that cyanobacteria dominate in eutrophic lakes because of their ability to fix nitrogen when the nitrogen : phosphorous (N : P) supply ratio is low and nitrogen a limiting resource.
2. Nitrogen fixation rates, estimated through acetylene reduction with \(^{15}\)N calibration, were compared with \(^{15}\)N-tracer estimates of ammonium and nitrate uptake monthly during the ice-free season of 1999. In addition, the natural N stable isotope composition of phytoplankton, nitrate and ammonium were measured biweekly and the contribution of N\(_2\) to the phytoplankton signature estimated with a mixing model.
3. Although cyanobacteria made up 81–98% of phytoplankton biomass during summer and autumn, both assays suggested minimal N acquisition through fixation (<9% for the *in-situ* incubations; <2% for stable isotope analysis). Phytoplankton acquired N primarily as ammonium (82–98%), and secondarily as nitrate (15–18% in spring and autumn, but <5% in summer). Heterocyst densities of <3 per 100 fixer cells confirmed low reliance on fixation.
4. The lake showed symptoms of both light and nitrogen limitation. Cyanobacteria may have dominated by monopolizing benthic sources of ammonium, or by forming surface scums that shaded other algae.

*Keywords*: ammonium uptake, cyanobacteria, N : P ratio, nitrate uptake, nitrogen fixation, stable isotope

Introduction

Cyanobacterial blooms are a frequent and unwelcome consequence of lake eutrophication. With rising nutrient inputs, the relative abundance of cyanobacteria increases, while first chrysophytes and cryptophytes, and then chlorophytes and diatoms, diminish in importance (Watson, McCauley & Downing, 1997). The cyanobacterial species involved are relatively large-celled, filamentous or colonial, and contain gas vacuoles for buoyancy regulation. Many, but not all, have heterocysts for N\(_2\) fixation in oxic well-lit waters.

The surface scums that these algae form during calm weather are unsightly, odiferous, and sometimes toxic (Reynolds, 1984). Anxious to prevent or reduce blooms, lake managers have sought understanding of the conditions that lead to their dominance. More than a dozen hypotheses have been put forth [see reviews of Shapiro (1990) and Hyenstrand, Blomqvist & Pettersson (1998a)], the more convincing of which suggest that the nature of resource limitation changes during the eutrophication process, promoting cyanobacteria from a poorly- to a highly-competitive position. Phosphorus limitation generally is accepted as the initial condition, while the hypotheses differ in identifying nitrogen, CO\(_2\) or light as the limiting resource under eutrophy. In addition, some hypotheses suggest that, once all resource limitations are

</page>

<page number="1">

relieved, algae grow at their intrinsic rate of increase and relative abundance is determined by differential mortality. While the bloom-forming cyanobacteria grow slowly, their grazing mortality is minimal because of large size, low lipid content and frequent toxicity (Lampert, 1987), and sinking losses are substantially reduced by vacuolation (Knoechel & Kalff, 1975).

Here we provide a test of the most widely accepted hypothesis about cyanobacterial dominance in eutrophic lakes, the low nitrogen : phosphorous (N : P) hypothesis. First proposed by Pearsall (1932), and later elaborated on and popularised by Schindler (1977) and Smith (1983), this hypothesis maintains that cyanobacteria are masters of survival in environments poor in N and that their dominance in eutrophic systems is related to the low N : P ratios of major anthropogenic pollutants (e.g. animal and human wastes). The unusually high demand to supply ratios of P and N suggest that these nutrients are the basis of most phytoplankton competitions. Pearsall (1932) noted an association between cyanobacterial presence and low N : P ratios in English lakes but knew too little about algal physiology to provide a convincing explanation. He speculated that, as prokaryotes, cyanobacteria may use more organic N than other algae. Schindler (1977) proposed the mechanism that is now an integral part of the hypothesis, that cyanobacteria gain dominance by fixing atmospheric nitrogen when water column supplies of dissolved inorganic N (DIN) are minimal and populations of eukaryotes (which cannot fix) severely N limited. Because the atmospheric supply of nitrogen is vast, substrate limitation of nitrogen fixation is not expected. Cyanobacteria exploit the rising P inputs no longer available to eukaryotes and match P uptake with nitrogen fixation, biomass ultimately being limited by self-shading. Schindler (1977) based this mechanism on observations made at the Experimental Lakes Area (ELA) in Ontario, Canada. Lakes experimentally enriched with N and P at ratios above the demands of phytoplankton developed chlorophyte dominants, while blooms of heterocystous Anabaena and Aphanizomenon occurred when the enrichment ratio was lower. Smith (1983) further promoted the hypothesis by showing that the relative abundance of cyanobacteria in 17 north temperate lakes correlated negatively with total N : total P (TN : TP) ratio.

Previous tests of the low N : P hypothesis continued the field enrichment studies and empirical analyses initiated by Schindler (1977) and Smith (1983), but with less straightforward results. Nitrogen additions to Manitoban and British Columbian lakes with blooms of Aphanizomenon and Anabaena, respectively, successfully reduced the biomass of these fixers, but the new dominants were Microcystis and Synechococcus, non-heterocystous (non-nitrogen-fixing) cyanobacteria, rather than the chlorophytes favoured in ELA lakes (Barica, Kling & Gibson, 1980; Stockner & Shortweed, 1988). Microcystis is a particularly toxic bloom-former, and thus was no improvement over Aphanizomenon. Schindler (1977) overlooked non-fixing cyanobacteria in his initial formulation of the low N : P hypothesis because they were not major respondents to whole-lake nutrient enrichment at the ELA. However, Levine & Schindler (1999) later urged the scientific community to restrict the low N : P hypothesis to prediction of dominance by heterocystous species, having shown in mesocosm experiments that several non-heterocystous cyanobacterial taxa (Oscillatoria, Pseudoanabaena and Lyngbya) increased in relative abundance along an N : P gradient. Unfortunately, most empirical studies have dealt with total cyanobacterial biomass. The result has been reports of positive (e.g. McQueen & Lean, 1987) as well as negative (Smith, 1985; Smith, Willén & Karlsson, 1987) relationships when data sets have been relatively small, and a finding of no relationship when more than 100 lakes have been included (Harris, 1986; Canfield, Philips & Duarte, 1989).

The more recently formulated low DIN hypothesis of Blomqvist, Pettersson & Hyenstrand (1994) and Hyenstrand et al. (1998a,b) suggests that heterocystous versus nonheterocystous cyanobacterial dominance is determined by whether there is a benthic ammonium source available during water column DIN depletion. Vacuolated filamentous or colonial cyanobacteria such as Microcystis and Oscillatoria can migrate vertically with little energy expenditure and with greater speed than flagellated algae (Reynolds, 1984). Bringing stored N back to the surface, they may grow more quickly than heterocystous species that have stayed in the epilimnion and fixed nitrogen. Dominance by fixers is predicted only when both epilimnetic and benthic DIN sources are inadequate to meet demands. A shortcoming of the low DIN hypothesis is its failure to acknowledge that most heterocystous cyanobacteria also are vacuolated and colonial. They may be as likely to migrate as non-

</page>

<page number="2">

heterocystous forms, and thus may dominate both when there is a benthic N source and when fixation is required to obtain adequate N.

Our test of the low N : P hypothesis was unique, although simple. Inverse logic dictates that N₂ must be the principal species of N used by heterocystous cyanobacteria during blooms if these algae have gained and maintained dominance through fixation. Consequently, we assessed N sources in a hypertrophic lake over the course of an ice-free season, looking for a relationship between periods of heterocystous cyanobacterial dominance and dependency on atmospheric nitrogen. Three independent assays contributed to our conclusions, monthly assessments of ammonium, nitrate and N₂ incorporation rates through in-situ incubations with \(^{15}\)N tracers and acetylene (referred to as the ISI assay), biweekly natural N stable isotope analysis (NSID assay), and biweekly determination of heterocyst density on fixer filaments. The last variable was useful because cyanobacteria with access to ammonium produce few heterocysts, ensuring that the high energetic cost of fixation (12 moles of ATP per mole of nitrogen fixed) is not incurred unnecessarily (Paerl et al., 1981). Consequently heterocyst density is a good indicator of reliance on atmospheric nitrogen. To allow for evaluation of hypotheses about cyanobacterial dominance other than the low N : P hypothesis, we measured light availability throughout the study and examined biweekly water chemistry (N, P and inorganic C forms) and zooplankton populations.

Methods

Study site

Shelburne Pond, 16 km southeast of Burlington, VT, U.S.A. (44°23′N, 73°9.5′W), was the study site. Shallow (mean depth 3.4 m; maximum depth 7.6 m) and moderately sized (176 ha), this lake is ice-covered in winter (December to April) and polymictic in summer. An epilimnion approximately 1 m in depth develops between May and October, but is destroyed periodically (typically 3–4 times per year; DeYoe, 1981) by storm mixing. Agricultural runoff and soluble P-rich dolomite in the 20-km² catchment create hypertrophic conditions. For the period 1977–98, spring and summer TP concentrations averaged 3.3 and 5 \( \mu \)M, respectively; chlorophyll \( a \) concentration, 88 \( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\); and Secchi depth, 0.78 m (N. Kamman, Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation, pers. comm.). The mean TN concentration for 1997–99 was 124 \( \mu \)M (Lescaze, 1999; this study).

Macrophyte beds (primarily Potamogeton crispus L.) cover much of the lake bottom in spring and early summer (DeYoe, 1981; our observations). The winter and spring phytoplankton communities are dominated by diatoms and chlorophytes (DeYoe, 1981; our observations). Vacuolated cyanobacteria appear in May, and generally by June reach bloom densities. Aphanizomenon flos-aquae L. Rolfs, a nitrogen fixer, is the most frequent dominant, but this role is sometimes assumed by Anabaena species (including A. flos-aquae (Lyngby) Brébisson, A. circinalis Rabenhorst, and A. planctonica Brunnth.), or by non-heterocystous Planktothrix agardhii (Komarek) Anagnostides (probably what DeYoe (1981) called Oscillatoria subbrevis Schmidle) or M. aeruginosa Kuetz. emend. Elenkin (DeYoe, 1981, Lescaze 1999, current study). The zooplankton community consists of a mixture of cladocerans (especially Daphnia galeata mendotae Birge and Chydorus sphaerida O.F. Müller), copepods (mostly Acanthocyclops vernalis Fischer and Diaptomus minutus Liljeborg) and rotifers (e.g. Brachionus, Keratella, and Filinia) (Schuyler, 1972; this study). Yellow perch (Perca flavescens Mitchell) and golden shiner (Notemigonus crysoleucas Mitchell) are the most abundant fish (B. Chipman, Vermont Fish and Wildlife, pers. comm).

Nitrogen fixation

Nitrogen fixation in the lake was estimated monthly using the methods and numerical model of Levine & Lewis (1987). Integrated epilimnetic water samples were incubated with acetylene in 50-mL glass syringes suspended from a floating frame at depths of 0.02, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 m for 3 h (all analyses done in duplicate). The ethylene produced was measured on a Shimadzu GC14A gas chromatograph (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) with a Hayesep T pre-column and S primary column, and a flame ionization detector. Temperatures for the column, injector and detector were 45, 100 and 120 °C, respectively. ‘Calibration’ factors for conversion of the acetylene reduction (AR) values to nitrogen fixation rates were obtained by incubating duplicate surface samples (0.02 m) with \(^{15}\)N₂, determining the isotopic content of phytoplankton

</page>

<page number="3">

collected on pre-combusted GF/C glass fibre filters, and comparing the results with AR values for the same depth.

Nitrogen fixation is known to be a highly light-sensitive process, as light provides both reductant and ATP for the splitting of the triply bound N atoms (Paerl et al., 1981). Light inputs during incubations were estimated for each of the five incubation depths from incident solar radiation (I_0) measured on shore with a LiCor Li-190 SA light meter (LI-COR, Lincoln, NB, U.S.A.), and the light extinction rate, using the equation:

\[
I_z = I_0 e^{-\varepsilon z},
\]

where \( I_z \) is light at depth \( z \); \( I_0 \) is light at the surface; and \( \varepsilon \) is the light extinction coefficient measured with a LiCor Li-192SA submersible probe. The relationship between fixation rate and light availability was determined using the equation:

\[
N_i = N_s - N_s e^{-a} + D,
\]

where \( a = \alpha I N_s^{-1} \). \( N_i \) is the fixation at light intensity \( I \) (Ei m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)); \( N_s \) is fixation at light saturation; \( D \) is fixation in the dark; and \( \alpha \) is the slope of the rising limb of the relationship between fixation and light intensity. \( N, N_s \) and \( D \) may have the units nanomol \( N \) L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) (volumetric fixation rate) or nanomol \( N \) (million heterocysts)\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) (heterocyst-specific fixation rate).

The numerical model first determined average light intensities for 0.1-m depth intervals within the lake hourly, and then used the light response relationship to determine volumetric rates. These were multiplied by layer volumes and integrated over the depth of the epilimnion (1 m) and the 5-day period to arrive at molar estimates for the whole epilimnion.

Ammonium and nitrate uptake

Nitrate and NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates generally were measured within a day of the N fixation assay. \(^{15}\)N-labelled tracer (approximately 98 atom per cent enrichment, Cambridge Isotope Laboratories, Andover, MA, U.S.A.) was added to 300 mL glass bottles as NH\(_4\)Cl (0.83 \( \mu \)M) or NaNO\(_3\) (0.13 \( \mu \)M) and the bottles incubated in the lake at a depth of approximately 33 cm. The incubated bottles were filtered in the field over a time course (generally after 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 h) onto precombusted GF/C glass fibre filters. The filters were oven-dried at 60 \(^\circ\)C, sealed in quartz tubes containing CuO (3.0 g), CaO (approximately 0.5 g), and Cu (2.5 g) and combusted at 900 \(^\circ\)C (Kendall & Grim, 1990). The resulting nitrogen gas was analysed to determine its \(^{15}\)N/\(^{14}\)N ratio on a VG/Isogas Sira II isotope ratio mass spectrometer (VG/Isogas, Middlewich, U.K.). The following equation from Fisher et al. (1988) was used to calculate the rates of uptake:

\[
U = \frac{d(\text{atom}\% \text{P}^{15}\text{N})}{dt} \times \frac{\text{PN}}{\text{atom } \% \ ^{15}\text{NH}_4^+ \text{ or } ^{15}\text{NO}_3^-},
\]

where \( U \) = uptake rate in \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\), d(atom % P\(^{15}\)N) is the change of the isotopic composition of the PN pool over time); PN is the size of the particulate nitrogen pool; and atom per cent \(^{15}\)NH\(_4^+\) or \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) is the isotopic composition of the N pool at the midpoint of the experimental time interval. Only the initial linear portion of the labeling curve (before isotope dilution through regeneration reduced the curve slope) was used to calculate d(atom per cent P\(^{15}\)N)/dt.

A problem with using stable isotopes as tracers is that their detection requires fairly substantial isotope additions, sufficient to augment uptake rate if the process is substrate limited. We sought to minimize this effect by keeping our additions at approximately 10% of what had been mean ambient values in past years. However, DIN concentrations in summer 1999 were lower than expected, and tracer additions raised substrate concentrations by as much as 100%. Consequently, the estimates reported here [what we will call direct tracer (DT) estimates] must be viewed as potential, rather than ambient, rates. Their usefulness is mainly in assessing whether uptake was substrate limited. Nitrogen-sufficient algae should take up N near the maximum uptake velocity (\( V_{\text{max}} \)) with and without substrate addition, as in both cases uptake rate is determined by enzyme activity or other physiological variables, not substrate concentration (Levine, 1989).

Rates of substrate uptake at ambient concentrations may be obtained by determining Michaelis–Menten relationships for the processes and solving the equations for ambient substrate concentrations (Dowd & Riggs, 1965). We carried out this procedure on 19 August. Water samples were treated with \(^{15}\)N-label and either KNO\(_3\) or NH\(_4\)Cl at six different concentrations (0, 0.07, 0.15, 0.36, 0.71 and 1.79 \( \mu \)M) and incubated at a depth of 0.33 m for 4–5 h. Rate constants for uptake were obtained from the difference in particulate \(^{15}\)N content at the beginning and end of the incubation period. To facilitate the use of

</page>

<page number="4">

the relationship to estimate ambient uptake on dates other than 19 August, we normalised the equation to chlorophyll \( a \). Consequently, the following equation was used to acquire what we refer to as Michaelis–Menten (MM) estimates of ambient uptake rates:

\[
U_a^c = U_{\text{max}}^c \frac{S}{K_m + S} \times \text{chl.},
\]

where \( U_a^c \) is the ambient uptake rate (\( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\)); \( U_{\text{max}}^c \) is the maximum uptake velocity [\( \mu \)mol (\( \mu \)g chlorophyll \( a \) L\(^{-1}\)) h\(^{-1}\)]; \( S \) is the substrate concentration (\( \mu \)M); \( K_m \) is the half-saturation constant (\( \mu \)M); and chl. is the chlorophyll \( a \) concentration (\( \mu \)g L\(^{-1}\)). Because temperature changed little over the summer and cyanobacteria were consistently dominant, we believe the equation obtained on 19 August was roughly accurate for the summer period. In spring and late autumn, however, temperatures were lower and diatoms dominant, so the equation was inappropriate. Fortunately, substrate concentrations were high during these periods, so that the direct tracer measures are probably good estimators of ambient rates.

On 20 August, we examined the relationship between NO\(_3^-\) and NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates and light intensity. Samples were treated with \( ^{15}\)N-labelled substrate and incubated at four depths (0.02, 0.25, 0.5, 1 or 2 m) in the lake for 4–5 h. The light intensities experienced at each depth were determined using solar radiation and light extinction data obtained with a LiCor light meter, and use of eqn 1. The generation of light response curves for ammonium and nitrate uptake was not necessary, however, as light-stimulated uptake was not observed (see below). Thus, whole epilimnion uptake rates were obtained by simply multiplying the volume of this layer by the volumetric uptake rates measured at 0.33 m.

Natural stable isotope distribution

Determination of the relative contributions of DIN and nitrogen fixation to phytoplankton N nutrition from the distribution of N isotopes in lakes is possible because the isotopic signatures of NH\(_4^+\) and NO\(_3^-\) generally differ from that of atmospheric nitrogen. The phytoplankton signature reflects the ‘mix’ of source use. Specifically,

\[
\text{PC} = \frac{(\delta^{15}\text{N}_i - f_i) - \delta^{15}\text{N}_p}{(\delta^{15}\text{N}_i - f_i) - (\delta^{15}\text{N}_a - f_a)} \times 100,
\]

where PC is the percent contribution of nitrogen fixation to N incorporation; \( \delta^{15}\text{N}_i \), \( \delta^{15}\text{N}_p \), and \( \delta^{15}\text{N}_a \) are the isotopic signatures of DIN, phytoplankton and atmospheric N\(_2\), respectively; and \( f_i \) and \( f_a \) correct for isotopic fractionation during DIN uptake and nitrogen fixation, respectively (modified from Shearer & Kohl, 1989). Delta \( ^{15}\)N is defined as

\[
\delta^{15}\text{N}(\%) = \frac{(\frac{^{15}\text{N}}{^{14}\text{N}})_{\text{sample}} - (\frac{^{15}\text{N}}{^{14}\text{N}})_{\text{standard}}}{(\frac{^{15}\text{N}}{^{14}\text{N}})_{\text{standard}}} \times 1000,
\]

where the standard is atmospheric nitrogen (the signature of which is defined as 0\%). \( \delta^{15}\text{N}_i \) is generally a composite variable, as NH\(_4^+\) and NO\(_3^-\) may have different isotopic signatures. However, we use only the value of \( \delta^{15}\text{NH}_4^+ \) here because NH\(_4^+\) concentrations typically were much greater than NO\(_3^-\) concentrations, and uptake rates for ammonium were much greater than those for nitrate (see below). We assumed that \( f_a \) was −2\%, as this is the amount of fractionation normally reported for cyanobacteria growing in culture with N\(_2\) as their sole N source (Wada & Hattori, 1976; Macko, Estep & Hoering, 1982; Gu & Alexander, 1993b; Lescaze, 1999). The value of \( f_i \) is dependent on substrate concentration when algae are not N limited, but approaches 0\% with substrate limitation (Fogel & Cifuentes, 1993; Lescaze, 1999). Fogel & Cifuentes (1993) found 0\% fractionation during ammonium uptake by marine diatoms at concentrations <20 \( \mu \)M. We used a more conservative threshold for the decision to assume no fractionation, ammonium concentrations <5 \( \mu \)M, plus other symptoms of N limitation. We chose not to use the model in spring and autumn, when concentrations exceeded the threshold because relationships between \( f_i \) and substrate concentration have not been determined for lacustrine species.

We collected water for natural stable isotope distribution analysis from the epilimnion of Shelburne Pond biweekly during the ice-free season of 1999 (May to November), and then monthly from December to February. Samples were taken on or within 2 days of the ISI assessments. Integrated duplicate samples were obtained by lowering a 5-cm diameter, 1.83-m long PVC pipe into the water, stoppering it, and allowing the water to drain through a 150 \( \mu \)m sieve (to remove macrozooplankton) into 20-L plastic containers. Within 3 h of sample collection, seston

</page>

<page number="5">

was separated from the water through filtration onto pre-combusted Whatman GF/C glass fibre filters (nominal pore size 1.2 μm). These filters were oven-dried (60 °C) and analysed for \(^{15}\mathrm{N}/^{14}\mathrm{N}\) ratios using the method of Kendall & Grim (1990) described above. The isotopic signature obtained was assumed to be that of phytoplankton, although the seston retained on filters inevitably includes detritus and some microzooplankton and heterotrophic bacteria.

The water used in \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) analysis was filtered through Gelman Aquaprep 600 groundwater filters (pore size 0.45 μm) and stored frozen. Isotope extraction on thawed samples was according to the procedure of Downs et al. (1999). Ammonium and nitrate (2–15 μmol) were collected onto DOWEX-50W and DOWEX-1 resins, respectively, by pumping or gravity-dripping water through 2 cm diameter columns at a flow rate of 1.5 mL min\(^{-1}\). Samples were ‘dripped’ for an average of about one day, and samples with so little N present that more than 4 days were required to process them were discarded because of concerns about microbial contamination and other factors. The concentrated N was eluted with 2 M KCl, and then gathered onto precombusted and acidified 5 mm diameter GF/C filters by placing the solution and packets containing filters in sealed Nalgene bottles along with MgO (2 g L\(^{-1}\)) and, in the case of nitrate extraction, Devarda’s Alloy (4 g L\(^{-1}\)), and agitating the solution on a shaker table (speed 100 rpm) for 7 days. The filters were dried in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid (approximately 60 °C), and sealed in tin capsules (5 by 9 mm) prior to combustion and analysis for \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) abundance on a Finnigan Delta isotope ratio mass spectrometer (run by R. Michener at Boston University). Although Downs et al. (1999) reported minimal isotopic fractionation during the extraction of ammonium from water, we included NH\(_4\)Cl standards in our analyses to detect and quantify fractionation rates.

Phytoplankton and heterocysts

Samples for phytoplankton and heterocyst counts were preserved in the field with acid Lugol’s solution. Phytoplankton was concentrated in settling chambers and measured and counted under an Olympus CK2 inverted microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) at 400× magnification (Utermöhl, 1958). At least 100 fields or 100 heterocysts were counted for heterocyst density determination, but only five fields were counted for determination of species composition (these counts included >100 cells). Zooplankton samples were collected with a 64-μm mesh net hauled through the depth of the water column, and preserved with sugar-buffered formalin (Haney & Hall, 1975). Species were identified and counted under the inverted microscope.

Other measurements

To determine whether the uptake results obtained were realistic, primary production rates were measured on 20 August and multiplied by the C/N ratio of seston (4.98 by weight) to arrive at estimates of N demand. The method of Fee et al. (1992) was used to estimate whole-lake primary production from a light response curve, data on light availability in the lake and bathymetry. The light response curve was obtained by incubating duplicate light and dark bottles at four depths (0.3, 0.6, 1.0 and 1.4 m) for 4 h and estimating CO\(_2\) fixation from the change in dissolved oxygen concentrations (Wetzel & Likens, 1991). Light data were obtained as for nitrogen fixation. Particulate C and N were determined through combustion of seston collected on precombusted GF/C filters in a CE Instruments C/N analyser. These results did not take into account phytoplankton respiratory losses at night. Consequently, we used the increase in phytoplankton biomass between our samplings on 10 and 19 August to provide a second estimate of phytoplankton N demand. Phytoplankton was assumed to have a dry weight of 0.47 pg μm\(^{-3}\), a C content of 50%, and a C : N ratio of 6 : 1 by weight (Reynolds, 1984).

Temperature, pH, alkalinity, Secchi depth, light extinction rate, chlorophyll \(a\) concentration, and the concentrations of total nitrogen (TN), ammonium-N, nitrate-N, total phosphorus (TP) and soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) were measured during each of the natural stable isotope distribution samplings. Water was collected with the integrated sampler and filtered through GF/F glass fibre filters to separate particulate and dissolved phases. Chlorophyll was extracted in hot ethanol, and its colour intensity measured on a Shimadzu 1600 UV/VIS spectrophotometer (Sartory & Grobbelaar, 1984). Lorenzen’s method of acid addition (Lorenzen, 1967) was used to correct for phaeophytin pigments. Ammonium, nitrate/nitrite and phosphate

</page>

<page number="6">

were analysed on a Lachat flow injection autoanalyser (QuickChem 8000) using methods described by Patton & Crouch (1977); Anderson (1979) and Murphy & Riley (1962), respectively. Alkalinity was determined by sulphuric acid titration with phenolphthalein and bromcresol green-methyl red indicators (Rainwater & Thatcher, 1960), and used along with pH to calculate dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and free CO₂ concentrations (Wetzel & Likens, 1991).

Statistical analyses

Use of a mixing model to determine the relative contributions of atmospheric nitrogen and DIN to phytoplankton nutrition requires that the two sources have distinct isotopic signatures. We used a t-test (\( P = 0.05 \)) to confirm that the mean \( \delta^{15}N \) value of NH\(_4^+\) was significantly different from \( -2\%_{oo} \), the normal value for phytoplankton totally reliant on fixation as a N source. One-way ANOVA using the Student–Newman–Keuls (SNK) test was used to test for differences in NH\(_4^+\) uptake rates during the light-uptake experiment. To investigate the role of environmental parameters on NH\(_4^+\) and NO\(_3^-\) uptake and N\(_2\) fixation rates, and on natural stable isotope distribution results, Pearson product moment correlation analysis (Darlington, 1975) was performed using at a significance level of \( P = 0.05 \).

Results

Physicochemical conditions

Shelburne Pond displayed many symptoms of eutrophy during our study, including a TP concentration of 0.9–7.0 \( \mu \)M (0.1–0.4 \( \mu \)M present as SRP) and a TN concentration of 66–137 \( \mu \)M (Fig. 1a,b). Ammonium and nitrate concentrations were substantial (26.7 and 1.6 \( \mu \)M) when the study began in May, but were greatly reduced (to 1.45 and 0.01 \( \mu \)M) by the first cyanobacterial bloom in June (Fig. 1b). Decomposition of this bloom later in the month may have been responsible for the pulse in NH\(_4^+\) (34 \( \mu \)M) observed on 29 June; otherwise both fractions were present at very low concentrations (NH\(_4^+\), 0.7–1.6 \( \mu \)M; NO\(_3^-\), 0.01–0.05 \( \mu \)M) until late August. Ammonium concentration reached 31 \( \mu \)M on 4 September, and remained above 23 \( \mu \)M for the remainder of the growth season. Nitrate concentration rose gradually from mid-September into winter, probably because of nitrification of accumulated NH\(_4^+\) as well as catchment inputs.

Molar TN : TP and DIN : TP ratios (Fig. 1c) were relatively high during late autumn and winter (83–151 : 1 and 19–75 : 1, respectively) but, in summer, fell below the thresholds for N limitation suggested by Morris & Lewis (1988), 33 : 1 and 3 : 1 respectively. TN : TP ranged from 24–34 : 1, while DIN : TP was normally between 0.2–0.5 : 1 (except on 29 June when it rose to 10 : 1). Throughout the growth season, TN : TP ratio was no more than half the threshold level above which Smith (1983) predicts cyanobacterial scarcity.

The lake was circumneutral (pH 7.5–7.8) in winter but during the growth season slightly alkaline (pH 8.2–9.2) (Fig. 2a). Consequently most of the DIC available to phytoplankton was bicarbonate and carbonate rather than CO₂. DIC concentration over the growth season was relatively stable, 2.32–2.62 mM, but free CO₂ varied widely with shifts in temperature and pH (from 0.01 to 0.31 mM; Fig. 2a). However, free CO₂ concentration did not fall below the compensation concentration of chlorophytes (approximately 0.01 mM, Shapiro, 1990).

Light extinction coefficient was high (1.12–3.80 m⁻¹) and Secchi depth low (0.40–1.68 m; Fig. 2b) in summer because of high algal turbidity. Although the lake was frozen in winter and cool in early spring and late autumn, temperatures of 21–28 °C were maintained from late May to mid-September (Fig. 2b).

Biological conditions and nitrogen demand

Chlorophyll a concentration was relatively low in May (5–9 μg L⁻¹) but rose to 60 μg L⁻¹ by mid-June, and for the remainder of the summer stayed above 30 μg L⁻¹ (Fig. 3a). Blooms occurred in mid-June, from mid-July to mid-August, and in mid-September, yielding chlorophyll a concentrations of 60, 88–92 and 69 μg L⁻¹, respectively. Surface scums were visible during calm weather throughout most of the ice-free season.

Diatoms dominated the phytoplankton community from late autumn through spring but were replaced by cyanobacteria in May (Fig. 3b). Aphanizomenon flos-aquae, a nitrogen fixer, was the most abundant species in the lake in early and late summer, but was overwhelmed numerically by non-heterocystous P. agardhii during much of July and August. Microcystis aeruginosa also was present in appreciable numbers during the period of P. agardhii dominance, and Anabaena species (including A. flos-aquae, A. circinalis and A. planctonica) were found in samples throughout the ice-free season and for two months under ice. Although Aphanizomenon numbers increased in autumn, following loss of P. agardhii from the lake, Anabaena species were more important fixers during this period. Heterocyst densities were consistently low for the amount of Aphanizomenon and Anabaena present. We measured 809 mL⁻¹ in mid-June, but <200 mL⁻¹ during the remainder of the growth season (Fig. 3a). The average number of heterocysts present per 100 fixer cells was never greater than three (Table 1).

Zooplankton grazers were most abundant in spring, declined to a late summer minimum, and then reached a smaller autumn peak. Rotifers made up much of the community in spring, whereas cladocerans were particularly important in summer. Daphnia galeata mendotae was the most abundant cladoceran, but was outnumbered by Chydorus sphaeridus for a few weeks in midsummer. Copepods (especially Acanthocyclops varians and Diaptomus minuta) were present throughout the ice-free season as subdominants.

Light response curves for primary productivity on 20 August indicated that carbon fixation saturated at a light intensity of 200 μEi m⁻² s⁻¹ (Iₖ; Table 2). The mean daytime light intensity in the mixed layer of the lake (upper 1 m) was only about one third as high, 67 μEi m⁻² s⁻¹; consequently, primary productivity was largely light limited at this time. Our primary production model indicated that 370 kmol C were fixed in the epilimnion during the 5 day period preceding our 20 August NSID sampling. Consequently,
