The control was made up as suggested by (15), in order to detect production of endogenous ethylene. To avoid oxidation of endogenous ethylene, we added 500 ml. l-1 acetylene (16). After incubation, 3 ml of the gaseous sample was transferred to vacuntainers of 7 ml capacity; these were conditioned in a refrigerator for later injection into a chromatograph. To determine the concentration of ethylene produced, 0.5 ml was injected into a Varin Star 3400® gas chromatograph, with a Poropak Q® 80/100 3 m x 8 mm column, FID at 220 °C, column temperature 60 °C, injector at 100 °C, using N2 as the carrier gas. The concentration of organic carbon in the sediment was determined by oxidizing the samples with 0.4 N dichromate as recommended by (17). Extraction of ammonia and nitrate in the sediment was done using 2 M KCl as described by (18). To determine the concentration of ammonia, we used the method proposed by (19). For nitrate, we used the continuous flow injection technique (FIA) (20). Pearson's linear correlation was used to test the degree of association between the rate of biological nitrogen fixation and the ammonia concentration. RESULTS The air temperature varied from 10 to 23°C during the experiment period, with the lower values at night (table II). In spite of this large variation, no significant correlation between temperature and biological nitrogen fixation was observed (table III). The values of fixed molecular nitrogen varied during the period, and also varied among replicates. Highest mean fixation was observed during the first incubation (19:00 hours) (table II). No clear difference was observed between the morning and evening periods, but the results obtained initially (between 19:00 and 04:00 hours) were higher than those obtained during the period following. The smallest mean value obtained for biologically fixed nitrogen was 0.02 (nmol g-1 dw h-1), and the highest was 0.46 (nmol g-1 dw h-1). In two samples the biological nitrogen fixation rate was 0; in the remaining replicates the values obtained were low. There was no variation in values of organic carbon in the sediment. The lowest value obtained was 10.9%dw and the highest was 14.0%dw. The concentration of ammonia varied more but showed no clear pattern corresponding with the period of the experiment. The highest concentration was measured in the sediment of the samples incubated at 19:00 hours on the second day (table III). The expression of the rate of biological nitrogen fixation as a function of nutrient availability demonstrates very clearly the relationship between nutrient concentration and the activity of diazotrophic bacteria. The results indicate that the concentrations of carbon and nitrogen were not directly responsible for the observed rates of nitrogen fixation (tab. III). No significant linear correlation was obtained between temperature, organic carbon and ammonia and the rates of biological nitrogen fixation, which indicated that the observed rates were independent of these factors. DISCUSSION In this study there was no huge difference between the rates observed during the day and night periods, although the highest rate, observed at 19:00 hours (table II), may have resulted from an interaction between the plants and the diazotrophs. Recent studies have demonstrated that the diazotrophic organisms are capable of utilizing photosynthesis products as a carbon source; these products are then leached out, thus making possible higher fixation rates during the night (21). The availability of oxygen and carbon in the sediment is in great part dependent on the metabolism of rooted aquatic macrophytes, which demonstrates the importance of the association with the diazotrophs. The plants can affect bacterial growth by reducing the availability of oxygen, by competing for available nutrients, or by providing a carbon source (22). Many species of plants use nitrogen fixed by diazotrophic organisms as a source of nutrients (23, 24, 25). In oligotrophic ecosystems, biological nitrogen fixation can contribute significantly toward the total nitrogen that might be available to the primary producers (26). Thus, nitrogen fixation can be an important nitrogen source for aquatic ecosystems, as pointed out by (27). However, eutrophic systems shows high rates of nitrogen fixation (28, 29), suggesting that biological nitrogen fixation is independent of the trophic state of the lake, or other preponderant factors in determining nitrogenase activity. The sharp decrease observed at 07:00 (tab. II) was not a result of temperature differences, since higher fixation rates were recorded in samples incubated at lower or higher temperatures. This is corroborated by the low linear correlation between temperature and fixation. A similar result was observed for the concentration of organic carbon and ammonia in the sediment. This demonstrates that in the samples studied, other factors than temperature, organic carbon, and ammonia are responsible for the results obtained. However, not only the quantity of available carbon is important, but also its quality. In the sediment of Imboacica Lagoon there is a large quantity of refractory carbon derived from the decomposition of aquatic macrophytes (30). So, the process of biological nitrogen fixation, which generates a high energy demand, would be limited by the quality and not the quantity of the organic carbon present in the sediment. But, the concentration of oxygen in the sediment, which was not estimated in this study may have been the controlling factor for the activity of the diazotrophs, since it is an important regulatory factor (8). The drying sediment resulted from the opening of the sand barrier separating the lagoon from the sea was insufficient to interrupt the activity of the diazotrophs. The lack of total drying sediment (high moisture content) provided minimum necessary conditions for the diazotrophs to continue nitrogen fixation. However, we do not have results permitting us to compare the rates observed before the opening of the barrier with those obtained in this present study. It is possible that although the opening of the barrier did not totally interfere with the diazotrophs, nevertheless it may have drastically reduced nitrogen fixation. This is due tho the biological nitrogen fixation wich is more representative at the surface fraction of the sediment under stable physical conditions such as low turbulence and a stratified water column (31). Fewer data are available on the effect of different types of effluents on nitrogen fixation (32). Imboacica Lagoon, impacted by several different human activities, wich may provide a natural laboratory for future investigations in this area. De Assis Esteves VOLUME: 40.1 ISSUE: MONTH: YEAR: 1997 PAGES: 143-151 ISSN: 0365-0979 OCLC #: 1514223 PATRON: Fulweiler, Robinson Processed by RapidX: 6/8/2022 11:46:06 AM BIOLOGICAL NITROGEN FIXATION IN A BRAZILIAN COASTAL LAGOON Andre L. dos S. Furtado¹ & Francisco de A. Esteves² ¹Limnologie Geschiteten Seen, Institut für Gewässerökologie und Binnenfischerei, Alte Fischerhütte, D-16775 Neuglobsow, Deutschland (present address). ²Lab. de Limnologia, Depto. de Ecologia, Inst. de Biologia, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Cidade Universitária, Ilha do Fundão, Rio de Janeiro, 21941-590, Brazil Recebido para publicação em 21 de outubro de 1996 ABSTRACT The objective of this study was to quantify biological nitrogen fixation in the sediment of Imboacica Lagoon after the opening of the sand barrier separating the lagoon from the sea. The activity of the diazotrophs was greater at night; the highest fixation rate was 0.48 nmol g⁻¹ dw⁻¹. No significant linear correlation was observed between nitrogen fixation rates and the air temperature, carbon concentration or ammonia in the sediment. This had demonstrated that other factors were determining the rates measured. The activity of the diazotrophs was not limited by the concentration of organic carbon although the quality of this carbon may be responsible for the measured rates. Inspite of the breaching of the sand barrier and a consequent draining of most of the lagoon caused the sediment to be directly exposed to solar radiation. This process did not impede the nitrogen-fixing activity of the diazotrophic organisms, this might be because of the large amount of water retained in the sediment maintaining the minimum necessary conditions for the diazotrophs. key-words: diazotrophs, coastal lagoon, biological nitrogen fixation, sediment INTRODUCTION The coastal lagoons in the northern part of the State of Rio de Janeiro are located in an intensively developed by the local community and for tourism. In recent decades, these lagoons have been directly affected by different anthropomorphic activities. The effect of such activities on Imboacica Lagoon, wich is located in the suburbs of the Municipality of Macaé ,is a clear example of the lack of an environmental protection policy. Evaluations of water quality parameters, although important for the biota, are generally not efficient indicators of human impact (1). This is basically because of the lack of informing about the effects of many toxic agents on organisms, and on the environmental variations intrinsic. In addition, it has been observed that the first effects are seen on some species, wich are considered "key-species", and/or at the level of processes (2). Among these processes there is nutrient cycling, particularly the nitrogen cycle, which is an essential element for protein synthesis. In lacustrine systems, biological nitrogen fixation is carried out by organisms called diazotrophs. These may be autotrophic or heterotrophic, and can be facultative or obligate nitrogen- fixers. Two methods have been used to estimate biological nitrogen fixation: the radioactive isotope (N^{15}), and the acetylene reduction. The acetylene reduction technique has the advantage of practicality being inexpensive, sensitive, and operates very fast in obtaining results (3, 4). This technique has been found in comparative studies to be an efficient means of estimating biological nitrogen fixation (5). Variations in nitrogen fixation rates may result from the interaction of several factors. Levine & Lewis (6), in studying diazotrophs presence in water column observed that the vertical distribution of these organisms was responsible for the pattern observed. In an irrigated ricefield, nitrogenase activity was determined by temperature and radiation (7). However, it had also been suggested that nitrogen fixation was regulated by oxygen concentration and availability of organic carbon (8). The acetylene reduction method is relatively old (9), and numerous studies had been carried out in tropical as well as temperate ecosystems. However, there was in coastal lagoon only a study to measure the nitrogen fixation by phytoplankton in Pel-harvey Lagoon, Australia (10). Nevertheless, the present study is the first in the coastal lagoon system in northern Rio de Janeiro to estimate biological nitrogen fixation. In recent years, in spite of its socio-economic importance to the region, Imboacica Lagoon has been constantly impacted by human activity. These impacts consists of three basic kinds: landfills for residential construction, now covering about 15% of the area; dumping of untreated domestic waste; and occasional lowering of the water level by opening the sand barrier separating the lagoon from the sea. This last factor causes in the direct exposure of the sediment to solar radiation, resulting the death of aquatic macrophytes present in the littoral zone, and benthic macroalgae in the central part of the lagoon. Thus, the objective of the present investigation was to quantify biological nitrogen fixation in the sediment of Imboacica Lagoon after the opening of the sand barrier. We intended also to determine whether temperature, concentration of organic carbon, or ammonia content of the sediment are correlated with biological nitrogen fixation. STUDY AREA Imboacica Lagoon is located in the Municipality of Macaé (22° 50'S - 44° 42'W), and has the following morphometric characteristics: area 3.26 x 10^6 m^2; volume 3.56 x 10^6 m^3; maximum depth 2.2 m; mean depth 1.09 m; perimeter 27.6 km; maximum effective length 5.3 km; and maximum effective width 1.3 km. The regional climate is warm and humid and the period of greatest precipitation occurs in the summer, and the least in winter (11). About 30% of the present area of Imboacica Lagoon is occupied by the aquatic macrophyte Typha domingensis, but other macrophytes, such as Eleocharis cf. fistulosa, Eichhornia crassipes, Salvinia sp. and Nymphaea sp. also occur with more restricted distribution. In the littoral zone, the sediment consists of a high proportion of very fine silts and clays. The daily input of total nitrogen and phosphorus through a single sewage canal is 70 kg and 7 kg respectively (12). The mean concentration of total nitrogen, available phosphate and organic carbon in the sediment varies respectively from 0.04 to 0.24 mmol/g, 1.56 to 7.51 mmol/g, and 0.28 to 4.88 mmol/g. The granulometry of the lagoon sediments is diverse, varying from pebbles to clays. Near the sea, fine sand (22.3%) and very fine silt (19.3%) predominate, with smaller percentages of granules (0.9%), medium silt (1.6%), and coarse silt (2.0%). The sediment of the littoral region near the mouth of the Imboacica River has a higher percentage of very fine silt (24.7%) and clays (15.1%), and a lower proportion of pebbles (0.1%) and granules (0.9%). The concentration of nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus) in the water column is shown in table I. MATERIAL AND METHODS The nitrogen-fixing activity of diazotrophic organisms in Imboacica Lagoon estimatly using the acetylene reduction method (9) quantifies the activity of nitrogenase; the enzyme responsible for this process. The theoretical conversion factor was 4 moles of ethylene produced per 1 mole of nitrogen fixed (13). For estimatimation of nitrogenase activity by the acetylene reduction method, samples are not to be incubated longer than 6 hours, then the inhibition of bacterial growth may lead to errors (14). Thus, the samples were incubated for 3 hours. The samples of the upper 5 cm of sediment were collected ten days after the opening of the sand barrier, near the edge of a stand of Typha domingensis Pers. (Typhaceae). There was no surface water at the site, but the sediment was moist and covered with detritus from decaying T. domingensis. The samples were incubated in 120 ml glass flasks. For each interval time four incubations were carried out, i.e. three replicates and one control. The samples were incubated according to the following schedule: 19:00, 22:00, 01:00, 04:00, 07:00, 10:00, 13:00, 16:00 and 19:00 hours. ![Map showing the location of the experiment in Typha domingensis Pers. stand in Imboacica lagoon](page_1012_1342_627_388.png) Figure 1. After incubation, 3 ml of the gaseous sample was transferred to vacuntainers of 7 ml capacity; these were conditioned in a refrigerator for later injection into a chromatograph. To determine the concentration of ethylene produced, 0.5 ml was injected into a Varin Star 3400® gas chromatograph, with a Poropak Q® 80/100 3 m x 8 mm column, FID at 220 °C, column temperature 60 °C, injector at 100 °C, using N2 as the carrier gas. The concentration of organic carbon in the sediment was determined by oxidizing the samples with 0.4 N dichromate as recommended by (17). Extraction of ammonia and nitrate in the sediment was done using 2 M KCl as described by (18). To determine the concentration of ammonia, we used the method proposed by (19). For nitrate, we used the continuous flow injection technique (FIA) (20). Pearson's linear correlation was used to test the degree of association between the rate of biological nitrogen fixation and the ammonia concentration. RESULTS The air temperature varied from 10 to 23°C during the experiment period, with the lower values at night (table II). In spite of this large variation, no significant correlation between temperature and biological nitrogen fixation was observed (table III). The values of fixed molecular nitrogen varied during the period, and also varied among replicates. Highest mean fixation was observed during the first incubation (19:00 hours) (table II). No clear difference was observed between the morning and evening periods, but the results obtained initially (between 19:00 and 04:00 hours) were higher than those obtained during the period following. The smallest mean value obtained for biologically fixed nitrogen was 0.02 (nmol g-1 dw h-1), and the highest was 0.46 (nmol g-1 dw h-1). In two samples the biological nitrogen fixation rate was 0; in the remaining replicates the values obtained were low. There was no variation in values of organic carbon in the sediment. The lowest value obtained was 10.9%dw and the highest was 14.0%dw. The concentration of ammonia varied more but showed no clear pattern corresponding with the period of the experiment. The highest concentration was measured in the sediment of the samples incubated at 19:00 hours on the second day (table III). The expression of the rate of biological nitrogen fixation as a function of nutrient availability demonstrates very clearly the relationship between nutrient concentration and the activity of diazotrophic bacteria. The results indicate that the concentrations of carbon and nitrogen were not directly responsible for the observed rates of nitrogen fixation (tab. III). No significant linear correlation was obtained between temperature, organic carbon and ammonia and the rates of biological nitrogen fixation, which indicated that the observed rates were independent of these factors. DISCUSSION In this study there was no huge difference between the rates observed during the day and night periods, although the highest rate, observed at 19:00 hours (table II), may have resulted from an interaction between the plants and the diazotrophs. Recent studies have demonstrated that the diazotrophic organisms are capable of utilizing photosynthesis products as a carbon source; these products are then leached out, thus making possible higher fixation rates during the night (21). The availability of oxygen and carbon in the sediment is in great part dependent on the metabolism of rooted aquatic macrophytes, which demonstrates the importance of the association with the diazotrophs. The plants can affect bacterial growth by reducing the availability of oxygen, by competing for available nutrients, or by providing a carbon source (22). Many species of plants use nitrogen fixed by diazotrophic organisms as a source of nutrients (23, 24, 25). In oligotrophic ecosystems, biological nitrogen fixation can contribute significantly toward the total nitrogen that might be available to the primary producers (26). Thus, nitrogen fixation can be an important nitrogen source for aquatic ecosystems, as pointed out by (27). However, eutrophic systems shows high rates of nitrogen fixation (28, 29), suggesting that biological nitrogen fixation is independent of the trophic state of the lake, or other preponderant factors in determining nitrogenase activity. The sharp decrease observed at 07:00 (tab. II) was not a result of temperature differences, since higher fixation rates were recorded in samples incubated at lower or higher temperatures. This is corroborated by the low linear correlation between temperature and fixation. A similar result was observed for the concentration of organic carbon and ammonia in the sediment. This demonstrates that in the samples studied, other factors than temperature, organic carbon, and ammonia are responsible for the results obtained. However, not only the quantity of available carbon is important, but also its quality. In the sediment of Imboacica Lagoon there is a large quantity of refractory carbon derived from the decomposition of aquatic macrophytes (30). So, the process of biological nitrogen fixation, which generates a high energy demand, would be limited by the quality and not the quantity of the organic carbon present in the sediment. But, the concentration of oxygen in the sediment, which was not estimated in this study may have been the controlling factor for the activity of the diazotrophs, since it is an important regulatory factor (8). The drying sediment resulted from the opening of the sand barrier separating the lagoon from the sea was insufficient to interrupt the activity of the diazotrophs. The lack of total drying sediment (high moisture content) provided minimum necessary conditions for the diazotrophs to continue nitrogen fixation. However, we do not have results permitting us to compare the rates observed before the opening of the barrier with those obtained in this present study. It is possible that although the opening of the barrier did not totally interfere with the diazotrophs, nevertheless it may have drastically reduced nitrogen fixation. This is due tho the biological nitrogen fixation wich is more representative at the surface fraction of the sediment under stable physical conditions such as low turbulence and a stratified water column (31). Fewer data are available on the effect of different types of effluents on nitrogen fixation (32). Imboacica Lagoon, impacted by several different human activities, wich may provide a natural laboratory for future investigations in this area. Sediment accumulation and organic material flux in a managed mangrove ecosystem: estimates of land–ocean–atmosphere exchange in peninsular Malaysia

D.M. Alongi a,*, A. Sasekumar b, V.C. Chong b, J. Pfitzner a, L.A. Trott a, F. Tirendi a, P. Dixon a, G.J. Brunskill a

a Australian Institute of Marine Science, PMB No. 3, Townsville M.C., Qld. 4810, Australia
b Institute of Biological Sciences, University of Malaya, Kuala Lumpur 50603, Malaysia

Received 13 May 2002; accepted 14 April 2004

Abstract

Rates of sediment accumulation and organic matter decomposition in mangrove forests of different age were examined at the Matang Mangrove Forest Reserve in peninsular Malaysia. These data were used with previous findings to construct a first-order mass balance of carbon to determine whether the ecosystem is net heterotrophic or autotrophic, and to estimate land–ocean–atmosphere exchange. Measurements of various carbon and nitrogen processes in sediments suggest that organic matter is rapidly and efficiently mineralized to a depth of 1 m. Rates of total carbon oxidation in sediments (\( T_{COX} \)) ranged from 77 to 118 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) with no significant differences with forest age. Sulfate reduction (range: 19–53 mmol S m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) appeared to be the dominant decomposition pathway, accounting for an average of 51–75% of sediment \( T_{COX} \). Aerobic respiration (range: 5–20 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) accounted for \( \approx 5–20\% \) of mean \( T_{COX} \). Methanogenesis was not measurable. Denitrification (range: 0.4–11.0 mmol N\(_2\) m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) was rapid but very variable, and may have accounted for \( \approx 25\% \) of \( T_{COX} \) at the old-growth forest. Rates of sediment mass accumulation (range: 2.2–11.4 kg m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\)) were rapid compared with previous measurements in mangroves. Efficiency of carbon burial (range: 23–29 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) in sediments increased from 16% to 27% from the youngest to the oldest forest. The ratio of sediment \( T_{COX} \) to mangrove net primary production decreased from 28% to 7% with increasing forest age. The efficiency of N mineralization (range: 67–81%) and burial (range: 10–29%) in sediments showed the opposite pattern. Tree N demand required from 8 to 22 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). Surface N\(_2\) fixation was measurable only in two of six trials, but was rapid (range: 2.3–3.0 mmol N\(_2\) m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)). A mass balance of carbon for the entire reserve suggests that the ecosystem is currently net autotrophic, with a net ecosystem production of \( \approx 21 \times 10^9 \) mol C year\(^{-1}\) and an ecosystem \( P/R \) of 1.4. Despite considerable uncertainty, forest production and respiration clearly dominates carbon flow, accounting for \( \approx 95\% \) of total inputs and \( \approx 79\% \) of total outputs, respectively. River inputs, phytoplankton primary production and trash fish inputs to fish cage aquaculture in the waterways were comparatively minor. Export of mangrove detritus equated to 25% of net canopy production; only 2% of total carbon input to the ecosystem was buried in mangrove sediments. Clear felling and thinning of forests accounted for \( <1\% \) of total outputs; 73% of total carbon

inputs to the ecosystem were respired. Our budget indicates that the major exchange of carbon in this managed ecosystem is between forest and atmosphere.

Keywords: carbon cycle; nitrogen cycle; mass balance; mangrove; diagenesis

1. Introduction

The tropical coastal zone is one of the most biogeochemically active regions of the biosphere, representing a potentially important sink or source of carbon. Mangrove forests are dominant ecosystems along tropical coastlines and are important interfaces in the exchange of sediment, organic materials and gases between land, atmosphere and ocean. Twilley et al. (1992) estimated global storage of mangrove carbon at \( 3 \times 10^{14} \) mol C with 70% of this carbon stored within 10° of the equator; net ecosystem production of mangroves was estimated to be \( 1.5 \times 10^{13} \) mol C year\(^{-1}\). More recently, Gattuso et al. (1998) estimated that global mangrove gross primary production averages \( 4.6 \times 10^{13} \) mol C year\(^{-1}\) with mean net ecosystem production of \( 1.8 \times 10^{13} \) mol C year\(^{-1}\) and an ecosystem \( P/R \) ratio of 1.4. Mass balance models of other mangrove ecosystems (Alongi et al., 1998a, 2000) support current global estimates that most mangroves are net autotrophic.

At the ecosystem level, mangrove trees dominate carbon and nitrogen flow, being among the most productive plants in the ocean (Alongi, 2002). Despite this high productivity, most labile carbon fixed by the trees appears to be retained within the ecosystem (Twilley, 1988). Nitrogen also appears to be efficiently assimilated and retained, due possibly to the evolution of various conservation mechanisms. At the forest level, trees and microbial consortia constitute a tight energetic link in concert with crabs, that as keystone species, intensively bioturbate sediments fostering microbial growth and soil conditions beneficial to tree growth (Kristensen et al., 1995; Alongi et al., 2002).

In Southeast Asia where 35% of the world’s mangrove forests are located, rapid economic and population growth has resulted in severe environmental problems, including soil erosion, pollution and increased reliance on mangroves for aquaculture and wood products. In the future, it is predicted that these pressures will continue and may even increase until late this century (Alongi, 2002). An understanding of how mangrove forests functionally relate to land, sea and atmosphere is crucial for their survival and for an understanding of potential impacts on mangrove ecosystems from problems in adjacent catchments, offshore and in the atmosphere.

In this paper, we describe sediment carbon and nitrogen flows in relation to forest production and construct a preliminary mass balance of carbon to identify the extent of interaction between mangroves and the environment. The Matang Mangrove Forest Reserve in northwestern peninsular Malaysia was chosen as our study area for several reasons. First, the reserve is arguably the best example of a managed mangrove ecosystem. It has been managed on a sustainable basis mostly for wood since first gazetted in 1906 (Watson, 1928; Gan, 1995). A better understanding of this ecosystem is important since it is often used as a model for other regional countries to follow. Second, the reserve is one of the best-studied mangrove ecosystems in Southeast Asia, offering an opportunity to use data accumulated over at least two decades to construct a mass balance to identify the major sources and sinks of carbon. Few such budgets exist for a complete mangrove ecosystem, and such information is needed to assess the potential impact of global climate change and the increased environmental threats in Southeast Asia. Finally, long-term management of the reserve means that the age of all of the forests are known, giving us an opportunity to gain possible insights into the influence of forest age on carbon and nitrogen cycling.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Study area

The Matang Mangrove Forest Reserve is situated in the state of Perak, on the northwest coast of

</page>

<page number="2">

peninsular Malaysia (Fig. 1). The reserve, with a total surface area of 48,804 ha, is comprised of 40,151 ha of mostly Rhizophora apiculata forest ranging in age from 1 to 30 years, and forms a large crescent-shaped embayment stretching for \( \approx 50 \) km along the coast bordering the Straits of Malacca. A small area is reserved for virgin forest that is roughly 85 years old and harvested only once early last century (Gan, 1995). Tides are semi-diurnal with a mean tidal range of 2.5 m (Sasekumar et al., 1994).

The reserve has been able to sustain a continuing need for charcoal and other wood and non-wood products for nearly a century (Gan, 1995). A total productive forest area of 32,746 ha is currently managed on a sustainable basis using a 30-year rotation cycle, with two thinnings between 10 and 15 years and between 20 and 25 years (Gan, 1995). The area of productive forest is equally proportioned between the 1–10-, 11–20- and 21–30-year-old age classes. About 2500 ha of forest are felled annually in small lots. The slash is left to decompose naturally. Roughly, one-half of these lots are allowed to regenerate naturally, the remainder are manually replanted. The waterways of the reserve make up a total surface area of 8653 ha with a mean water depth of 5 m (Sasekumar et al., 1994), and are the sites for a growing fish cage aquaculture industry (Alongi et al., 2003). Other commercial and traditional fishing activities include mudflat cultivation of cockles (Anadara granosa), raft culture of mussels (Perna viridis) and oysters (Ostrea folium), and baited trap catching of mud crabs (Scylla serrata). Total fisheries yield is about 28,000 million metric tons year\(^{-1}\) (Gan, 1995; Perak State Fisheries Department, unpublished data).

Three mangrove forests were sampled in August 1998 and July 1999. Stn. M5 (4°51.57' N, 100°36.93' E) is a 5-year-old R. apiculata forest consisting of moderately reducing (Eh range: –50 to –210 mV), acidic (pH range: 6.2–6.8) sediments with 81% silt and 19% clay (Alongi et al., 1998b). Stn. M18 (4°51.04' N, 100°36.72' E) is an 18-year-old R. apiculata stand that had undergone its first thinning at 10 years. A.marina is present at the seaward edge with a dense understory of the mangrove fern, Acrostichium aureum; the forest floor is thickly layered with leaf litter and slash. Sediments at Stn. M18 are reducing below 10–15 cm depth but acidic throughout a sediment profile (pH range: 6.3–6.7) that is 80% silt and 20% clay (Alongi et al., 1998b). Stn. MVR (4°50.27' N, 100°37.02' E) is an 85-year-old forest (incorrectly stated as a 60-year-old forest in Alongi et al., 1998b) located within the Pulau Kecil Virgin Jungle Reserve, dominated by R. apiculata with Bruguiera gymnorrhiza as subdominant and a sparse understory of A. aureum. The forest floor is carpeted with a thick layer of leaf, twig and bark litter. Sediments at Stn. MVR are reducing (Eh range: –50 to –330 mV), acidic (pH range: 6.1–6.5) silt (84%) and clay (16%). All three sites are at roughly the same tidal height, being inundated an average of 5–6 days (20%) per month (Putz and Chan, 1986; Alongi et al., 1998b).

2.2. Above-ground forest biomass and productivity estimates

Within each forest, three separate sets of measurements were made usually over a 100–200 m^2 area (where all sediment samples were taken) for species identification, basal area and diameter-at-breast-height (DBH) using the angle count cruising method (Clough, 1997). This method does not sample a fixed area of forest. Instead, it uses angular sighting, covering an area of forest in accordance with the size classes of the trees that fall within the scale used on a relascope, an optical device with a measuring scale of alternating black and white bands (Cintron and Novelli, 1984). Trees appearing within the field of view are compared with band width on an appropriate scale (Bitterlich, 1948). A scale factor is then applied to the raw counts to give true basal area. Stand density is then obtained from tables for number of stems per hectare based on DBH (Cintron and Novelli, 1984). These data were then used to calculate above-ground biomass based on the allometric relationships for R. apiculata obtained within the Matang Reserve by Putz and Chan (1986).

Daytime canopy production was estimated using a modified light interception method (Clough, 1997). Measurements of light absorption (n = 100 per plot) by the forest canopy were used to estimate leaf area index (LAI) (L = m^{-2} leaf area m^{-2} ground) using the formula,

\[
L = [\log_e (I)_{\text{mean}}] - [\log_e (I_0)_{\text{mean}}]/k
\]

where (I)_{mean} = mean photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) under the canopy; (I_0)_{mean} = incident PAR; and k = canopy light extinction coefficient (0.5). L was corrected to a solar zenith angle (\theta) of 4° for the latitude of these forests. Leaf area index was converted to daytime canopy photosynthesis (\(P_g\)) using the formula,

\[
P_g = A d L
\]

where d = day length (10 h) and A = average rate of photosynthesis per unit leaf area. A has been repeatedly measured in the Matang forests by Gong et al. (1992), Ong et al. (1995) and Clough et al. (1997). Based on these data, empirical values used were 0.26, 0.38 and 0.43 g C m^{-2} leaf area h^{-1} for the 5-, 18- and 85-year-old forests, respectively. A night-time foliar respiration rate of 0.06 g C m^{-2} leaf area h^{-1} (Gong et al., 1992; Clough et al., 1997; Clough, unpublished data) was used to estimate total tree respiration, assuming 14 h of effective darkness and that respiration of the woody tissues and fine roots is equivalent to leaf respiration.

2.3. Mass sediment accumulation

Mass sediment accumulation rates were determined from gamma spectrometric measurements of \(^{210}\)Pb, \(^{226}\)Ra and \(^{137}\)Cs made on sequentially sliced duplicate 95–100-cm-long cores taken at each site using a 1.5-m-long (6 cm i.d.) stainless-steel corer. Cores were taken equidistant from trees in order to minimize impacts from roots and crab burrows. Each core was cut with a clean stainless-steel cutting blade into 2-cm slices from the sediment surface to 20 cm of depth, then into 4-cm slices to the bottom of the core. Gamma ray measurements were made on 50–150 g dried and ground sediment from each slice packed by a 10 metric ton hydraulic press into a custom designed gas-tight plastic container. Direct estimation of \(^{210}\)Pb was obtained from the 46.5-keV gamma emission. After storage for 3–4 weeks, radon daughter ingrowth allowed estimation of \(^{226}\)Ra from the gamma photopeaks of \(^{214}\)Pb at 295 and 351 keV, and \(^{214}\)Bi at 609 keV. Thermonuclear bomb fallout nuclide (\(^{137}\)Cs) was estimated from the 661.6 keV gamma emission of \(^{137m}\)Ba. Four planar germanium detectors and one well germanium detector inside 10-cm-thick lead walled castles with steel liners were used. Energy spectra were calibrated with Amersham and CANMET standards of known low activity spikes of suitable nuclides in cleaned silica sand. IAEA marine reference material was used to check calibrations. Counting precision for \(^{210}\)Pb and \(^{226}\)Ra was \( \leq 10\% \), but \(^{137}\)Cs precision was 30% due to very low activities in these sediments.

Interpretations of the radiochemical profiles were done with several sub-models incorporating weighted least-squares regression analysis (Robbins, 1978, 1979). These models utilize a sediment mixed layer thickness, a decadal–century scale average input of excess \(^{210}\)Pb (total \(^{210}\)Pb minus parent \(^{226}\)Ra), and diffusion coefficients for \(^{210}\)Pb and \(^{137}\)Cs in marine sediments (Li and Gregory, 1974).

2.4. Gas and solute fluxes

Gas fluxes across the sediment–air interface were measured using one set of three opaque closed chambers (volume: 1 l; area: 82 cm\(^2\)) for O\(_2\) and CH\(_4\) fluxes, and one set of three semi-closed chambers for CO\(_2\) fluxes, placed in replicate boxcorer samples (0.027 m\(^2\) surface area) taken from each site at low tide. Each chamber had a propeller-electric motor unit and two sampling ports on opposite sides of the chamber through which a stream of airflow was maintained (in the CO\(_2\) chambers) by the propeller unit to minimize gas buildup (Alongi et al., 2001). The other chambers were closed completely and sampled via the side ports. The chambers were incubated in a field laboratory in a shaded water bath maintained at ambient seawater temperature. Water was up to, but not over, the sediment surface in each chamber. CO\(_2\) gas flux represents total carbon oxidation in exposed sediments. The O\(_2\) flux represents total oxygen consumption (chemical oxidation + aerobic respiration) from exposed sediments. Gas measurements were made via the airflow port (for CO\(_2\)) or a closed port (for O\(_2\) + CH\(_4\)) connected to a MTI Analytical Instruments P200 gas chromatograph and checked using certified standards. All gas measurements were made every 30 min until a linear change was detected (usually 2–3 h). The detection limit for all gases was 0.045 \( \mu \)M.

Solute flux was measured from identical opaque chambers submerged in a water bath with ambient seawater flowing over the entire unit. In one set of three chambers, dissolved oxygen was measured using O\(_2\) probes (TPS™ Model WP-82 DO meters) placed into one sampling port, and solutes (\( \Sigma \)CO\(_2\), DOC, DON, NH\(_4^+\), NO\(_2^-\), NO\(_3^-\), Fe, Mn) were measured by taking samples from a second port on each chamber. Water samples were taken from each chamber every 45 min for 3 h. Samples were processed in the field and analyzed in the laboratory as described in Alongi et al. (2001). Detection limits were 0.025 \( \mu \)M for dissolved C, 0.05 \( \mu \)M for NH\(_4^+\) and DON, 0.05 \( \mu \)M for NO\(_3^-\), 0.02 \( \mu \)M for NO\(_2^-\), 0.09 \( \mu \)M for Mn and 1.0 \( \mu \)M for Fe.

Another set of three opaque chambers were each poisoned with 100 ml of 37% HCHO, then flooded with ambient seawater after waiting for 20 min, closed and fitted to DO probes to measure DO changes. DO flux in these poisoned chambers represents chemical oxidation of reduced solutes diffusing from the sediment. Aerobic respiration by organisms was estimated by the difference in DO flux rates between unamended and poisoned chambers.

2.5. Sediment, leaf and rainwater nutrient pools

Porewater concentrations of NH\(_4^+\), NO\(_2^-\), NO\(_3^-\) and SO\(_4^{2-}\) were determined from duplicate cores taken at each site to a depth of 1 m. Each core was cut at 2-cm intervals and processed as described in Alongi et al. (2001, 2002). Adsorbed + exchangeable NH\(_4^+\) was measured using the KCl extraction procedure of Rosenfeld (1979).

The squeezed sediment slices were dried and ground and processed for total organic carbon and total nitrogen on Perkin-Elmer 2400 CHNS/O Series II Analyzer and a Shimadzu TOC Analyzer with solid sampler. Green leaves were collected from several trees at each site, washed in distilled water, dried to constant weight, ground to a powder and analyzed for carbon and nitrogen content on the Perkin-Elmer analyzer.

Methane concentration in the porewater was determined by placing segments of sediment slices (see above) into 50-ml Plexiglas syringes containing 10 ml of a 1-M NaOH solution. The syringes were sealed with a rubber-stopper plunger, shaken and allowed to sit for \( \approx 1 \) h (Alongi et al., 2001). Gas in the headspace was examined by gas chromatography by extruding headspace gas directly into the sampling port of the gas chromatograph. Pure methane gas was used as standard with a detection limit of 0.045 \( \mu \)M.

Rainwater was collected at the field station using a sterile bottle mounted on a retort stand placed atop a 25-cm-high plastic container. The rainwater was filtered (0.45 \( \mu \)m Minisart) using a sterile syringe and stored frozen for analyses. Rainwater and porewater N were determined by standard automated techniques (Ryle et al., 1981; Ryle and Wellington, 1982). Sulfate was determined gravimetrically by BaSO\(_4\) precipitation and filtration.

2.6. Sulfate reduction

To minimize compaction, intact cores for sulfate reduction were taken by inserting 120-cm-long plastic

</page>

<page number="5">

tubes (2.7 cm diameter) into larger (6 cm i.d.) stainless-steel cores as they were being inserted into the soil at low tide. The inner cores were extruded from the steel outer cores, capped with rubber stoppers, washed, and then injected with carrier-free \(^{35}\)S (Fossing and Jorgensen, 1989). Cores were injected at 2-cm intervals, incubated for 6 h, then sliced under a N\(_2\) atmosphere and terminated by fixing sediments at 2-cm intervals in 20% zinc acetate. Samples were then frozen until a two-step distillation procedure was used to determine the fraction of reduced radiolabel shunted into the acid-volatile sulfide (AVS) and chromium-reducible (CRS) sulfur pools.

2.7. Denitrification and nitrogen fixation

Denitrification was measured from replicate sediment samples taken from each site using the N\(_2\)-gas flux technique (Nowicki, 1994). Open-ended bottles were carefully pushed 6–10 cm into the sediment (volume: 230–385 cm) so as to avoid large roots and other biogenic structures. Any obvious infauna was removed with tweezers before each sample was extruded into a gas-tight glass chamber (height = 23.5 cm; i.d. = 7.6 cm). Sediments in each chamber were covered with \( \approx 500–800 \) ml of creek water which was sparged with either 80%He/20%O\(_2\) mixture (four experimental chambers per site) or 100% He (one to two control chambers per site, see below) to remove N\(_2\) and, in the case of the experimental cores, to maintain dissolved O\(_2\) concentrations. The overlying water in each sealed chamber was stirred continuously. All chambers were incubated for 9 days in the dark at ambient temperatures to mimic field conditions as closely as possible.

In the experimental chambers, the gas phase was flushed repeatedly with 80%He/20% O\(_2\) mixture after the water overlying sediments was periodically replaced with low-N\(_2\) seawater. The water exchanges maintained O\(_2\) and an adequate NO\(_3\) supply.

The control chambers were incubated under anaerobic conditions (100% He gas and deoxygenated water exchanges) in order to block nitrification and denitrification (Nowicki, 1994). A water exchange was carried out on day 3, followed by a 3–5 min gas flush immediately after, and 8 h after the water exchange. After day 3, each chamber was sealed and gas samples were withdrawn for measurement of O\(_2\) and N\(_2\) concentrations in the headspace. The accumulation of N\(_2\) gas in the headspace was measured each day for the next 5 days by withdrawing samples through the chamber ports with a He-flushed syringe. Samples were analyzed using a MTI Analytical Instruments P200 gas chromatograph. Calibration standards were run with each set of samples using a certified gas mixture (3% N\(_2\), 20% O\(_2\), 77% He).

Despite denitrification being blocked in the control cores, there can be significant de-gassing of N\(_2\) from the sediment porewater that diffuses into the overlying water and gas. This background flux of N\(_2\) (\( F_{dg} \)) measured in the control chambers was subtracted from the total N\(_2\) flux (\( F_t \)) measured in the experimental chambers to derive the rate of N\(_2\) flux due to denitrification (\( F_{dn} \)), where \( F_{dn} = F_t - F_{dg} \) (Nowicki, 1994). Denitrification rates were calculated as the average rate of triplicate cores from each site, from three to four individual incubation periods.

Nitrogen fixation in sediments at each site was measured in three clear and two dark chambers using the acetylene reduction technique (Capone, 1993). Samples were taken by inserting open-ended chambers (surface area: 64 cm\(^2\)) into the sediment to a depth of 5 cm. The chambers were then gently withdrawn with minimal disturbance. After return to the laboratory, the samples (sediment volume: 320 cm\(^3\)) were sampled immediately and hourly for 3 h, with a final sampling at \( \approx 20 \) h. Acetylene and ethylene were analyzed simultaneously by gas chromatography. The acetylene reduction rates were converted to rates of N\(_2\) fixation using the theoretical factor of 4 C\(_2\)H\(_2\) molecules equalling 1 N molecule.

3.2. Gas and solute fluxes from sediments

Daytime flux of CO\(_2\) gas and \( \Sigma \)CO\(_2\) from sediments (Table 2) was variable among sites and sampling intervals. There were no clear site differences in rates of gas emission, but solute flux was fastest at Stn. MVR in 1998, and at Stns. MVR and M5 in 1999. \( \Sigma \)CO\(_2\) flux was significantly slower (ANOVA, \( P < 0.05 \); Sokal and Rohlf, 1995) than gas efflux from exposed sediments at Stns. M18 and M5. CH\(_4\) flux was not detected at any of the three sites in both years.

O\(_2\) gas flux, measured only in 1998, was equivalent at Stns. M18 and MVR, but flux was slower at Stn. M5 (Table 3). 3.7. Estimates of tree N demand and a preliminary sediment N budget

Nitrogen requirements of the trees (Table 8) were estimated by multiplying net canopy production (Table 1) by leaf N content (Table 1). Tree N demand increased with increasing forest age, ranging from 8 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) at Stn. M5 up to 22 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) at Stn. MVR (Table 8). We assumed that the nitrogen required for tree growth was ultimately derived from NH\(_4\) produced by bacterial decomposition or root-associated N\(_2\) fixation, or a combination of both processes; other measured sources of N were accounted for (e.g., uptake from tidal water, Table 4).

The nitrogen data, coupled with the data on sediment mass accumulation rates, allowed construction of first-order nitrogen budgets for sediments at all three forests (Table 9). Nitrogen burial was estimated by multiplying the mass sediment accumulation rates (Table 5) by the average sediment TN content (see Section 3.3). These calculations gave increasing N burial rates of 2.6, 2.8 and 3.5 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) with decreasing forest age (Table 9).

The averaged process measurements were used to estimate total N input as the sum of the burial rate, flux of N from precipitation and tidal water, surface N\(_2\) fixation, and gross ammonification/root-associated N\(_2\) fixation (=tree N demand), assuming total inputs must equal total outputs plus accumulation at steady state (Berner, 1980). Groundwater inputs were not measured. Total N inputs increased with increasing forest age, ranging from 11.9 to 27.3 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) (Table 9). The bulk of the sediment N flow was through the ammonium pool via ammonification/root-associated N\(_2\) fixation, with comparatively slow flux across the air/water–sediment interface. The efficiency of sediment N mineralization was greatest at the old-growth forest (Stn. MVR). Burial efficiency showed the opposite pattern with the lowest burial efficiency at Stn. MVR (10%).

Our budget implies rapid turnover of the ammonium and nitrate pools, on the orders of hours to 1–2 days. On average, denitrification was a large loss in relation to N loading at Stns. M5 (93%), MVR (71%) and M18 (39%).

3.8. Estimates of sediment carbon pathways and total flux

The contribution of individual metabolic pathways to total carbon oxidation (\( T_{COX} \)) rates to a depth of 1 m were estimated for each forest (Table 10) using the diagenetic equations in Canfield (1993). Methanogenesis was not detected, but mean rates and estimates of the other pathways suggest a pattern of a proportional decrease in sulfate reduction relative to \( T_{COX} \) with increasing forest age,

</page>

<page number="12">

from 75% of \( T_{COX} \) at Stn. M5 down to 51% at Stn. MVR (Table 10). Conversely, aerobic respiration (estimated as the difference between total DO flux and DO flux in poisoned chambers) appeared to account for a smaller proportion (4%) of \( T_{COX} \) at the youngest forest (Stn. M5) than at the other two forests (18–20% of \( T_{COX} \)). Denitrification may have accounted for a significant fraction of \( T_{COX} \) especially at the old-growth forest (25% at Stn. MVR). Fe and Mn reduction, estimated by difference between \( T_{COX} \) and the sum of the other metabolic pathways, may have accounted for a moderate percentage (6–12%) of \( T_{COX} \) with the contribution decreasing with increasing forest age (Table 10).

The rates of C burial and metabolism enabled construction of a preliminary sediment carbon budget for each forest (Table 11). Summing the rates of burial and mineralization, rates of total carbon input tended to decrease with increasing forest age, ranging from 141 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) at Stn. M5 to 106 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) at Stn. MVR. Burial efficiency increased, as mineralization efficiency decreased, with increasing forest age (Table 11). This is reflected in the percentage of the ratio of total sediment carbon oxidation to forest net primary production, as the ratio decreased from 28% at Stn. M5 to 7% at Stn. MVR.

4. Discussion

4.1. Sediment–forest relations and nutrient budgets

The various measurements of sediment carbon and nitrogen metabolism suggest some influence of forest age. This is not surprising as greater primary productivity with increasing forest age would be expected to drive rates of carbon and nutrient cycling, as found in other mangrove ecosystems (Alongi et al., 2001). It appears that net primary production of R. apiculata forests in Southeast Asia does not decline until at least 80 years of age (Alongi, 2002). This pattern is contrary to most terrestrial forests, which experience age-related declines in production and nutrient cycling (Ryan et al., 1997).

There were no significant differences in total carbon oxidation among the forests because of tidal variations (more gas flux at low tide than solute flux when flooded) and intrinsic small scale variability, but there were a few patterns in the dominance of the various metabolic pathways in sediments. Sulfate reduction

</page>

<page number="13">

most often dominated organic matter decomposition, ranging from 51% to 75% of \( T_{COX} \). There was a trend toward a proportional decline in the contribution of sulfate reduction to total carbon oxidation with increasing forest age, but there was no clear age related pattern in sulfate reduction, if one considers the scatter in the data among years (1995, 1998, 1999) and variability among replicate cores and sediment depths (Alongi et al., 1998b).

Rates of sulfate reduction measured in these forests were equivalent to rates measured in other mangroves (Nedwell et al., 1994; Kristensen et al., 1995, 2000; Alongi, 2001; Alongi et al., 2001), but most previous measurements were made only to depths of <20 cm. Our data indicate that slow, but nearly constant, rates of sulfate reduction occur to 1 m. It is probable that measurable rates of sulfate reduction occur to the maximum depth of penetration of living fine roots, which can be to depths of >2–3 m in mature forests (Komiyama et al., 1987) as sulfate reducers are probably fueled by root exudates. This was implied in earlier mangrove studies that found a significant positive correlation between living fine root biomass and rates of sulfate reduction (Alongi, 2001; Alongi et al., 2001).

Rates of iron and manganese reduction were not measured, but the rates estimated by difference between \( T_{COX} \) and the other metabolic pathways suggest a moderate contribution at all three sites. This is similar to results obtained using a core incubation technique in mangroves in Western Australia (Alongi, 2001) and in Thailand (Alongi et al., 2001), but contrary to measurements by Kristensen et al. (2000) in southern Thailand using a similar incubation method. There is no direct method available to measure rates of iron and manganese reduction in sediments, so it is likely that indirect methods underestimate true reduction rates (Canfield, 1993).

Our estimates of aerobic respiration must be considered with caution, as there are no direct methods to measure only biological uptake of oxygen in sediments (Canfield, 1993). We assumed that poisoning of sediment with formaldehyde to kill all biota results in only chemical oxidation, with only minor chemical reaction between formaldehyde and oxygen. Nevertheless, the differences between gross oxygen uptake and oxygen uptake in poisoned chambers suggest that 50–60% of total \( O_2 \) uptake may be due to oxidation of reduced solutes diffusing from the sediments. There may be some aerobic respiration within roots and rhizomes, but these were not measured.

Our budget of sediment carbon (Table 11) indicates that most (73–84%) carbon transported to the forest floor is oxidized. This range is an overestimate as the rates of \( T_{COX} \) include root respiration, which is derived from atmospheric carbon fixed by the tree and is carbon not included in the measurements of sediment mass accumulation. Our model assumes steady state based on the equation, \( OC_{IN} = OC_{OUT} + OC_{ACCUMULATION} \) (Berner, 1980); there may be lateral or groundwater losses of carbon not unaccounted for, or conditions may not always be in steady state, given the fact that some forests are clear-felled and disturbed, and that some organic pollution is dumped into the waterways. Non-steady-state conditions have been attributed to mangroves in macrotidal estuaries where massive sediment movements and tidal pumping foster large variations in carbon gains and losses (Alongi, 2001). Soil disturbance is an important factor to consider as felling of trees results in extensive destruction of redox horizons and deep, extensive mixing to sediments by trampling and dragging of timber to the water’s edge (Ibrahim, 1991). Presumably, steady-state redox conditions are not restored until the forest recolonizes and roots penetrate the soil horizons.

Carbon burial rates were rapid (range: 8.5–10.7 mol C m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\)) in these Malaysian forests compared with a grand mean burial rate for mangroves of 8 mol C m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\) calculated by Twilley et al. (1992) but slightly less than the burial rate of 12.5 mol C m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\) calculated by Ong (1993) for the Matang forests. All six cores showed exponential decay profiles of excess \( ^{210}Pb \) requiring average annual \( ^{210}Pb \) fluxes ranging from 161 to 397 Bq m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\) (Table 5), which are roughly three to eight times that of atmospheric supply (Turekian et al., 1977; Feichter et al., 1991). This can be interpreted as focusing of fine sediment from a larger area of sediment resuspension and transport, to a smaller area of deposition. The \( ^{137}Cs \) inventories were small compared with the expected fallout of \( \approx 700–1000 \) Bq m\(^{-2}\) (UNSCEAR, 1977) suggesting either that these sediments have been well leached by seawater (Cs \( K_d = 10^2 \) to \( 10^3 \), Bruland, 1983) or that the deposited sediment is greatly diluted by old pre-bomb soil or marine sediment. Earlier studies indicate that net

</page>

<page number="14">

material flow is seawards (Sasekumar et al., 1994; see next section), but this does not exclude the possibility that some sediment is transported into the waterways from the Straits of Malacca. Another possibility is that sediments from eroded banks within the system undergo cycles of deposition and resuspension. Gan (1995) points out that most riverbanks appear to be accreting, but there are expanses of mangrove banks that are eroding, especially at waterway junctions.

Our rates of total carbon oxidation and burial are in good agreement with the well-known relationships between sediment carbon oxidation and deposition rate in marine sediments (Canfield, 1993). Rates of sulfate reduction were at the mid-portion of the range of rates measured in marine sediments under similar rates of sediment accumulation (Henrichs, 1993). The proportion of sediment \( T_{COX} \) to mangrove net primary production decreased with increasing forest age. This is primarily a reflection of the increased burial rates with increasing forest age and concomitantly greater rates of primary production with stand age.

The measurements of nitrogen metabolism suggest that ammonification and root-associated nitrogen fixation, or a combination of both processes, must supply most of the nitrogen required for tree production as nearly all other directly measured N inputs were much slower than estimated N demand of the trees (Tables 8 and 9). When measurable, rates of nitrogen fixation were rapid compared to other studies (Zuberer and Silver, 1978) but were very variable between sampling intervals. Atmospheric supply of nitrogen was small as was supply of dissolved nitrogen from overlying tidal water (Table 4). These results are very similar to those measured in Thai (Kristensen et al., 2000; Alongi et al., 2002) mangrove forests. In mangrove forests, it appears that nitrogen is very rapidly mineralized and assimilated by bacteria and the trees; our data suggest mineralization efficiencies of 67–81% with comparatively low efficiencies of nitrogen burial (Table 9). Turnover of the small dissolved N pools (Table 9) in the Matang sediments is on the order of hours to a few days. In Rhizophora forests in Jamaica, Nedwell et al. (1994) calculated similar turnover times and measured ammonification rates within the same order of magnitude as our estimated rates of mangrove nitrogen demand (Table 8).

We did not measure ammonification directly, but our assumption that nitrogen demand for the trees is derived from ammonification and/or root-associated \( N_2 \) fixation is tenable given the small inputs of the other N pathways. Translocation of nitrogen within the trees was not measured but is likely to be within the range of 5–15% of total tree N flux based on differences in N content between green and senescent leaves, and litterfall measured in other forests (Li et al., 1999). Mass balances of nitrogen in other mangroves have pointed to the importance of ammonium uptake in tree nutrition (Kristensen et al., 1995; Alongi et al., 2002). As there was little, if any, significant algal flora observed on the trees or on the forest floor, mangroves must meet their N demands via \( N_2 \) fixation within roots and rhizomes, or there must be significant \( NH_4^+ \) and \( NO_3^- \) production in deeper sediment layers. \( N_2 \) fixation in deep roots in mangrove sediments has been detected (Zuberer and Silver, 1978; Holguin et al., 1992). Our measurements of \( N_2 \) fixation were in shallow cores with little or no live root material, so it is likely that our rates are underestimates.

Our measured rates of denitrification were highly variable among replicate chambers, but were rapid when measurable, greater than rates measured in most other mangrove forests (Rivera-Monroy and Twilley, 1996). In fact, our direct gas flux measurements indicate that denitrification equates to 71%, 39% and 93% of total N input to Stns. MVR, M18 and M5, respectively, suggesting that these rates are overestimates or that there are other sources of nitrogen.

The ratio of \( T_{COX} \) to total N flux (a rough estimate of C/N mineralization) varied from 3.5 to 7.3 to 14.8 at Stns. MVR, M18 and M5. These ratios are much less than the solid-phase C/N ratios in the sediments; neither do the mineralization rates of C and N correlate with the abundance of sediment carbon and nitrogen. This lack of agreement suggests that sediment carbon and nitrogen reflect what remains as residual material rather than their molar ratio being an indicator of organic matter quality. In fact, most of the carbon and nitrogen in these sediments likely reflects root material; the C/N ratio of mangrove roots is often within the range of 75:1 to 250:1 (Robertson et al., 1992). In Thai mangroves, 50–70% of total sediment carbon and nitrogen is derived from roots and rhizomes (Alongi et al., 2001). Such may be the case in the Matang sediments.

The low sediment mineralization ratios better reflect the stoichiometry of water-column organic mat-

</page>

<page number="15">

ter. The molar C/N ratio of pelagic material in the Matang waterways averaged 6.8 ± 1.9 (Alongi et al., 2003) which indicates that this material is rapidly mineralized when deposited to the sediments. The high quality of this water-column material has been attributed to aquaculture effluent, sewage from local villages, and other industries within the catchment (Alongi et al., 2003). The low mineralization ratios may be supported by low stoichiometric ratios of dissolved material from root exudates or from groundwater, although no such data is available.

4.2. Land–ocean–atmosphere exchange: a preliminary carbon mass balance model

Using our data in conjunction with previously published information (see Table 12 footnotes for references), we constructed a first-order mass balance of carbon flow in the Matang Mangrove Forest Reserve (Table 12). We used a simple mass balance equation (see Berner, 1980) assuming steady-state conditions, where the annual flux of carbon equals zero if the sum of inputs (gross autotrophic production, river and anthropogenic inputs) equals losses (respiration, harvesting, export, burial). If the inputs are greater than losses, the ecosystem is presumably net autotrophic, gaining more carbon than it loses. The opposite result would imply that the ecosystem is net heterotrophic, consuming more carbon than it gains. Carbonate carbon was not included as concentrations of carbonate carbon are negligible in these sediments (Alongi et al., 1998b). Our model does not account for possible carbon flow via groundwater or other sources; sedimentation to subtidal sediments is considered negligible as most of the waterway seabed is scoured (Sasekumar, unpublished observation). Nevertheless, the mass balance (Table 12) indicates that mangrove production and respiration dominates carbon flow within the ecosystem. Mangrove photosynthetic production accounts for 95% of total carbon inputs; estimated river inputs, phytoplankton production and inputs of trash fish to fish cage aquaculture are comparatively minor carbon sources. Our estimate of river inputs (see footnote b in Table 12) is based on the assumption that total carbon inputs to the sediments (minus litter and slash inputs likely accounted for in the MAR rates) represent the bulk of import from rivers. Most of the input of carbon is probably from land considering the high soil erosion rates and suspended sediment loads in rivers in peninsular Malaysia (Sasekumar et al., 1994; Sani, 1998; Chua et al., 2000). Recent evidence from estuarine and inshore muds in southeast Asia identify land-based sources for much of the organic fraction in these deposits (Kamp-Nielsen et al., 2002), and stable isotope studies (Newell et al., 1995; Chong et al., 2001) identify mangrove detritus as the main food for juvenile prawns and a limited trophic link between mangrove waterways and adjacent waters within a few km of the coast. This explanation may be at variance with the radiochemical analyses suggesting that there may be a marine source for the sediment, but as noted earlier, the low \(^{137}\)Cs inventory may be accounted for by erosion of adjacent mangrove banks as well as some import from the Straits of Malacca.

Tree respiration accounts for \( \approx 79\% \) of total ecosystem losses, and all respiration losses account for nearly 85% of total carbon output (Table 12). Harvesting of timber and poles from thinning stages constitute relatively small annual losses (\(< 1\%\) of total output), as are harvesting of natural and cultured finfish and shellfish within the reserve (3% of total output). Export of mangrove carbon to adjacent coastal waters appears to be a small loss compared with tree respiration, equating to only about 7% of total carbon inputs and 25% of mangrove net primary production. Similarly, only 2% of TOC input is buried in sediments.

Despite some uncertainty, it is reasonably apparent that the Matang Mangrove Forest Reserve is net autotrophic, currently producing more carbon than it is losing. The ecosystem \(P/R\) ratio averages 1.4, which compares favorably with the \(P/R\) ratio of other mangrove ecosystems (Gattuso et al., 1998; Twilley, 1988; Twilley et al., 1992; Alongi et al., 1998a, 2000). What is the fate of this excess organic carbon? It is reasonable to assume that most of this carbon is being stored in new forest growth on accreting mudbanks, considering that most of the forests are \(< 30\) years old and highly productive. Based on extensive surveys, Gan (1995) estimates that since its inception early last century (Watson, 1928), the reserve has gained \( \approx 1500 \) ha of new forest through accretion, of which 228 ha was gained in the last decade. This would only account for 5% of the excess carbon, but carbon may be retained in biomass below ground and on the forest floor. In Matang, Ong et al. (1984) and Ong (1993) estimated rates of carbon accumulation above ground to be 2–6 tons C ha\(^{-1}\) year\(^{-1}\) in 5–25-year-old *R. apiculata* stands. Recent evidence indicates that natural and some managed tropical forests have a century-scale capacity to store carbon in wood and roots (Chambers et al., 2001a,b). Mangrove forests may have a similar capacity for carbon storage.

Excess carbon may also be tied up in fish and invertebrate biomass. Although harvesting of natural and cultured fish and shellfish has been considered, not all are actually accounted for and these (uncaught) migrate offshore as adults. Another possible loss is carbon consumed by migratory birds, as the Kuala Gula Bird sanctuary is known to be a feeding ground for thousands of migratory birds (Gan, 1995). In the Pearl River estuary in China, Li and Lee (1998) found that birds consume over half of the estimated carbon fixed by marsh grasses and mangroves. However, such losses are difficult to quantify given the lack of data on invertebrate and fish consumption rates by coastal birds.

Our carbon budget supports data from other mangrove ecosystems that they are able to conserve and retain carbon and nitrogen. Nitrogen retention has been suggested for other ecosystems (Nedwell et al., 1994; Rivera-Monroy and Twilley, 1996; Alongi et al., 2002), and numerous processes have been offered to explain this phenomenon, including rapid deposition of particulate nitrogen, storage of humic nitrogen,

</page>

<page number="17">

leaf resorption and translocation, inhibition of nitrogen loss by anoxia, dissimilatory nitrate reduction, and microbial exudation of proteinaceous compounds and/or accumulation by microbes colonizing mangrove organic matter. Like other forests, a large fraction of the total detrital pool in mangrove forests is stored in the form of wood that decays slowly, acting as a long-term reservoir of nutrients. An analysis by Cebrian (2002) suggests that mangroves are accumulators of detrital carbon. Mangroves appear to be more functionally similar to other forests than to their estuarine wetland counterparts, with most carbon exchange being with the atmosphere rather than with adjacent coastal waters.

5. Conclusions

Our data suggest that the Matang mangrove ecosystem is currently accumulating sediment and organic carbon, the latter mostly in forest biomass. Carbon input to the ecosystem was estimated at \( 143 \times 10^9 \) mol C year\(^{-1}\) and total losses at \( 122 \times 10^9 \) mol C year\(^{-1}\) for a net ecosystem production of \( \approx 21 \times 10^9 \) mol C year\(^{-1}\) and an ecosystem \( P/R = 1.4 \).

There were a few age-related patterns in rates of net primary production and nutrient cycling among the forests, but sediment organic matter was rapidly and efficiently decomposed in all forests with carbon burial rates ranging from 16% to 27% of total C input to the sediments. Despite rapid sediment accumulation (range: 2.2–11.4 kg m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\)), carbon burial equated to only 2% of total carbon inputs to the entire ecosystem. Sulfate reduction appeared to be the major decomposition pathway, ranging from 19 to 53 mmol S m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) to a sediment depth of 1 m. The ratio of total sediment carbon oxidation to net mangrove primary production decreased with increasing forest age, from 28% in a 5-year-old stand to only 7% in an 85-year-old forest.

Nitrogen cycling was dominated by high requirements by the trees, with uptake of N on the order of 8–22 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). Sediment nitrogen was efficiently mineralized (67–81%) with moderate efficiency of burial (10–29%). Sediment–water exchange of nitrogen was minor. Denitrification was very rapid, ranging from 0.4–11.0 mmol N\(_2\) m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\), but highly variable.

Our results suggest that this managed mangrove ecosystem is currently net autotrophic. Unlike other marine ecosystems, but like other forests, most carbon exchange occurs between the trees and atmosphere during carbon assimilation and respiration.

Sediment accumulation and organic material flux in a managed mangrove ecosystem: estimates of land–ocean–atmosphere exchange in peninsular Malaysia

D.M. Alongi a,*, A. Sasekumar b, V.C. Chong b, J. Pfitzner a, L.A. Trott a, F. Tirendi a, P. Dixon a, G.J. Brunskill a

a Australian Institute of Marine Science, PMB No. 3, Townsville M.C., Qld. 4810, Australia
b Institute of Biological Sciences, University of Malaya, Kuala Lumpur 50603, Malaysia

Received 13 May 2002; accepted 14 April 2004

Abstract

Rates of sediment accumulation and organic matter decomposition in mangrove forests of different age were examined at the Matang Mangrove Forest Reserve in peninsular Malaysia. These data were used with previous findings to construct a first-order mass balance of carbon to determine whether the ecosystem is net heterotrophic or autotrophic, and to estimate land–ocean–atmosphere exchange. Measurements of various carbon and nitrogen processes in sediments suggest that organic matter is rapidly and efficiently mineralized to a depth of 1 m. Rates of total carbon oxidation in sediments (\( T_{COX} \)) ranged from 77 to 118 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) with no significant differences with forest age. Sulfate reduction (range: 19–53 mmol S m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) appeared to be the dominant decomposition pathway, accounting for an average of 51–75% of sediment \( T_{COX} \). Aerobic respiration (range: 5–20 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) accounted for \( \approx 5–20\% \) of mean \( T_{COX} \). Methanogenesis was not measurable. Denitrification (range: 0.4–11.0 mmol N\(_2\) m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) was rapid but very variable, and may have accounted for \( \approx 25\% \) of \( T_{COX} \) at the old-growth forest. Rates of sediment mass accumulation (range: 2.2–11.4 kg m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\)) were rapid compared with previous measurements in mangroves. Efficiency of carbon burial (range: 23–29 mmol C m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)) in sediments increased from 16% to 27% from the youngest to the oldest forest. The ratio of sediment \( T_{COX} \) to mangrove net primary production decreased from 28% to 7% with increasing forest age. The efficiency of N mineralization (range: 67–81%) and burial (range: 10–29%) in sediments showed the opposite pattern. Tree N demand required from 8 to 22 mmol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). Surface N\(_2\) fixation was measurable only in two of six trials, but was rapid (range: 2.3–3.0 mmol N\(_2\) m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\)). A mass balance of carbon for the entire reserve suggests that the ecosystem is currently net autotrophic, with a net ecosystem production of \( \approx 21 \times 10^9 \) mol C year\(^{-1}\) and an ecosystem \( P/R \) of 1.4. Despite considerable uncertainty, forest production and respiration clearly dominates carbon flow, accounting for \( \approx 95\% \) of total inputs and \( \approx 79\% \) of total outputs, respectively. River inputs, phytoplankton primary production and trash fish inputs to fish cage aquaculture in the waterways were comparatively minor. Export of mangrove detritus equated to 25% of net canopy production; only 2% of total carbon input to the ecosystem was buried in mangrove sediments. Clear felling and thinning of forests accounted for \( <1\% \) of total outputs; 73% of total carbon

</page>

<page number="1">

inputs to the ecosystem were respired. Our budget indicates that the major exchange of carbon in this managed ecosystem is between forest and atmosphere.
